While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning by leveraging permutations of factorization order and, due to its autoregressive formulation, rectifies the limitations seen in BERT. Moreover, XLNet incorporates key aspects from the advanced autoregressive model, Transformer-XL, thereby achieving notable advancements. According to comprehensive evaluations on multiple benchmarks, XLNet consistently outperforms BERT across eleven tasks, including long-range dependencies, and notably improves the state-of-the-art results for question answering and hypernym discovery. Furthermore, XLNet outperforms Transformer-XL when trained on large language models, while its performance gains on the SQuAD1.1 benchmark surpass BERT by 1.0 and Transformer-XL by 0.4. When applied to the SQuAD2.0 benchmark, XLNet surpasses the current best model by 3.2. These advances significantly reduce the required training time for a large language understanding model. By cross-validating the pretraining data with samples of varying factorization orders, XLNet dynamically adapts to the properties of each dataset, thereby enhancing its robustness and consistency of pretraining-finetune performance. This research introduces a new method for natural language pretraining based on autoregressive language modeling and establishes comprehensive evaluations to compare XLNet with prior approaches. The source code for this method will be made accessible via https://github.com/zoering/xlnet. Currently, research focuses on developing advanced computational models that can effectively capture the intricate processes involved in tsunami behavior. A discontinuous Galerkin solution with a spatial resolution of 100 meters in the ocean and 10 kilometers on land is employed, accompanied by a high-resolution wind field with a 1 kilometer grid. Furthermore, the study incorporates a novel wind model that utilizes an optimal control theory and linearized optimization to drive the simulation. Through a series of calculations, the research demonstrates the significance of incorporating various factors, including ocean depth, friction, atmospheric conditions such as wind, pressure, and temperature, as well as the critical role of time-dependent wind simulations in accurately representing tsunami propagation. Additionally, the study assesses and promotes the application of advanced processing techniques for optimizing and accelerating these complex simulations. As an example of the methodology's potential, the research recreates and showcases a high-resolution simulation of the massive Chicxulub asteroid impact's impact on Martian rivers, first simulated in 2019. Nevertheless, the ultimate aim of this work is to utilize this methodology to reenact one of the most catastrophic events in asteroid collisions, specifically the massive Chicxulub asteroid impact that led to the extinction of dinosaurs on Earth. An effort is made to contrast the results with a recent and similar simulation of a tsunami from a asteroid impact on Mars, in a parallel context.

Recent observations of deeply embedded star-forming galaxies have uncovered a novel phenomenon, where massive galaxies remain obscured from our view by dense dust and gas. Data collected by the JWST has provided new insights into these buried galaxies, showing that they are highly luminous in the infrared, but impossible to detect in visible light. As a result, a significant number of these hidden galaxies are likely to be missed by current observational studies, affecting our understanding of their overall density among these heavily obscured populations. Lately, representation learning in taxonomies has received considerable attention, 
but most existing studies assume a fixed structure for the taxonomy and focus 
on addressing its distortions using Euclidean geometry. In contrast, this study 
explores using hyperbolic geometry to improve taxonomy representation and growth. 
We introduce HyperExpan, a novel approach for expanding a taxonomy represented in
hyperbolic space. Based on a minimal graph representation of the taxonomy, we use
graph embedding models to calculate node positions and determine new concept 
locations. We then apply a bilevel optimization process within a hyperbolic 
framework to identify suitable child concepts in the expanded taxonomy. 
Computational assessments demonstrate that HyperExpan outperforms existing 
methods in terms of structural accuracy and scalability for hyperbolic 
taxonomy representation, also showing significant improvements in concept 
similarity comparisons over traditional Euclidean-based taxonomies. We also 
showcase HyperExpan's potential in supporting human-centered knowledge management 
for taxonomy structure and growth. The proposed method's source code is 
available for research purposes at https://github.com/atl-ncar/HyperExpan. Our 
experiments have been conducted using a Google Cloud-based environment with 
approximately 25 GPUs. Due to the innovative nature of HyperExpan, we have 
submitted it to the Emerging Trends track at ACM 2022. We acknowledge the 
research support provided by NSF Award SAPPHIRE and DOE Award FASTNET.  Our 
data and other related resources can be accessed at https://atl-ncar.github.io/

We explore various forms of roughness in a diffusion equation on a complete manifold. By establishing certain conditions on the diffusion coefficient and the manifold's geometry, we prove that the equation's gradient can be approximated locally. This approximation depends on the metric, the diffusion coefficient, and the manifold's curvature. It's notable that our results are largely impartial and applicable to different types of diffusion coefficients and manifolds. Additionally, we show that our method is practical by implementing it to derive explicit gradient estimates for a specific diffusion equation on smooth domains in Euclidean space, illustrating the connection between the manifold's geometry and the potential and diffusion semigroups' properties. Furthermore, our investigation also covers convergence issues and provides an alternative approach to existing results, such as those by Kiuhler and Sturm, using our method to derive the potential operator's explicit expression. Finally, we use the established approximation to establish the well-posedness of a nonlinear diffusion equation with a roughness of $\alpha=\frac{1}{2}$ and a non-Lipschitz diffusion coefficient in Euclidean space. The diffusion equation now solves for a more extensive class of initial conditions than before. We introduce a generalized version, which can automatically encapsulate any monoid within the transition function. This leads to a higher-level description of hidden phenomena using categories of monoids. By considering two specific categories - abelian groups and monoids with invertible elements - we derive corresponding HMMs that can measure data flow both quantitatively and qualitatively. An explicit definition is provided for the former, which models the preservation of data equivalency under the data transition process, and for the latter, which models the data transition process itself. Furthermore, we offer a theoretical explanation for the difficulty of implementing an HMM description of non-commutative groups and outline the necessary modification to achieve this for any abelian group. The discussion will primarily focus on the HMM formulation, but similar concepts apply to the more general Markov models. The decision to utilize groups instead of general monoids allows for the implementation of probabilistic backwards induction, which facilitates the reconstruction of data transition probabilities. As a result, our description deviates from the standard probabilistic HMM approach. The HMM formulation provides a concise definition of data preservation under the data transition process for the quantitative flow model, which we will outline next. The discussion will focus on the properties of data preservation in the objective formula of the general model, which leads to a concise definition of data preservation for the quantitative flow model: the set of all initial states that lead to a preservation state with positive measure. The transition process itself is defined as a left action of the corresponding monoid, which corresponds to the standard definition of the transition function in HMMs. The fundamental difference between the two models lies in the direction of the data transition process; in HMMs, the state transition is forward, whereas in our general model, the data transition is backwards. We investigate the potential consistency of a physically-based model for nonlocal elasticity and develop a statistical representation of nonlocality, incorporating both point-wise variability of material properties and the influence of distant nonlinear interactions. Focusing on nonlocal fracture mechanics, we derive the nonlocal stress intensity factors and examine their independence using principles from the Kolmogorov-Fernihew theorem, aiming to establish a fundamental measure of nonlocality in fracture mechanics. Building on this statistical representation, we develop an approach to determine the probability of nonlocal uniqueness of stress intensity factors under certain conditions and for specific fracture geometries, such as those in central and notched configurations. Furthermore, we establish a connection between our proposed method and the concept of ultracavity in nonlocal fracture mechanics, discussing its scalability with respect to the nonlocality parameter and modeling accuracy, along with numerical examples to demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. Validation through numerical simulations, conducted using a nonlocal finite-element model, confirms that the method can effectively capture nonlocal behavior in fracture mechanics. To better understand this issue, we developed a mathematical framework that enables efficient analysis of privacy risks in scenarios where the arrival times of a location visitor follow an Poisson process and the visitor's prior location history is uncertain and follows a Gaussian distribution. Our framework leverages properties of conditional priors and spectral theory, allowing us to derive a concise metric that quantifies the maximum possible information that can be inferred about an individual's location history, known as the susceptibility. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we applied it to the analysis of ocean currents affecting seagulls and the impact of bike-sharing on the privacy of its users. Our results show that the susceptibility can be used to identify key factors affecting an individual's privacy and to calculate the minimum amount of location history transparency needed to ensure their privacy. Furthermore, we found that the susceptibility is influenced by the individual's location history duration, their kinematic preference, and the stochastic process generating their location history, and that incorporating dynamic priors into the analysis generally reduces the maximum inferred information unless the kinematic preference or duration-specific features are significant. A novel localization method, specifically designed for large-scale 3D point clouds, has been developed, utilizing the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation. This approach employs a Transformer-based point cloud localization network that utilizes 3D point clouds and normal map images to generate a probability distribution function (PDF) and mean vector of estimated pose. The multifacibility of the Transformer architecture and the utilization of the NDT representation enable robust recovery of partial point cloud pose. In addition, a novel method for generating noise-free NDT representations via voxel clustering is introduced, enabling utilization of 3D point clouds collected from real-world scenarios. Extensive experiments validated the proposed method, demonstrating its superiority by achieving an average localization accuracy of 5.48 cm on the KITTI challenge with a processing speed of 16.7 frames per second on the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPU. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrated superior adaptability and 3D robustness on the SUNARM benchmark and SDKE lyft datasets. Furthermore, 3D point cloud-based lyft-localization benchmark was successfully solved by employing the proposed method, yielding a record-breaking accuracy of 60 cm. The proposed method has been successfully employed and demonstrated on various cloud-based platforms such as Uber Technologies self-driving sensor platforms and cloud-based platforms like Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud Platform. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have been met with growing interest from researchers and practitioners, leveraging word-level alignment to overcome language proficiency disparities. Although WordPiece-based models have achieved success, they suffer from inefficiency in capturing contextual variations and neglecting sequential connections, which are crucial for code-mixed texts. Furthermore, existing positional encoding methods rely on either fixed or training-set learned approaches that fail to adapt to the nuances of cross-lingual datasets at word or sentence levels. To address these shortcomings, this paper introduces positional encoding that adapts to switching points in sentences, effectively modeling contextual associations and sequential connections in code-mixed texts. The proposed method demonstrates a 2.02% improvement in accuracy on the CMNLP 2017 indotubid dataset and 1.31% improvement in F1-score on the WMT 2020 COVID19 shared task dataset. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/kelvinxv/PESTO. An extended version of this research is available at https://arxiv.org/submit/pdf/2105_00954.

This paper introduces a novel motion planning approach grounded in discontinuous spaces, which is particularly suited for handling dynamic obstacles in real-world applications. Building upon spatial segmentation, our proposed method aggregates areas with similar obstacle trajectories into composite regions, enabling us to treat them as static environments and efficiently plan collision-free paths. To adapt to changing obstacles, we propose updating the obstacle model by adjusting the boundaries of these regions, rather than re-planning entire paths. This leads to significantly improved execution speeds and enhanced safety features, as demonstrated through theoretical efficiency analysis and experimental evaluation. Our results show that this strategy can produce optimal solutions while reducing the overall computational complexity. A comparative assessment with existing state-of-the-art techniques confirms our method's superior performance in both efficiency and safety. Moreover, our method exhibits excellent practical performance in complex applications such as autonomous driving and racing games. Last but not least, we showcase the potential of this approach to tackle challenging environmental and planning issues through theoretical analysis of its effects on continuous and differentiable motion spaces. This adds valuable theoretical grounds to the established algorithmic results presented in this work. The implementation of the method, as well as the associated experiments and evaluations, is made publicly available through the GitHub repository https://github.com/ParisaRamezani/Spatial-Restriction-Generation, which is also the location for the supplementary material. The associated code is fully self-contained and can be directly executed by other researchers, allowing for easy replication and verification of the presented findings. Following the recommended guidelines, our contribution is structured into introduction, related work, method description, efficiency analysis, experimental evaluation and conclusions. Initially, we establish that a technique employing Stochastic Variations of a Constant, originally discovered by Dupuis and Strugowski, results in the convergence of certain expressions containing Q(x) and their derivatives. This research examines a specific type of two Higgs doublet model, known as 2HDM, after a global analysis of its theoretical and experimental predictions has been made. Considering the constraints from the alignment of electroweak parameters and the measurement of the W boson mass, a likelihood function of the 2HDM is constructed. From an analysis of nearly 15,000 simulated points, a posterior probability distribution of the 2HDM's parameters, $m_{H_1}$, $m_{H_2}$, $\sin^2\theta_w$, and $\sin^2(\beta-\theta)$, is obtained. Furthermore, the research determines the alignment of the 2HDM's properties with four forthcoming collider results: the values of $\sin^2\theta_w$ from the HL-LHC, the International Linear Collider (ILC), the Circular Electron Positron Collider (CEPC), and the Future Circular hadron Collider (FHCC); the mass of the Higgs-like boson from ILC and CEPC; and the mass of the extra Higgs bosons from HL-LHC, ILC, and CEPC. From the alignment of the 2HDM's properties with these collider results, the research obtains the allowable ranges of the 2HDM's parameters. Additionally, the research determines the alignment of the 2HDM's properties with other physical quantities, such as the $\Z'$ mass in left-right models and the electric dipole moments (EDMs) of the electron, neutron, and di-neutron. From the alignment of the 2HDM properties with these quantities, the research obtains the allowable ranges of the 2HDM parameters. Finally, the research discusses the potential consequences of future collider results on the 2HDM's properties and the predictiveness of its alignment, in particular its potential to determine its parameters completely. We demonstrate through simulated experiments that neuroevolutionary learning can be employed to develop agents capable of autonomous self-assemblage, which achieves complex functionalities by means of simple local interactions, thereby simplifying the process of achieving desired behaviors. By evolving agents with the ability to produce and exchange information-generating particles called 'blueprints' during brief interactions, we find that populations of these agents eventually acquire a collective behavior that enables them to produce and dissever these blueprints in a coordinated and strategic manner. This collective behavior is achieved through the evolution of a shared understanding and predictive model of their peers, referred to as the 'pluralistic cognitive paradigm,' which allows all agents to uniformly anticipate one another's actions and possess similar expectations. This shared predictive mechanism manifests as a uniform and situation-dependent strategy that other agents have come to expect from their counterparts, thereby facilitating cooperative behavior. Our results show that this 'pluralistic cognitive paradigm' facilitates effective and predictable cooperation and strategic coordination, even among diverse groups, and that this predictive framework can emerge and address issues of trust and social concern through the transformation of individual and collective risk preferences. Additionally, we find that the 'pluralistic cognitive paradigm' is exceptionally resistant to manipulation by simplistic models of agency, and that robust and complex strategic interactions are required to generate this predictive mechanism, which has implications for the emergence of this shared thinking in human societies. Overall, our experiments illustrate the effectiveness of self-assemblage as a means of achieving complex cooperative behavior and the possibility of embedding nuanced cognitive and social structures through the use of such self-assemblage processes. Finally, we reflect on the potential applications of these findings and the interest of delving into the interaction between the 'pluralistic cognitive paradigm,' self-assemblage and multi-agent reflective learning. One of the key challenges is demonstrating that the 'pluralistic cognitive paradigm' can actually emerge in environments that are inherently competitive and the possibility of applying similar self-assemblage processes to such environments is explored. Moreover, we reflect on the interest of a new line of research that focuses en environments in which the characteristics of the 'pluralistic cognitive paradigm' can be set a priori as the desired behavior. In these environments, we can use evolutionary learning to directly generate the necessary CoCoStrategies, thereby simplifying the process of achieving such behaviors. This lines of research are proposed as potential areas for extension. A comprehensive execution of these ideas is proposed as future work. To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are used widely in many down-stream NLP tasks, a new method called Dict-BERT is introduced. This approach involves enhancing BERT's vocabulary with a thesaurus during pre-training. A new word embedding technique is proposed to fill in word substitutions from the thesaurus, and it is combined with BERT's original word embeddings through a linear combination. Additionally, PLMs can benefit from incorporating dictionary-related features such as word synsets and semantic vectors, which can be incorporated into the model as additional inputs. The Dict-BERT model is evaluated on several NLP tasks, including word sense disambiguation, paraphrasing and sentiment analysis, and it is compared with baseline models and thesaurus-enabled models that use word replacement, synonym insertion and other techniques. The results show that Dict-BERT outperforms the baseline models and many previous thesaurus-enabled models in these tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving NLP performance with a thesaurus. Furthermore, an ablation study is conducted to verify the contribution of each component in Dict-BERT. The study's outcomes reveal that the thesaurus-enhancement of BERT's vocabulary is the primary factor contributing to the model's success in these tasks. Finally, the study highlights potential strategies for choosing a thesaurus and word substitution for different NLP applications, providing valuable insights for practitioners. The Dict-BERT code and data are available on GitHub at https://github.com/dungminh184/Dict-BERT. The research findings are reported at the IJCA 2021, ICMR 2021 and NLPCK 2021 conferences. We investigate the minimal spanning acycles of random complexes generated from random geometric graphs in high-dimensional space under specific conditions. Our research reveals the relationship between the edge probability and the complexity size that maximizes the expected size of these minimal spanning acycles. Contrary to previous predictions, our study shows that this optimal point shifts as the dimension changes rather than remaining constant at a specific value. Additionally, we examine the minimum and near-minimum points for these optimal values and demonstrate similar behavior in minimal spanning trees. Furthermore, similar outcomes are derived for the extremal values of stability maps and homology norms in persistence diagrams, showing that they also change with the complexity dimension rather than remaining constant. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations in geometric spaces and simplicial complexes. Lastly, we discuss how these results have implications for the application of homological techniques to detect outliers in high-dimensional data sets, known as anomalies or extremes. The approach is particularly useful since it does not rely on any underlying model other than the structure induced by the data itself, referred to as a simplicial complex. The excellence of this technique is shown through its application in a real-world study involving the analysis of gene expression in breast cancer samples. A revised version of this article is included with additional figures and figures A1 to F, along with related supporting material collected on the GNU Savane repository. The corresponding R code and additional supporting data are also available on the repository. The related supporting material can be accessed through the link provided at the bottom of this document, specifically at the repository mentioned above. The approach proposed in this study leverages the use of algorithms such as hit-and-run, block importance sampling, and the walk algorithm developed by Edelsbrunner and Harer to efficiently compute the persistence diagrams and their associated elements, enabling computations that would otherwise take months to complete without these optimizations. The code and data for the study are publicly accessible. The study reveals that after optimizing parameters through numerical simulations in high-dimensional space, the near-minimum point for the homology norms shifts towards higher values than expected, contrary to previous predictions made by the CoCoPolis tool. A similar pattern is observed in minimal spanning trees. The technique does not rely on the assumption of a pre-defined shape or distribution other than the structure induced by the data itself, making it suitable for analysis. Researchers propose Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) to address privacy concerns in machine learning, specifically by consolidating training data from interconnected parties, enabling the creation of a comprehensive training dataset without the need for data exchange. Our study focuses on the implications of this framework by identifying potential exploitation of parties during VFL and developing two feasible attacks: a training-based attack discrediting a model's privacy, and an adversarial attack capable of evading privacy safeguards, both of which can be executed locally by the adversary with minimal computational requirements. Our analysis on the current implementation of Google's Federated Learning library demonstrates the effectiveness of these attacks in extracting sensitive information and compromising model accuracy. Our research aims to raise awareness about VFL's vulnerabilities and prompt the development of robust safeguard measures. The associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/steeltist/vfl-attack. A demonstration of the attack is available at https://steeltist.github.io/vfl-attack/privacy-assault. Furthermore, a privacy-assuring module developed in response to this study can be accessed at https://github.com/steeltist/vfl-module. The module's demo is available at https://steeltist.github.io/vfl-module/secure-inference. Our research finds that through enhanced module utilization, VFL can deliver comparable performance to local training, while preserving data privacy. In light of these findings, we encourage researchers to address and devise solutions to privatize deep learning models. A comprehensive theory of baryon decays to first-order in the fine structure constant has been developed, bringing together light-cone sum rules and perturbative QCD to predict key parameters for rare B-meson decays that produce proton showers and dark antibaryons. The analysis was based on four independent sum rules that allow for the determination of form factors, form factors' moments, and quark mixing amplitudes. The results show the dominance of perturbative QCD in these sum rules and confirm the significant role of final-state interactions in guiding baryon decay. The analysis used the previously established QCD-based rules for parton distributions to predict important properties for exclusive and rare processes, including baryon decays, heavy-to-light transitions, and Compton scattering. The results include predicted branching ratios for rare B-meson decays to proton showers and dark antibaryons at the Belle II energy range, informing experimental searches. The accompanying software uses the standard TCRC formula and standard CVGK analysis with the \textsc{LCSR-PC} library, simplifying the complex analysis required for these decays and opening a new path for determining the NGB mediation mechanism of dark matter. The analysis also offers a starting point for the analysis of similar rare B-meson decays at upcoming experiments. The resulting knowledge expands our understanding of baryon transition form factors, enabling new connections to hadronic physics and lattice QCD. The resulting general structures for these form factors (with some examples provided) will be widely applicable to various types of baryon decays, including those involving dark matter and proton showers. The resulting knowledge extends the range of baryon transition form factors from lattice QCD to multi-mesonic decays with proton showers and dark antibaryons. The resulting knowledge extends the range of baryon transition form factors from perturbative QCD to deep-inelastic scattering, parton distributions, and parton fragmentation. The resulting knowledge enables new insights and calculations for various physical processes, including matrix elements of parton distributions, kernels of parton distributions, jet production, wide-invariant-mass decays, scattering, decay, fusion, production, absorption, annihilation, fragmentation, and other important one-loop and tree-level processes. This research introduces the Intelligent City Defense Game (ICDG), a 2-player, 2-action game that simulates urban management and defense decision-making in the face of socio-cyber-physical attacks. In this game, the attacker's objective is to inflict maximal damage on physical infrastructure, while the defender aims to minimize both economic loss and disruption of social services. Each player's payoff depends on their respective strategy choices and two key factors: the fraction of affected and defended infrastructure. Notably, some of the physical infrastructure can be essential for carrying out socio and cyber operations within the city limits. Our analysis explores the game's equilibrium outcomes, presents two potential applications including binary search and fair resource allocation, and finds that in nearly 26.5% of scenarios the optimal attack results in the disruption of socio services despite the economic loss being preventable. Additionally, we observe that in approximately 7% of cases, the optimal defense strategy involves the physical defeat of the attacker. Our model also takes into account the economic variable influence on the optimal strategy choices. Furthermore, we present a binary search algorithm to determine which layer of the socio-cyber-physical target to attack that maximizes the optimal damage. Our paper also presents a fair resource allocation algorithm that minimizes the maximal loss and ensures the minimalization of socio service disruption. Notably, all of our models are solved exactly in polynomial time, presenting a significant difference in the paradigm of game theoretical modeling. Long documents serving as the foundational elements of search engine indexing necessitate efficient retrieval, which is typically achieved through a bag-based model adopting a ranking loss. Nonetheless, documents are often tainted by errors in labeling, leading to inconsistent word-to-label mappings and elevated word embedding dispersion. By choosing a bag sampling method, we separate the indexing and retrieval processes. Our proposed group-level loss function not only diminishes the impact of label noise but also learns to predict document levels of quality. Through theoretical analysis, we establish that the loss function is robust to label noise of arbitrary type and demonstrate the superiority of our bag sampling and group-level loss approach in handling label noise, as evidenced by its significantly greater accuracy and retrieval performance in noisy settings. Experimental results on diverse datasets further validate the effectiveness of our method. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/sustcsj/Bag-GNML. labelnoise
An extended version of this paper is published at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08462.

In applications of unsupervised graph learning, conventional methods train and validate models on labeled datasets, but several tasks, such as link prediction and node classification, often struggle due to a shortage of labeled samples. This challenge is exacerbated by the fact that partial labels can sometimes misguide the model's learning process, causing it to overfit early in training. To address this issue, we propose a method called informative pseudo-tagging (IPT), in which partial node labels are converted into comprehensive pseudo-node labels. This process integrates topological information and utilizes specialized neural networks to produce accurate pseudo-labels, leveraging both local structure and global constraint information. Additionally, IPT has a noise-tolerant mechanism that allows the model to withstand noisy pseudo-labels. Experimental results on diverse networks like Wikipedia and the North Western university dataset showcase IPT's superior performance in classification and link prediction tasks under different sceneries and noise levels. Analytical validation confirms that IPT's pseudo-labels are more informative than traditional methods. Furthermore, IPT's source code is made available to the research community. Overall, IPT facilitates effective learning on complex graphs with limited labeled data, and its noise-tolerant capabilities make it a reliable solution in real-world graph applications. IPT has outperformed state-of-the-art methods by a considerable margin, demonstrating strong generalizability in link prediction tasks. Ultimately, IPT's comprehensive pseudo-labels provide profound insights into node behavior in graph-structured data. The research codes for this study have been released on GitHub's star183590 repository for the research community's benefit. This comprehensive pseudo-labeling approach offers practical implications in numerous machine learning applications. Its effectiveness in pseudo-label generation and model training can likely be extended to other learning tasks and domains. Moreover, the research sheds light on the theoretical properties of graph neural networks trained using partial labels and pseudo-labels, inspiring the exploration of innovative training methods and graph neural networks for supervised learning tasks. The analysis of learned model behaviors offers valuable insights into the design of efficient graph neural networks. Most notably, the research reveals that graph neural networks trained using partial labels exhibit overfitting, whereas those trained using comprehensive pseudo-labels demonstrate consistent performance across various network settings without the need for label augmentation. This conclusion holds promise for the development of more effective learning algorithms in machine learning and data science applications. Additionally, the research offers practical guidelines for choosing an appropriate partial label selection method. Specifically, the analysis contrasts the effects of idealized and realistic plasma profiles in AWAKE Run 2, with further applications extending to other facilities employing similar techniques. This discrepancy further highlights the value of employing realistic, multi-dimensional plasma profiles, especially in cases involving witness particle off-center trajectories. Moreover, the study's findings demonstrate the potential for utilizing betatron radiation spectroscopy to quantify the proton's phase space, with accurate calculations yielding proton energies of 2.5 MeV and corresponding phases of around 1.5 π, thereby offering a promising new method for probing this crucial parameter in future research. In the context of differential privacy, learning distributed decision trees poses significant challenges, particularly when dealing with datasets from multiple sources with varying data sizes. The existing approaches for private learning are largely inextricable and exhibit excessive computational complexity. To address this issue, we have developed a new framework for large-scale distributed decision tree learning, achieving high accuracy and robustness. Our method leverages the Laplace Transformation framework, providing a comprehensive mathematical proof of privacy and accuracy. Furthermore, we have introduced a novel mechanism for selecting split candidates, which effectively mitigates errors and enhances accuracy. Our experimental findings demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing private learning techniques in terms of model accuracy and computational efficiency. To validate the accuracy of this approach, we have conducted a thorough threshold-based error analysis, providing a mathematical guarantee of its validity. This study focuses on a specific type of interplay between geometrical frustration and spin-orbit coupling in systems with square-planar metal or transition-metal ions. This specific configuration is found in certain real materials, such as claudyite and scheelite families. Using a combination of theoretical methods, such as variational Monte Carlo calculations and a perturbative approach, this study investigates the characteristics of these systems as they undergo structural transformations. By simulating these systems in their amorphous and polycrystalline states, this research reveals that these structural changes can lead to the emergence of a chiral spin liquid phase, characterized by a specific order parameter, when certain conditions are met. This study finds that this specific order parameter can be significant in the amorphous state but much weaker in the polycrystalline state, indicating that longer-range correlations are reduced in the latter case. Notably, this study also identifies another phase known as the chiral antiferromagnet, exhibiting antiferromagnetic ordering with a specific spin configuration, which can be realized in the polycrystalline state under different conditions. Overall, this study suggests that equilibrium transformations within these geometrically frustrated materials can result in the formation of a non-equilibrium phase, such as the chiral spin liquid, when certain conditions are met. However, this behavior is found to be more pronounced in the amorphous state due to the absence of long-range order. Nonetheless, this study also reveals the potential for realizing the chiral antiferromagnetic phase in the polycrystalline state. Lastly, it is the outcome of these equilibrium and nonequilibrium pathways that gives rise to the observed complexity and variability in the reported material properties. Our research investigates how to measure investment portfolio distribution diversity.
Existing methods, including the Shannon and Renyi entropies, can't distinguish between two portfolios, no matter how varied, as long as they have identical statistical properties.
To overcome this limitation, we've developed a novel approach combining a variant of the Autoencoding Conditional Generative Adversarial Network with the Wasserstein distance, allowing us to evaluate the diversity of a portfolio by comparing its density function with that of a reference, calibrated, diversified portfolio.
Through theoretical analysis and computational simulations involving real market data, we've demonstrated the effectiveness of this measure in assessing portfolio diversity.
Additionally, we've identified properties of reference portfolios that can be considered ideal candidates for calibration.
Our findings also suggest that market portfolios tend to be less diverse than theoretically predicted by models such as the Random Matrix Model. 
At the same time, we've observed a number of market characteristics that may contribute to diversity, including negative correlations with stock returns and trading volumes. 
To validate these insights, we've conducted a comprehensive analysis involving various S&P 100 market datasets. 
Our research provides a practical solution for conditional generation and portfolio diversity assessment, offering effective insights for investors and financial managers to make informed investment decisions.  It combines generative adversarial networks, autoencoding, and the optimal transport theory to develop a new diversity metric based on the distance between a portfolio's density function and that of a reference, calibrated, diversified portfolio.  Specifically, we've applied the Wasserstein distance and the adversarial training process to the underlying sequences of quantiles to construct a conditional model that's both computationally efficient and recognizable.  To test the accuracy of our metric, we've evaluated its performance using real market data, namely daily time-series for the S&P 100 index over a 7-year period.  Our research presents a new method for conditional generation and portfolio diversity assessment.  It's known that generating conditional models from observed, real data can be challenging due to the inherent difficulties of modeling partially observable variables, even after utilizing techniques like data augmentation.  To overcome this limitation, we've applied the autoencoding approach, combining it with the adversarial training process, to develop a recognizable and computationally efficient conditional model that can be used for various tasks, such as portfolio diversity assessment. A precision object classification method using Bayesian neural networks (BAYESNETs) is presented as an alternative to traditional probability thresholding methods for binary classification tasks. BAYESNETs utilize Bayesian estimation to determine the confidence levels of a neural network, which enables the calculation of a reliable classification area under a Receiver Operating Characteristic curve. This approach is applied to the analysis of 10, 11, and 12 years' worth of data from the Fermi-LAT experiment for BL Lacertae objects and Flat-Spectrum Radio Quasars respectively, resulting in the categorization of 2, 231, and 622 sample objects in the "EXTBL Lac", "MBl Lac", and "FSRQ" classes. A comprehensive study of the classification models and their potential biases or data limitations is performed using methods such as calibration metrics and part-per-cent probability scaling to determine the optimal classification strategy. By employing BAYESNETs, a comprehensive snapshot of the gamma-ray sky is produced and the classification results are compared to traditional gamma-ray blazar classifications, which helps establish the hierarchy of blazar classes and their spectral relationships. Furthermore, a link to a publicly accessible web tool that allows users to dynamically adjust classification thresholds and observe their impact on the results is provided. Our research focuses on identifying obstacles and opportunities related to making social media content accessible, with a particular emphasis on the technical and human aspects of creating accessible content online. Through in-depth interviews with experts from the US and the UK, we gained insight into their perspectives on accessibility and discovered that although there is a growing awareness and interest in the topic, the predominant social media providers have not adequately addressed the issue. Our research outlines specific areas where improvement can be made and suggests potential solutions to create more inclusive social media content. Our aim is to contribute to the development of accessible communication online and stimulate further research in this important but underdeveloped field. The research was conducted with funding from the ESRC IAA initiative and received ethical approval from the University of Cambridge's Experimental Research Ethics Committee, with documents available online (eResearch_22-027). Notably, the study was conducted despite various accessibility obstacles.

 - The platforms' terms of service are ambiguous and lack clarity.
 - The accessibility needs of social media users are diverse and often overlooked.
 - There is a shortage of research and engagement from social media companies on accessible communication.
 - The accessibility community is dispersed and lacks influence.
 - Experts are undervalued and face significant obstacles in advocating for inclusive design.
 - Cultural and human factors play a significant role in the accessibility of social media content.
 - Emotional accessibility is a crucial aspect of inclusive design.
 - Novel applications of emotional intelligence in accessible design remain an underdeveloped field.
 - The interplay of emotional cues, user feelings, and personal relationships influences accessible content authoring.
 - The accessibility of social media content is a complex field influenced by personal, cultural, and human factors.
 - Existing research has significant limitations.

Several modeling techniques employed in atmospheric science fall short of meeting thermodynamic equilibrium requirements. The fundamental issue with each of these methods can be pinpointed, and it's argued that correcting them to satisfy the first and second laws of thermodynamics is not only feasible but also straightforward. In contrast, we refuse to engage in the notion that thermodynamic coherence can be achieved by incorporating arbitrary constants into standard approximation formulas. Rather, we encourage the use of alternative formulas that have been derived from a single, self-consistent thermodynamic framework. Three instances of thermodynamic coherence being improved in this paper concern 1) the computation of total potential energy in reference to saturation point, 2) the formulation of a relative humidity principle, and 3) the distribution of conservation of energy and entropy in cases of thermodynamic processes affecting a system comprising air and water vapor. The validity of our approach is supported by a theoretical analysis, and it's applied to both simplified and comprehensive models of atmospheric states with variable potential temperature. The integration of this improved framework into models of planetary climate systems is straightforward, and it's envisioned that incorporating these corrections will yield notable improvements in continuous prediction models for short and long-term periods. The theoretical foundation of this improved framework, in which thermodynamic properties are represented by sums of correlation-based regression elements along with physically-driven approximations, is also discussed in detail in an accompanying work. This idea is supported by a nontrivial external algebra associated with the family of geometric matroids, discovered through investigating the combinatorial characteristics of polytopes utilizing Minkowski matrix algebra. This finding demonstrates the utility of external algebras as a tool in matroid theory, allowing for novel direct approaches to mature geometric matroid theory, independent of linear representations. This work also establishes a connection to the recently developed field of flag matroids and showcases polynomial matroids as a special case of flag matroids. Additionally, we utilize the combinatorial properties of polytopes to develop a natural and external algebra-based interpretation of geometric matroids, independent of linear structures, similar to the one used for transversal subfamily problems in linear matroids, but in a more general setting. This approach can potentially lead to the solution of some open problems in the field, similar to how geometric matroids were used to solve the rational cone ratio problem. Furthermore, it addresses a generalization of this problem, asking for the simplest rational convex polytope that incorporates a given set of rational vectors as its subset, distinct from linear structures. Our work addresses the challenge of the asymptotic bias in dialogue state tracking by taking into account the ambiguities in the system output in speech recognition. We develop a framework to address this issue by first constructing a confusion network representing various possible interpretations of the system output. We derive a confidence score for the ambiguity-considering confusion network from the one without consideration, and the score can be calculated via forward-backward algorithm in O(n^2) time. We show the established score has a connection with the one without consideration, and it serves as an upper bound. We also propose an effective method to address the high computational cost by approximating the ambiguity-considering confidence score with the one of lower ambiguity levels. We conduct experiments on a speech dialogue set from Air Travel Booking and observe that the proposed scoring approach results in a 5.6% relative improvement on F1-score compared to the one without consideration. Additionally, the computational efficiency of our method is verified with only a 9% increase in computation time and a 10% increase in memory usage, which is within a tolerable range. The source code of our method and the corresponding data are available at https://github.com/ParryPathak/ASR-ambiguity-ds-monitoring. Our method demonstrates a substantial improvement in performance with limited additional processing requirements. Notably, the study is the first to address the asymptotic bias in dialogue state tracking. We contribute to the research by developing a modeling framework to capture speech recognition ambiguities as confusion networks and proposing efficient ways to calculate an ambiguity-considerable confidence score, which can be an upper limit for the actual score, although it remains unclear how to obtain the true score. Our method assumes the ambiguity-considerable confidence score to be a tight lower bound for the actual score. The study is also an advancement from the previous research on end-to-end dialogue state tracking by incorporating ASR ambiguity into the research, which can lead to better dialogue state tracking performance, but it remains unclear how the ambiguities affect the performance in general. As its key resource, we show that the entanglement of a two-qubit system can be fully assessed using only three optimal measurement settings, a significant reduction from the typically vast number of settings required. Researchers propose that the significant performance gap in Continual Learning (CL) can be attributed to the inherent abilities of pre-trained models (PTMs), which are often unaccounted for in benchmark assessments. They contend that these capabilities compromise the validity of CL benchmarks and make it difficult to determine the true effect of each method on the CL outcome. To address this issue, they developed a basic approach that relies solely on minimal hyperparameter tuning and avoids utilizing any PTMs. This simple benchmark serves as a control group to isolate the CL performance impact of PTMs. The study showcases the substantial improvement that incorporating PTMs can yield in CL when done thoughtfully. In contrast, incorporating PTMs into learning processes on image nets often hinders CL performance across various learning tasks. This research's primary objective is to stimulate discussion about the CL evaluation benchmarks and the underlying principles of PTMs. The study's code and models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Degenerate/No-PTMCL. Our study demonstrates that a well-established CL benchmark may be susceptible to biases introduced by the inherent strengths of PTMs. We suggest employing an alternative approach – a control group for CL evaluation – to help researchers ascertain the genuine effect of new techniques on CL performance. Furthermore, our study contributes new CL evaluation benchmarks that operate independently of PTMs, thereby allowing researchers to independently assess the impact of tasks, architectures, and learning strategies on CL performance. Lastly, our study highlights the need for caution in drawing conclusions from CL evaluation results incorporating PTMs, particularly when comparing outcomes across multiple tasks, which may complicate the interpretation of findings due to the incorporation of PTMs in training. While using PTMs in training may accelerate task resolution and enhance task compatibility, it may not fully alleviate the catastrophic interference characteristic of the CL setting. In some instances, our study suggests that utilizing PTMs may impair CL performance and make it difficult to draw reliable comparisons. We provide several potential explanations for this phenomenon, which may shed light on the challenges in CL. In contrast to prior studies, our research's control group allows researchers to isolate the true effect of tasks, architectures, and learning strategies on CL performance, thereby providing a more accurate evaluation of these factors. By establishing a more nuanced understanding of the roles of tasks, architectures, and learning strategies in CL, our study aims to promote dialogue on the CL evaluation benchmarks and the inherent strengths of PTMs. Moreover, our study offers a practical solution – the No-PTMCL baseline – to help researchers and engineers independently assess the CL evaluation of new techniques.

The input distribution of the GIFC channel can switch between two distributions, $P_{X|A|B}(x|a,b)$ and $P_{X|a',b'}(x|a',b')$, in response to auxiliary random variables $a$ and $a'$ that are themselves conditioned on the channel inputs $x$. The paper establishes an information spectrum lower bound on this channel capacity region and verifies that this bound remains tight for the specific scenario of a binary input binary output (BIBO) channel with random input equivalence. Furthermore, this bound is shown to be tight in the case of a binary input binary output (BIBO) channel without memory (BIBO) when the probabilities of input equivalence and the probabilities of auxiliary random variables $a$ and $a'$ are both equal to $\epsilon$. In the case of a binary input binary output (BIBO) channel without memory (BIBO) when the probabilities of input equivalence and the probabilities of auxiliary random variables $a$ and $a'$ are both equal to $\epsilon$, the lower bound is shown to converge to $\max  (1-\epsilon-\epsilon/2,\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon)$ as $\epsilon$ approaches 0. As special cases, the study's findings can be simplified to two significant channel capacity regions: the capacity region of a memoryless channel with random input equivalence (referred to as the SEFC channel capacity region) and the capacity region of a memoryless channel with fixed input equivalence (referred to as the MFC channel capacity region). The lower bound is shown to converge to $\frac{1-\epsilon}{2}$ as $\epsilon$ approaches 0 in the case of a memoryless channel with random input equivalence (referred to as the SEFC channel capacity region). Similarly, the lower bound is shown to converge to $\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon$ as $\epsilon$ approaches 0 in the case of a memoryless channel with fixed input equivalence (referred to as the MFC channel capacity region). Finally, this study illustrates an encoding strategy that achieves the lower bound on the GIFC channel capacity region in the case of a binary input binary output (BIBO) channel without memory (BIBO) when the probabilities of input equivalence and the probabilities of auxiliary random variables $a$ and $a'$ are both equal to $\epsilon

Using flow assessments, we identified distinct points where different equation-of-state models diverge and found that flow measurements are highly responsive to the critical points of the system, making them extremely effective in detecting the characteristics of various quantum phases, such as the critical slope and second sound velocity. The timely detection of COVID-19 through sensing wearables' data allows for the prevention of infection spread and protects users with sensitive data, whose detection risks exposure. To address this, we developed a method for detecting COVID-related conditions such as fever and fatigue, while safeguarding users' sensitive data. This method utilizes a machine learning model trained on perturbed data which mimics unknown unprocessed information. As a result, the model excels in detecting COVID-19 infections on real, unperturbed test data with high accuracy, outperforming a conventional Baseline model. This research demonstrates a robust solution for early COVID-19 detection and highlights the significance of protecting users' privacy. To replicate this, a complete coronavirus disease COVID-19 detection kit is open-sourced at: https://github.com/stergiosss/covid-19_adversarial_training_for_sensing_data. This kit includes the code for our detection system, the Adversarial Train model, and the COVID-19 dataset used to train it. The dataset includes various levels of data perturbation to simulate what might be seen when data remains unperturbed. Additionally, the repository contains a simulator to mimic unknown unperturbed information and validate the model's performance on real, unperturbed test data. The method was tested using data from 220 subjects with COVID-19 and 988 healthy individuals, all wearing activity trackers. Notably, the method detected COVID-19 infections or conditions with a 88.5% accuracy and healthy individuals with a 91.5% accuracy in a study where the data was mimicked to resemble what would be seen when data remains unperturbed. In a second testing stage, the method was tested using real data with a 85.7% accuracy and 91.5% accuracy for COVID-19 infections and healthy individuals respectively. Lastly, the method was tested for its resiliency as real data is never shared, demonstrating that the method can withstand manipulations by counterfeits with a 84.2% accuracy in a study where the data was tampered with. To further strengthen this research, the method was tested for its ability to translate to different wearable devices by recreating the data from Apple Watch for the Garmin Forerunner 245 model. In recent decades, homicides in Brazil have exhibited significant increases, 
placing the country among the top global locations for homicide rates. 
This study examines temporal and spatial characteristics of homicides in Goias 
from 2002 to 2014, employing a spatial analysis approach to determine whether 
homicide rates are evenly dispersed throughout the state. Results from Morgan's 
test indicate a cluster of high homicide rates in the Northwest region of Goias, 
where cities such as Aragaras and Uruandi reported homicide rates exceeding 50 
per 100,000 residents in the analyzed period. Conversely, the Southeast region of 
Goias, incorporating cities like Anapolis and Aparecida de Goias, reported lower 
homicide rates below 10 per 100,000 residents. These findings suggest a need for 
region-specific approaches to address high homicide rates in Goias, including 
interventions aimed at improving law enforcement, social and economic conditions, 
and public policy implementations in the Northwest region. An effort to make these 
services more accessible could potentially reduce homicide rates in cities such 
as Aragaras and Uruandi, for example by enhancing the presence of police forces, 
which could in turn foster a sense of security among residents, thereby 
comprehensively addressing the root causes of homicide. Additionally, identifying 
the underlying causes of homicide in Goias will involve investigating a variety 
of factors including socioeconomic conditions, as these are known to be 
correlated with homicide rates, reflecting broader social issues that need to be 
addressed at their source. Ultimately, achieving lower homicide rates will depend 
on developing effective strategies that tackle the root causes of crime and 
promote a greater sense of community and public safety. Analysis of the economic 
health of Goias also identifies a need to address the state's economic challenges, 
including disparities in income distribution and the unevenness of economic 
opportunities across regions, for instance in the Northwest where higher 
homicide rates may indicate a breakdown in the social and economic fabric of 
these cities. In addition to these policy recommendations, further research is 
recommended particularly into the role of access to services and investment in 
these regions in contributing to homicide, for example by exploring the 
relationship between the deployment of police forces in these cities and their 
homicide rates, which could help to identify more effective policy interventions. 
Ultimately, achieving lower homicide rates in Goias will require a multifaceted 
effort to improve the overall social and economic well-being

Stochastic gradient descent in its accelerated form efficiently optimizes smooth, strongly convex objectives, but its effectiveness relies heavily on the quality of random data points generated across iterations. When these samples are biased, accelerated SGD often struggles, which can be a significant issue in real-world applications where data is often noisy and biased. A specific case study involving computer tomography also highlights these limitations in a practical context. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a new accelerated SGD variant that adapts and improves the quality of its random samples iteratively, effectively making it more resilient to noisy and biased data. This adapted algorithm is grounded in a new theoretical understanding of SGD's behavior and is motivated by a novel model that characterizes the relationship between data noise and its distributive properties. The proposed algorithm is further enhanced by incorporating a novel sample correction method, which aims to mitigate bias and improve the sample quality, leading to significantly improved performance in practical settings, especially for complex objectives with heightened convexity, as demonstrated through our theoretical and experimental results. Furthermore, our research also explores the practical applications of this algorithm in a range of tasks, including a successful deployment in a medical imaging application to improve tomography image reconstruction. Developing robots capable of skilled work in complex environments is an essential area of study, but a significant obstacle to achieving this goal is a reliable technique for determining a graspable object grasp. The creation of a grasp suitable for a dexterous robot end-effector is crucial in achieving a successful task, and it is crucial to assess the quality of proposed grasps using physics simulations. However, there is a shortage of comprehensive simulation tools for evaluating dexterous grasps across diverse objects. To address this shortcoming, we introduced DexGraspNet, a substantial dataset featuring dexterous grasps achieved by simulations using two arms. Our dataset includes samples from 125 different objects and is characterized by diverse objects, successful grasps, and variable arm positions in the workspace. Additionally, a tool called DexGraspNet-CNN was developed for predicting quality using a convolutional neural network, and it was trained and tested on the created dataset. When applied to other established datasets that focus on robotic grasps, the performance of DexGraspNet-CNN exhibited a notable improvement. We are making the DexGraspNet dataset and associated code available to the scientific community. Further research on DexGraspNet is envisioned to incorporate visual input in dexterous grasps and to evaluate the effectiveness of DexGraspNet-CNN in actual-world scenarios with a dexterous robot. Our research is the first step in achieving a skilled dexterous grasp, and it lays the groundwork for a sequence of tasks requiring multiple joint movements and object manipulation. In the long run, our goal is to integrate this knowledge into a pre-trained model that can be used for other challenging tasks once it is successfully demonstrated in a world-class robotic system. With the advancement of DexGraspNet-CNN to a level of near-perfect performance, it can be utilized as a control mechanism in a hierarchical planning system that is implemented with a reinforcement learning method called reinforcement learning from scratch, a technique that was successfully utilized in the achievement of a successful dexterous grasp by the team at MIT. In the future, we will further develop our research in achieving a successful dexterous grasp, and it may be utilized as a knowledge transfer method when applied to other challenging tasks once it is successfully demonstrated in a collaborative system. A novel, motion-correction technique is introduced for enhancing the quality of free-breathing MRI scans, specifically for abdominal organs. This approach can be applied to any turbo spin-echo sequence and employs a combination of canonic and selective partial Fourier methods to rapidly estimate respiratory movement and correct for artifacts caused by image acquisition timing. Using a correlation-based method, more accurate data is obtained and high-quality images are generated through the combination of partially sampled data. This approach is tested on healthy volunteers and individuals with liver metastases, demonstrating improved image quality and tumor visibility even at the lowest respiratory levels. Canonic method-based correction is identified as the primary contributor to image enhancement. Additionally, image reconstruction with motion correction significantly reduces the impact of respiratory levels on image quality. Our results show that this new technique yields superior image quality to gated yet less-than-optimal, fully-breathing MRI scans. This approach is now available for clinical use. Although knowledge distillation effectively trains stronger students with fewer parameters, its effectiveness depends on having a well-trained teacher. Obtaining a superior teacher through traditional supervised learning is impractical with limited resources and data. To address this issue, our research introduces a new model compression method called InDistill, which enables the direct transfer of important information from the teacher to the student without the need for a complete understanding captured by traditional teachers. By focusing on the flow of information, InDistill helps students learn more more efficiently and accurately, and we've found that our approach, which is generally applicable, significantly outperforms previous techniques in several key areas. Specifically, our results show that InDistill achieves better performance than other methods in reducing model size while maintaining top performance, and it's especially effective at handling complex data with high information content. Furthermore, through experiments and analysis, we've determined that InDistill helps identify and extract the most valuable knowledge from the teacher and reduces unnecessary information that can distract the student. Ultimately, our approach makes it easier to compress large neural networks into smaller models with better accuracy and takes a step towards achieving efficient model transfer. The source code for InDistill has been made available on the GitHub platform. Furthermore, incorporating the effects of soil moisture and movement across extended areas improved the simulated predictions compared to local theory which it built upon. An added benefit of expanding the theory to include these factors was the discovery of new predictive capabilities, including the effects of spatial distribution of grazing on population growth. The Well-Correlated Algorithm (WCA), a recent version of the CountSketch, claims to offer the most resilient estimate for frequency estimation in streams of elements. Notably, it can handle even the most challenging scenarios in which subsequent elements in a stream are deliberately chosen based on previous counts. Building on existing research that compared WCA's excess k-error sketched space complexity to the best possible outcomes for ObbR Sketches and Randomized Sign matrices, we expand on this research by providing an even more competitive result that surpasses current standards. Our improved result is achieved through the development of a new algorithm that focuses on avoiding the issue of adaptivity in the stream, ultimately leading to its own set of parameters that result in the most resilient frequency estimation solution to date for streams that are not well-structured. In contrast to previous methods that relied on either semi-random or Supero bbR sketches, we present a novel solution that results in better frequency estimation results using only the most basic concepts from linear algebra. Finally, we also present an application of our non-adaptive version of WCA that results in the best possible solution for streaming 2SUM problems, a fundamental problem with significant real-world relevance and various applications in statistics and machine learning. Specifically, we achieve an estimate whose expected value is within $O(\sqrt{ k\log k})$ of the true sum, a result that surpasses current standards for 2SUM solutions that were previously established by Erdos-Renyi random graphs and achived an expected error of $O(n\log n)$. A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its implementation on central and graphical processing units and interfacing with PySCF. Preliminary timing benchmarks compared to existing C++ codes show ipie performs equally well or better on both CPUs and GPUs. AFQMC results for the isomerization of [Cu$_2$O$_2$$]^{2+} were achieved using ipie with selected configuration interaction trials, achieving convergence for small basis sets. Additionally, results for a quadruple-zeta basis set with an estimated error of less than one kcal/mol were reported, involving 52 electrons and 290 orbitals with $10^6$ determinants in the trial wavefunction, highlighting ipie's utility for systems with strong correlation and dynamic effects. Furthermore, the program's adaptability is shown by using it to perform time-evolution simulations on hydrogen chain with a time step of one third an femtosecond using its native time-evolution method, or resorting to lower approximation methods due to the limitations of ipie at such short time scales. All these examples suggest ipie is a versatile tool for performing quantum chemistry simulations with precision quantum Monte Carlo methods. The program will be continuously updated to become a more usefull quantum chemistry simulation tool. This could enable the swift exchange of electro-magnetic waves for negotiating contract terms, providing a competitive advantage through early knowledge of a quantum partner's decisions. To illustrate this concept, a multi-frequency version of the quantum prisoner's dilemma game was developed, which included modelled HFT decisions based on binary choices and binary contract terms. Three rounds of the game were played with various combinations of classical and quantum players, revealing that human players could achieve the highest level of cooperation with other human players, followed by a quantum player making non-coercive decisions and a human player. However, if a player makes coercive choices, it achieves the highest level of profit regardless of the other player's decisions. This concept could be taken further to create a more efficient HFT system on a quantum network, providing an opportunity to study the interactions between human and non-human decision-makers. This research demonstrates the potential benefits of using quantum technology in financial applications and contributes to a broader understanding of cooperation between different types of decision-makers. We examine how agents working as intermediaries affect the market equilibrium and optimal allocation when they are able to improve upon the outcomes without exerting effort. We investigate ways to maximize income for all participants in the market, focusing on a scenario involving consumer-product pairs and intermediary-consumer connections. We explore two scenarios: one where intermediaries have complete knowledge of prices and another where they do not. We consider a setup with multiple products and show it by extension. For the case with perfect knowledge, we show that the best allocation is achieved by having the fewest possible intermediary-consumer connections and that intermediaries are connected to consumers who have the highest demand for the shared product. However, collecting and preparing human-written labels for this task is complicated because it requires selecting and formatting relevant words from summaries, which is time-consuming. In response to these challenges, we present a novel approach where instead of using pre-defined lists, we use prompts as lists dynamically generated from a pre-trained model based on a document. We test this approach on two datasets and find that it leads to an improvement of up to 3.6 points in their performance scores, outperforming a method that uses pre-defined lists and showing comparable results to a method that uses no lists at all. When we examined this approach, we found that it often produces summaries that are simpler and easier to understand. Our study indicates that this approach is a viable solution for generating abstractive summaries and can serve as a starting point for future research on non-exhaustive generation methods. This approach takes into account that emotional contexts can affect the way people speak and respond to one another. It is based on a mathematical model that was tested using a dataset from the Rembrandt Project, which studied letters between Henry James and Robert Browning. In contrast to lambda-B, which can approximate all quantum operations with infinite precision, lambda-S1 achieves a more practical model by introducing a new abstraction mechanism focused on the structural composition of quantum operations. This paper demonstrates the potential for infinitesimal steps in the composition of operations in lambda-S1, and verifies that the resulting model accurately captures the category of rotations. In the future, this approach may be extended to accommodate more complex quantum circuits. Ultimately, this paper highlights the utility of lambda-S1 as a powerful tool for analysing quantum operations and facilitating communication about quantum algorithms. By categorising quantum operations according to their composition, this model offers a novel perspective on the field that may shed new light on established quantum operations and the development of future quantum algorithms. In the framework of finite element methods, we investigate the numerical analysis of a Stokes variational inequality with a semi-coercive condition. This specific problem arises in the study of glaciology, where the Navier-Stokes equations are used in an optimal control context with a free boundary constraint. Assuming a 2D setting with an analytic, Lipschitz-continuous and convex domain $\Omega$, we consider the associated semi-coercive Stokes variational inequality. Implementing a weak formulation of this problem, we derive the Galerkin approximation, leveraging the $C^{0,1}$ regularity of the stress tensor to establish the convergence of a Galerkin sequence. Moreover, we showcase the convergence order of a standard finite element method in space and temporal domains, specifically $C^{0,1}$ in space and $C^{0,\tau}$ in time, using the conditions specified in Cholewa's theorem. This analysis is complemented by an error estimate for a time-discrete scheme, resulting in a $C^{0,\tau}$ convergence order in time. Lastly, we verify these theoretical predictions through various numerical experiments under diverse mesh configurations. These endeavors ultimately facilitate the implementation of an efficient, stable, and convergent algorithm for solving the Stokes variational inequality, with practical implications in solving the Navier-Stokes equations through optimization. Following the numerical analysis, we validate our approach by applying it to real-world glaciology data with impressive results, specifically for the West Antarctic ice sheet. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation drives gas outflows through research conducted at the centers of this galaxy. By analyzing multiple wavelengths and scales, our data revealed distinct gas clouds located near the centers that are characterized by the emission of ionized and molecular gases. Measuring the densities and temperatures of these gas clouds in the near-infrared and submillimeter ranges allowed us to investigate the control that star formation has over gas outflows. We discovered that one cloud is hotter than typical for starbursts but features extremely high temperatures, and we estimated that the mass of ionized gas in the central region is significantly lower than that of the solid-angle average of ionized gas observed across the rest-frame ultraviolet spectrum. Additionally, our data indicate that the majority of the stellar population in the central region is older than the gas, and widening our analysis to include nearby starburst galaxies from the SPERS survey showed that outflows are less common in areas of high star formation rate-to-gas density. However, it's unclear whether this relationship holds true in galaxies with the high mass of this galaxy, and it's also unclear what role age plays in this potential connection. Furthermore, our data show that the high temperatures in the central region could be the result of both the energy from young stars and the interaction between gas clouds, and we suggest conducting similar observations to study the clouds in the nearby M87 system to gain insights into its central gas temperatures. Finally, our data show that the evolution of the central region in the far ultraviolet spectras will differ based on whether or not outflows occur, and we recommend conducting long-term monitoring of known starburst galaxies in the far ultraviolet spectras to investigate the impact of outflows on human vision and photography. Contrary to expectations, both models revealed an almost linear relationship between the initial geometry's anisotropic factor and the flow's anisotropic coefficient, although the relationship did not perfectly match theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we discovered that initial geometry's anisotropic characteristics tended to become increasingly unpredictable as collision energies decreased, which may contribute to difficulties in accurately constraining initial conditions using anisotropic flow in such cases. Our study found minimal flow differences between Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, which did not support theoretical hypotheses. Finally, we observed that in the current model, triangular flow from initial geometry was largely sustained throughout the evolution process, with approximately 60% of the final value being retained at a specific time threshold, which may serve as a reference for future model developments. Our study does not address how anisotropic flow is generated, but rather, it provides insights to aid in interpreting experimental results using this model.
