A collaborative framework called Simbot Framework was developed to facilitate learning and experimentation with robotic systems. This platform supports multiple robotic configurations, including ABB IRB 9600 six-degree-of-freedom (6DOF) robots, as well as specific variants with integrated force-tensors. To enhance user experience, the framework includes an intuitive graphical user interface based on Java Swing, accompanied by a range of methods leveraging Robot Operating System (ROS) and Java Automated Testing for Robotics (JAT) tools. These include methods related to motion planning, using the ros-geometry package to calculate trajectories and optimize motion, and image processing, leveraging OpenCV and ROS image tools to facilitate analysis. Additionally, the framework incorporates methods for calculating joint trajectories, managing robot movements over time, and integrating force into robot motion, allowing examination of stability using the Lyapunov indirect assessment method, and simulating force impact in cases where direct measurement is not possible. Furthermore, the framework includes access to previously recorded data from ABB robots, allowing for its retrieval and reuse. Lastly, the framework supports the synchronization of data between multiple robots, enabling concurrent execution of tasks on a robotic fleet. The phenomenon of edge intelligence in automotive networks is becoming increasingly prominent, with applications such as enhanced safety features and intelligent navigation systems requiring access to high-resolution sensor data. Unfortunately, sharing sensor data with a central authority by conventional methods poses a significant risk to user privacy as it necessitates the data source's identification. To address this concern, we are motivated to explore the realm of privacy-preserving edge intelligence (PPEI), which aspires to safeguard users' personal information while enabling intelligent decision-making on the edge. PPEI is characterized by two core functionalities: a unified framework for privacy preservation (UFPP) that safeguards users' personal information and one of two intelligent decision-making algorithms that either prioritize speed or maintain data accuracy. Notably, the latter category includes traditional machine learning methods, which as we will demonstrate, can be modified to prioritize speed by leveraging distortion techniques and facilitate accurate decision-making by utilizing partial information. Our framework subsumes recent PPEI approaches, empowers users to exert fine-grained control over privacy settings, and showcases its capability to attain an optimal balance between utility and privacy loss through the application of a linear optimization technique, thereby distinguishing it from existing frameworks. Furthermore, we have introduced a speed-oriented algorithm, which amplifies the scalability of PPEI by transferring computation tasks from the edge to fog nodes, which offer a resource-efficient environment compared to the cloud. Our comprehensive analysis evaluates the performance of the proposed framework using numerical simulations, which demonstrate the efficacy of the UFPP in achieving a range of desirable metrics including privacy guarantee, utility guarantee, and optimal privacy-loss tradeoffs. To demonstrate its practicality, we have applied the UFPP to an real-world application, namely, autonomous vehicles navigating through uncharted terrain. Our results verify that the UFPP not only attains a balance between utility and privacy loss but also exhibits a considerable decrease in privacy loss and a meaningful increase in utility compared to an existing baseline PPEI approach. With the rapid advancement of edge computing technology and its growing availability, our work on PPEI is positioned to become a practical solution, which can effectively address the tradeoff between privacy and performance in edge intelligence applications. We explore the properties of this optimal set of numbers, which we call the Euler characteristic family, through multiple examples and demonstrate its extensive applications in various exponential transformations. We further extend this concept to the level of categories, which is particularly useful in studying the effects of discrete transformations on stratified spaces. By applying this idea, we are able to determine the conditions under which the Euler characteristic remains unchanged after a discrete map, which ultimately enables us to calculate this optimal set of numbers for any finite reflection group. The idea of oscillating the Liouville operator within the Lindblad equation allows for the creation of dynamical maps that mirror the behavior of oscillating quantum evolution operators, effectively mimicking classical nonlinear Schroedinger dynamics with weak dispersion and a linearly unstable limit cycle. By developing an initial high-frequency expansion for the oscillating Liouville operator, we can establish an expansion for the oscillating Lindblad generator, which effectively acts as a perturbation in cases of weak oscillations, and also derive a key identity involving weakly oscillating Kontinuous projectors. Furthermore, we investigate the applicability of this expansion in the context of an example system: the Gaussian oscillator. Our analysis shows that through the application of a certain transformation, one can determine the asymptotic forms of key terms within the expansion, which in turn reveal insights into the Markovian nature of the system in question. Our research marks the first instance where such an expansion for the oscillating Liouville operator has been achieved, and has also demonstrated the applicability and utility of this method in the context of oscillating dynamical systems within a Lindblad framework. The research further shows that many of the difficulties associated with developing a general theory for oscillating Lindblad generators may be overcome by employing high-frequency expansions, and in doing so, we can effectively develop markers of the oscillation strength required to produce desired effects. The research presented marks a significant breakthrough in the field of quantum non-equilibrium thermodynamics through the use of classical nonlinear dynamics, and has also opened the door for further investigation into the utility of classical methods in the creation of effective quantum dynamical models, especially in cases of weak dispersion and complex, high-dimensional systems where classical behaviors may be produced via perturbative methods. Our research further highlights a number of additional potential applications and should not be viewed in isolation from related works on oscillating quantum dynamics within non-Markovian frameworks. The theoretical framework developed in the present study may effectively be generalized for any Hermitian Hamiltonian that includes time-varying components, and in doing so, we can effectively produce desired effects within quantum systems in accordance with a predetermined plan through the use of classical methods. Our research further opens the door for effective utilization of classical methods in the creation of quantum dynamical models and may effectively be generalized for application in strongly nonlinear systems within a dual formalism. Deep neural networks have shown remarkable performance in image processing tasks by leveraging large, self-consistent training datasets. However, these networks often struggle when applied to unfamiliar testing data with differing characteristics, such as varying colors, structures, or image contents. This issue can be mitigated through datasets created from multiple sources, but simply combining these datasets often results in inferior results due to inconsistencies between them. In contrast, domain adaptation techniques aim to reduce discrepancies between training and testing data, thereby enhancing generalization. Although various methods have been proposed to address this challenge, evaluating and selecting the most effective approach can be a complex task. In our work, we introduce a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess the performance of deep neural network domain adaptation techniques. We employ a broad classification of these methods into feature extraction and label information alignment, and illustrate the efficacy of our approach using three widely recognized image classification datasets, effectively showcasing how our framework can be used to achieve state-of-the-art results in image classification. Moreover, this article outlines how its methodology can be adapted to other deep learning architectures and performance metrics, and discusses potential applications of domain adaptation in other machine learning tasks. Ultimately, our framework serves as a resource for researchers to understand the strengths and limitations of domain adaptation methods and to identify promising approaches for advancing the field. The code for our work is publicly available at https://github.com/alexkilonzo/DADA. This repository contains the implementation of our domain adaptation framework as well as detailed examples of how to use it with different network architectures. Notably, our technique builds upon existing ideas but offers a more precise and efficient evaluation procedure, and our work differs from current research by assessing domain adaptation methods in a broad classification system and evaluating them across multiple datasets, and extending our findings to other machine learning tasks beyond image classification. The purpose of this evaluation is to inform future research directions and provide a comprehensive understanding of domain adaptation methods for researchers and practitioners. With our framework, researchers can replicate and verify the results, and conduct more in-depth investigations of domain adaptation techniques, and expand the scope of our work to other machine learning challenges. Furthermore, our findings can serve as a foundation for developing more sophisticated domain adaptation methods and evaluating their performance using our proposed framework. In summary, our paper contributes to the research in domain adaptation by introducing an comprehensive evaluation framework, promoting generalization in deep neural networks, and serving as a resource for researchers to advance the field of domain adaptation. The recent introduction of the Legendre Memory Module (LMM) has provided a significant improvement in recurrent neural network (RNN) performance by utilizing the properties of Legendre memory. This module serves as a proxy for long-term memories that are difficult for RNNs to retain. Building upon this module's success, researchers developed the Legendre Memory Block (LMB), which is an enhanced version of the LMM. This paper presents a parallel training method for the LMB that is more efficient than before, making it easier to implement. There are two primary challenges associated with training the LMB, including differentiating the Legendre memory and optimizing the Fisher information. To address these issues, we developed a spectral method for differentiating the Legendre memory and reinterpreted the loss function to make differentiation more straightforward. To further improve the training process, we used the stochastic gradient descent with a momentum-based optimizer for both the LMB parameters and the Legendre memory. This experimental study evaluated the performance of the proposed method on real-world datasets, including speech, text, and digital images, resulting in significant improvements in model accuracy and a better understanding of the characterisitcs of the Legendre memory. Furthermore, we explored additional insights into the long-term consistency of the LMB using theoretical analyses and numerical computations. To the best of our knowledge, this research presents an efficient training method for RNNs that is capable of maintaining their consistency over arbitrarily long periods. The proposed method has achieved state-of-the-art performance on speech and text benchmarks, outperforming existing top-tier models. Language development is a pivotal aspect of cultural maturation, and research into its processes is plentiful but often confined to artificial settings. In the context of a multi-ethnic society, we've created a complex scenario where diverse groups encounter each other, and their members engage in creative exchanges that may lead to linguistic convergence. To simulate this process, we've developed an original naming game model with movable agents and two unique characteristics: the ability of individuals to speak multiple languages and to relocate in search of better linguistic understanding among their community. Leveraging advanced computational methods, we've explored scenarios with a range of mobility levels and observed that local homogeneity can coexist with global diversity, and that lower-level agents are more likely to improve their language skills through interaction while pursuing their endeavors. Furthermore, we found that agents speaking multiple languages have a greater impact on linguistic change than those with limited proficiency and that varying levels of mobility and understanding can result in distinct language development patterns. These findings offer practical insights for individuals seeking to expand their cultural competence and contribute to the understanding of language development as part of cultural evolution. They also have immediate relevance for real-world applications, such as second-language learning and language teaching. In the field of AI, deep reinforcement learning has been successful in solving complex tasks, but the understanding of its learned knowledge and rules remains complex and difficult to interpret. This study aims to improve machine transparency by using a novel approach that combines hierarchical reinforcement learning with inductive logic programming. Our proposed method features two key components: ILP and hierarchical reinforcement learning networks. We implemented the ILP method using clp(Blog), which enables automatic extraction of logic rules from agent interactions. We then developed a two-layered reinforcement learning network system. The high-level layer uses clp(Blog) to generate logic planning strategies, and the low-level layer trains policy networks for actual actions. Our framework demonstrates its effectiveness through challenging gridworld and tileworld challenges, offering up to an 85.7% improvement in performance and breaking down complex problems into simpler sub-problems. We validated the interpretability of our ILP-RL method through the evaluation of its extracted logic rules and execution efficiency, resulting in significant performance gains and insight into the learned rules and sub-problems. This study showcases the potential collaboration of deep RL and logical AI to achieve transparency in agent behavior. The ILP-RL code is available for review on GitHub at https://github.com/jaykim9876/ILP-RL.

correct alternatives. A key benefit of this research is the potential to use 
language models that specialize in linguistic analysis to improve specification 
writing. A future project will involve integrating this approach with linguistic 
models to lower the specification development barrier and make formal verification 
more accessible. A tool called NatHL, supporting this goal, is available for 
download at https://github.com/natHL/.

Achieving consensus in the face of clock synchronisation challenges and diverse hardware leads to the design of low-latency consensus protocols, such as canopus. Existing protocols have typically overlooked the most harsh failure pattern - Byzantine faults, resulting in potential bottlenecks being introduced through faulty network connections or hardware malfunctions. This study presents a new canopus protocol, RCanopus, demonstrating for the first time the ability of a distributed consensus protocol to withstand multiple Byzantine faults during the process of reaching consensus. For instance, even if up to 39 out of 40 sites fail with distinct fault types, agreement will still be reached. Moreover, RCanopus surpasses existing DLT protocols in performance and is capable of achieving lattices comparable to DLT's lattices while also outperforming them in terms of execution latency. Finally, we observe that our protocol is efficient enough to support machine learning workloads on GPU and concurrently run with such workloads. Overall, this enables the widespread adoption of canopus in practical scenarios involving distributed systems. Lastly, using practical parameters, we estimate that our protocol could reduce communication overhead to approximately 8.5% of total canopus communications. Despite adding overhead, we find that our protocol outperforms pure canopus in terms of execution delay by up to 4.6% and discover canopus to be the most energy-efficient at 77.9% less energy consumption. Furthermore, we suggest canopus to be utilised in canopus-less environments, resulting in canopus gaining a 4.6% higher execution delay. Ultimately, we envision canopus to be the most trustworthy consensus protocol in future consensus systems. Following a thorough analysis, our experimental outcomes demonstrate the canopus consensus protocol to be robust, trustworthy and efficient. Moreover, our study indicates canopus to be the most performant and energy-efficient at 14.52% and 73.15% respectively in comparison to other DLT's. Our research demonstrates that certain cosmological models, including black holes, neutron stars, and the Big Bang, can be accurately explained by loop quantum mechanics. We derived the Hamiltonian for loop quantum gravity using the Arnowitt-Deutsch-Misner formalism and subsequently obtained the corresponding equations of state. By applying these equations to relativistic stellar models, we found that they predict mass-loss phenomena for both black holes and neutron stars at certain critical densities, and also briefly considered a potential link between loop quantum gravity and the inflation theory. Our findings reveal that they are consistent with established astrophysical observations of compact star behavior. Additionally, we identified notable similarities and differences between predicted behavior and experiments involving the GRANATA device, which demonstrates quantum effects under high acceleration. Finally, we explored the potential meaning of certain features in the neutron star spectrum that were previously attributed to gravity-like quantum effects. Our research indicates that it is possible that the gravitational field, rather than other areas of study, may serve as a means of testing quantum mechanics in inanimate objects. Our model also predicts certain characteristics of black hole and neutron star behavior that have yet to be independently verified. Object detection with deep learning models largely relies on empirical loss functions that fail to provide reliable measures of uncertainty in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we have developed BayesOD, a novel framework that integrates a novel loss function and a simplified approximation to enhance both the precision and computationally efficiency of uncertainty estimation for deep object detectors. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple benchmark datasets, including COCO and PASCAL VOC, have demonstrated the efficacy of BayesOD in predicting uncertainty levels, showcasing its ability to identify out-of-coherence detections and distinguish difficult object categories. Furthermore, classification and localization tasks on datasets such as CIFAR-10 and DTD have validated the robustness of BayesOD under varying data augmentation conditions. The performance of BayesOD surpasses existing methods reporting on the same benchmark datasets as of our knowledge cutoff date. The implementation of BayesOD is freely accessible on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/zheyangw/Bayes-OD. Additionally, our research has been motivated by several real-world applications of deep uncertainty estimation. The detailed analysis is currently published in a separate research paper on https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.13432. To gain a deeper understanding of our research, we have implemented a web-based uncertainty estimation platform for deep object detectors, which can be accessed at http. The proposed platform enables users to generate out-of-distribution data samples, identify confident object detections, and visualize challenging detection tasks that warrant further investigation. The research findings presented in this implementation are currently available on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/zheyangw/Bayes-OD-Web. The research is further supplemented by associated demos, which can be accessed at https://bayes-od-web.herokuapp.com/. The objective of this implementation is to facilitate the detection of unusual events in smart cities through the precise estimation of uncertainty levels produced by the BayesOD framework. By combining the functionality of object detection and uncertainty estimation, we have demonstrated the potential of BayesOD in identifying challenging object categories such as vehicles without faces or objects with heavy occlusion. To promote the use of uncertainty estimation in practice, we have released two publicly accessible challenge platforms, including the Uncertainty Estimation for Deep Object Detection challenge on the Baseline Challenges platform at https://baselinechallenges.github.io/ue-deepod, and the Generalisation and Uncertainty in the Classification Challenge on the WinCLEF platform at https://www.winCLEF.com/. The future of transportation depends heavily on intelligent traffic systems that can accurately forecast traffic conditions, allowing drivers to reach their destinations quicker. Current traffic forecasting systems, however, often struggle to paint an accurate picture of the overall traffic pattern due to the complex nature of traffic movement. They commonly rely on a limited set of key indicators, such as point data collectors and cameras, which offer a narrow perspective on the traffic situation. Furthermore, traffic prediction challenges are compounded by the absence of clear connections between traffic conditions in the past and future, the need to predict a long-term, point-in-time traffic situation, and the requirement for seamless traffic movement over extended periods of time. To address these issues, we present a novel approach called TraNet, which focuses on predicting traffic patterns within specific segments of the road. By using a deep learning model to analyze road snippets from multiple sources, including road-mounted sensors and external images, we ensure our results are accurate and reliable. Our approach outperforms existing methods by utilizing spatial and temporal traffic patterns in the road snippets, which provides a more comprehensive understanding of the traffic pattern. We also present a data preparation tool to generate training data for this model and share our code with the community. Our study, which was conducted using real-world data from road sensors and external images, demonstrates the effectiveness of this model in predicting traffic patterns at specific points along the road. By applying this model to road snippets from the past, we are able to make accurate traffic pattern predictions up to 4 hours in the future. Our results also indicate that incorporating external images with the traffic data significantly enhances the model's predictive capabilities, which is particularly evident when the number of images increases. Overall, our approach offers a breakthrough in intelligence for urban transportation systems by addressing the challenges of predicting traffic patterns at specific times and locations. With this model, we are able to achieve a low level of detail in our predictions, which demonstrates that the relationship between past and future traffic patterns is crucial for making accurate predictions. Our results also emphasize the importance of incorporating visual information from external images to improve the model's predictive capabilities. Due to the need for more extensive data to fully evaluate its capabilities, we are currently working to create a dataset that represents diverse road shapes and patterns to further optimize this model. Our ultimate goal is to use this model to help drivers reach their destinations quicker by providing them with accurate and reliable traffic forecast. Given the increasing dependence of modern transportation on accurate forecasting, we believe that the future of urban transportation relies heavily on intelligent systems like this model to ensure safe and efficient travel

Accurate hippocampus segmentation is crucial for identifying hippocampus volume, which is often used to assess brain disorder progression, including epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. We developed a multi-input, multi-pooling convolutional neural network to improve hippocampus segmentation in MRI images, which outperformed single-input networks by incorporating region-of-interest pre-training and used transfer learning for network development. This approach also employed quantitative features trained on hippocampus and Alzheimer's disease datasets as an additional input layer for improved segmentation accuracy. When tested on a dataset of MRI images related to hippocampus volume in epilepsy patients, our network successfully identified the hippocampus with 98.1% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity, compared to the rule-based method used as a gold standard. A pairwise t-test confirmed the superiority of our network over other automated hippocampus segmentation methods. Background Trapping, a critical issue for spacecraft, is caused by interactions between Galactic Cosmic Rays and the Earth's magnetic field, producing anisotropic particle distributions. To address this challenge, we conducted a comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation to analyze the anisotropic particles produced at low Earth orbits. The simulation captured the complex characteristics of the Galactic Cosmic Rays and their subsequent production, propagation, and localization. The results of our simulation revealed the anisotropic properties of particles produced at low Earth orbits, which align with actual space-borne measurements. The anisotropic amplitude increases in proportion to the power of the magnetic field index, consistent with existing theories. Our simulation establishes a foundational framework for further simulations and theoretical developments related to trapping phenomena. The anisotropic particle data, generated through this simulation, is now being utilized in SPADIL system calibration processes for the ADITYA-1 spacecraft, and is also expected to contribute significantly to the calibration of similar missions in the future. The anisotropic particle data and results of this simulation have been made available for the scientific community to utilize. The anisotropic particle data can be accessed at http://www.iiap.ernet.in/research/scientific-publications/publications/2022/ANIS.html. Network traffic forecasting involves predicting future traffic levels based on past and current road link conditions. Accurate forecasting depends on understanding the dynamic relationships between these road links. This paper presents a novel framework using Deep Graph Neural Networks to model these interactions and forecast traffic. It introduces two innovative modules: a module that simplifies the graph representation by reducing node numbers through hierarchical linking, and another that reconfigures link connections among road links of varying lengths. Experimental tests using highway data from Texas demonstrated that our framework achieved a low forecasting MAE of 5.66 km/h and MAPE of 0.26%. Furthermore, the framework outperformed existing models with significant improvements of 18.8% and 12.9% in forecasting accuracy in terms of MAE and MAPE respectively. Analysis confirmed that the initial framework successfully captured the underlying traffic dynamics between these road links. This research makes two important contributions: (i) a new graph representation method using Deep Graph Neural Networks, and (ii) a new link reconfiguration method to improve the accuracy of traffic forecasting using these networks. Our results show promising potential for graph neural networks in traffic forecasting, and encourage further exploration of their use in transportation research. In the context of differential privacy, we've developed a technique to complete a low-rank matrix based on a small portion of its constitutionally private entries and noise from sampling mechanisms. This method is particularly effective in a scenario where we've been excluded from the matrix. Our novel approach is called the Huber method, named after Andrew W. Huber, and is founded on the principles of iterative selection and replacement of private entries with pseudorandom data, generated by the user. We've demonstrated that the Huber method is private, efficient, and supersedes several established methods including the currently reigning champion, APF. This new technique is made even more robust by its ability to operate blindlessly, a first of its kind in differential privacy. Our experiments reveal the Huber method to be a resounding success in a variety of matrix completion trials, outperforming the current state-of-the-art. One intriguing discovery from these trials was the emergence of an 'optimal ignorance' trend, indicating that the most effective results are achieved when the user remains unaware of the matrix's inner workings. Based on these findings, we've proposed the concept of 'ignorance as a privacy mechanism,' offering a crucial performance boost in differential matrix completion. This concept is further explored and substantiated through accompanying theoretical trials and analytical examinations, which have further fortified the Huber method's status as the state-of-the-art in differential privacy. We have developed a novel dust model consisting of larger grains and smaller PAH particles.  The 'Astrodust' grain model, comprising three types of grains, accurately replicates the extinction and emission spectra observed in the interstellar medium.  The model also accounts for the overall abundance of C and O in the ISM.  Additionally, our model includes polarizable PAH particles that effectively replicate the polarization spectra obtained from various ground-based and space-based observations, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of dust polarization in the ISM.  The combined Astrodust+PAH model has been successfully incorporated into a complex model of the ISM, where it generates results consistent with the majority of observations.  Specifically, our model indicates a dust-to-gas ratio of 100:1 and a C/O ratio of 0.40:1, both of which are in line with the abundance predictions from astrochemical models.  Furthermore, our model shows that larger grains dominate extinction, while the emission and polarization spectra are primarily influenced by PAH particles.  Specifically, PAHs generate most of their emission in the 15-30.5 $\mu$m range and contribute significantly to polarization throughout the 1-30 $\mu$m wavelength range.  The combined Astrodust+PAH model has been applied to various environmental conditions, such as different gas densities and temperatures, and is even applicable to those as low as those found in some diffuse clouds and snowflake nucleation sites. The model indicates a significant gas density threshold, beyond which PAHs are destroyed by gas kinetic energy, and this threshold is at least 10$^5$ cm$^{-3}$. The Lights Out problem is well-known on graphs, which involves tapping switches to deactivate them by traversing the network. This tap strategy has a significant limit that the number of successive taps per switch cannot exceed $k+1$ where $k$ is the minimum degree of the graph. A particular instance of this problem has been studied in the context of a $j$-fold identity graph, which is created by connecting vertices in a straight line, and it was observed that the minimal number of taps required to solve the problem has a lower bound of $j+2$ and can be solved with $j+3$ steps. Furthermore, it was also discovered that if the problem allows $k+3$ steps, then the identity graph of degree $j$ can be equivalently represented as the union of $j$ simple paths connected to each other. As a result of this finding, the minimal number of taps required to solve the problem has also been determined for certain types of graphs including complete graphs, ring structures, and ladders. Key algorithms that solve the problem have also been developed and analyzed. Firstly, an $\epsilon j$-efficient algorithm was created to tap all switches in the network and then modified to have a time complexity of $O(j)$, and finally, another $\epsilon j$-efficient algorithm was modified to have a time complexity of $\sqrt{j}$. Lastly, an additional algorithm to solve the problem had a time complexity of $O(\log j)$. Analysis of these algorithms revealed that the minimal number of taps required to solve the problem has a lower bound of $j+2$. We have demonstrated the algorithm's correctness, and it has also been shown to be optimal in its performance by disproving several non-optimal taps strategies that included the algorithm itself in its previous state and the Best Edge Algorithm, which had a simple and efficient design by requiring only an edge's incidence and degree to facilitate the tapping process. Moreover, the algorithm's design has also been used to simplify an existing expression for ladders in terms of their height and the number of taps required to solve the problem, which is $2h+2$. With the image segmentation task serving as a constraint, it achieves image restoration minimax optimization. The model is theoretically analyzed and experimentally verified using synthetic and real-world data for image segmentation, which shows its efficacy compared to existing methods. Additionally, the model is applied to semantic image segmentation in convolutional neural networks, demonstrating its potential benefits in semantic image segmentation tasks. The model's performance is showcased through several image segmentation and image restoration experiments, highlighting its advantages. Notably, the model exhibits stronger image segmentation performance than a leading approach, while yielding comparable results in minimal dataset conditions. Furthermore, the model displays less dependence on initialization than state-of-the-art semantic image segmentation algorithms in baseline training, indicating its potential for improved semantic image segmentation performance with additional training data. Recent interest has been given to personalizing recommender systems and making their results more relevant to users' individual preferences. Although existing research has successfully achieved user-centered recommendation by leveraging user reviews and item attributes, it is often overlooked that users' comments often focus on specific items rather than being overall statements. Moreover, the interaction between reviews and items is commonly modeled as being uniform, which does not reflect real-world scenarios where reviews are often biased towards particular items. This paper investigates a user-centered recommendation task and proposes the SIFN model, an innovative approach that uses sentiment-awarely fused review-influenced item features to produce review-centered item recommendations. To achieve this, the SIFN model first generates sentiment-aware item features by mapping user reviews to items and then merges these features in a way that is sensitive to real-world review biases. This resulting review-centered representation is then used to produce recommendations that are more aligned with users' individual preferences, and the model also uses a feedback mechanism to further refine its results interactively. Experiments conducted on two public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the SIFN model and its components, and highlight the importance of reviewing-centeredness and interactive personalization in achieving high recommendation quality. The implementation of the SIFN model is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhangdeng1988/SIFN. Results indicate that the SIFN model outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, with a notable improvement of up to 11% in terms of top-10 accuracy in the tested case. The model also outperforms a recently published state-of-the-art interactive recommender model by up to 3% in terms of top-10 accuracy in the tested case. The research presents the first comprehensive study of the sentiment-awareness of user reviews and provides important insights to researchers working on personalizing recommender systems. This work introduces an innovative, computationally efficient approach to analytical Lag modeling for silicon-on-insulator (SOI) PMOS transistors with varying lengths. By leveraging Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox with polynomial or spline options, the modeling process becomes significantly more efficient, enabling the creation of high-quality, analytical Lag models within hours, even when incorporating multiple geometrical and temperature-dependent variables. To facilitate this process, a Matlab script is provided that supplements the required tools and data types, including a pre-designed fitting procedure for SOI PMOS Lag modeling, as well as a detailed user manual for optimizing the modeling strategy and data preparation. Building upon this foundation, the fitting procedure can be adapted to accommodate a broad range of MOSFET devices, encompassing both finite-channel length effects and varying gate materials. By utilizing this analytical Lag modeling approach, known as SOI-Lag, designers and researchers are empowered to perform precise predictions, complemented by Complementary Lag (CLag), enabling the accurate simulation and modeling of Lag effects in complex, spice-based circuit designs. Additionally, SOI-Lag serves as a reliable tool for characterizing physical MOSFET channels, obtained through channel extraction, and validated against 3D-simulations. Importantly, the presented approach offers a well-established framework for the analytical modeling of MOSFETs in general, including the derivation of parameter extraction methods for accurately determining device-independent target functions such as channel length, intrinsic output conductance, and contact resistance. Furthermore, SOI-Lag has been extended to incorporate a comprehensive understanding of variability, facilitated by the model's integration with Monte-Carlo simulations, as demonstrated in the evaluation of thermal noise in FinFET circuits. Ultimately, the presented methodology is universally applicable for the analytical modeling of various transistor types, including FinFETs, where it has been successfully implemented in the context of. Reinforcement learning commonly utilizes a discrete action space in real-world applications, but implementing algorithms with truly discrete actions is often impractical due to the need for a finite number of actions. To address this issue, we propose a new concept of coarse-grained continuity in metric spaces that serves as the foundation for our Q-learning algorithm. This approach is derived from the intuition that actions in a finite domain form a compact structure when mapped to a higher-dimensional space, and it can facilitate the extension of continuity-based results to domains with arbitrary dimensions. Furthermore, we show that our Q-learning algorithm based on this new concept is almost always near-optimal and has near-optimal regret. We demonstrate the applicability of this idea to discrete action spaces with arbitrary cardinality, and we test its effectiveness in various continuous control tasks. We also present additional experimental results that illustrate its utility for solving composite optimization problems and its connection to policy gradient methods. Overall, these findings make a significant contribution to the field of reinforcement learning. The extent to which animals are aware of their own existence and the lives of other creatures plays a crucial role in their behavior, interaction with each other, and understanding of the world. This "animacy" factor has been shown to influence various cognitive tasks and play a significant part in animal social behavior. From a neural perspective, it is still unclear how animacy is recognized and what specific mechanisms are involved. In a study, we have developed a comprehensive dataset consisting of over 6,000 videos featuring a wide range of animals, from insects to primates, and humans, which are categorized into animacy groups. By using this dataset, we have identified animacy-related brain areas by conducting functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans. In another experiment, we have created animacy-based stimuli by combining face and body parts, which are used in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans to reveal the underlying neural mechanisms. Through these experiments, we have found that the integral part of animacy processing in the human ventral temporal cortex involves the integration of social and autonomic face information and embodied body signals. In a computational model, we have developed an animacy map that reflects the hierarchy of animacy levels, which is based on face recognition alone and secondly on body signals with face information, which is used to replicate and validate our fMRI findings. This research provides the first comprehensive understanding of the animacy organization in the human ventral temporal cortex and suggests that face recognition systems play a crucial part in animacy perception. We are presenting a pioneering approach termed the Convex Optimization-Based Filter (COBF), which maintains the geometric structure of the computational grid in convex multi-dimensional environments. This technique is highly versatile and can be incorporated into a wide variety of geophysical simulation tools that rely on solving partial differential equations (PDPDEs). By converting an unstable, shock-producing equation into a stable, smooth counterpart, the COBF method prevents the formation of spurious oscillations and numerical shocks at a relatively low computational cost. In contrast to traditional PDPDE filters, the COBF method does not introduce additional diffusion, thus enabling the reproduction of precise solutions even after the formation of numerical shocks. Furthermore, we are implementing this algorithm in the OpenMFELab framework, which is a Python library used for finite element-based geophysical simulation. The framework's efficiency and user-friendliness provide an accessible platform for researchers to quickly prototype and iterate new algorithms. In line with the spirit of reproducibility, the source code for the COBF method and the corresponding project files can be found at the specified GitHub repository: https://github.com/tejas-i18/COB-Filters. In dynamic, collaborative environments with inherent challenges and limited resources, effective teamwork relies on strategic decision-making and adaptive interaction among members.  We propose a novel approach based on transfer empowerment that enables agents to focus on achieving the team's goals by leveraging their social connections.  By incorporating a quantitative measure of transfer empowerment, our method reveals the benefits of mutual support and guides agents to maximize their contributions based on each member's capabilities and the overall team effort required.  Through a simulation with two cooperative agents in a scarce resource setting, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in fostering a positive social dynamic and efficient cooperation, outperforming existing methods that promote cooperation through optimism and generosity.  Additionally, our method offers a significant advantage by enabling agents to adapt quickly to changes in the level of effort required and can be applied to any cooperative task without any task-specific assumptions.  Based on these outcomes, we validate the promise of the concept of transfer empowerment and its potential to improve cooperation among agents consistently and consistently well. A widely used technique for deriving the vector magnetic field (VMF) structure of the solar atmosphere relies on combining photospheric magnetic field polarization measurements from different wavelengths. However, this technique comes with significant biases, particularly in certain wavelength data, which severely impacts the resulting VMF reconstruction. In this study, we examine the effects of treating noisy, bias-infused data as if it contains accurate VMF information, and we explore two corrective methods - outbound extrapolation and polarization correction. We apply these techniques in a realistic simulation and find that outbound extrapolation yields more reliable VMF reconstructions than the unbiased technique. Furthermore, we suggest that using polarized magnetic field maps to determine horizontal VMF orientation can yield more accurate results than the unbiased technique. This finding is subsequently verified using actual data from various instruments. Ultimately, we believe that incorporating these corrective methods can greatly enhance the precision of VMF reconstructions in solar atmosphere studies. Additionally, we provide clear guidelines for properly using the unbiased technique in solar atmosphere research. Such best practices revolve around distinguishing between the intrinsic electron beam shape and the overall polarization structure, and we find that using polarized magnetic field maps can aid in this distinction. Our study was conducted primarily to refine the precision of VMF reconstructions in solar atmosphere research, but the techniques and methods we've outlined could also be applied to other complex multi-component data sets in various fields. At the very least, we believe that understanding the source of biased data and addressing it through corrective methods can only serve to further advance the associated research. Nonetheless, we do acknowledge the considerable efforts and accomplishments of prior researchers who have made significant contributions to our current understanding of the solar atmosphere. Upon reviewing the existing literature, we find that previous studies have largely failed to consider the significant biases present in biased data, and as such we've decided to introduce corrective methods to standardize the techniques for deriving VMF structure. This paper investigates the problem of optimizing ads to maximize revenue per user, taking into account the cost of ad display and individual user budgets. A novel solution is introduced that adapts to changing display costs and user budgets to maximize total revenue. Due to the ad display cost per click variability and uncertainty of user budgets, a high-performance bidding strategy is extremely challenging to establish. Therefore, a risk-averse bilevel optimization model is proposed to address this challenge. The model uses a budget constraint level optimization top model and a variance-reduced lower Bilevel Optimal Solution (BOS) model in the bottom level, minimizing the expected and variance of total revenue loss. The upper bilevel model optimizes the budget allocation, while the lower bilevel model uses the derivative of the upper bilevel model's optimality condition to calculate the derivative of the revenue loss and apply the Newton method, incorporating the constraint that no more ads can be displayed to minimize expected variance. Additionally, a constrained adaptive optimization algorithm is introduced to dynamically update the bidding parameters, which can rapidly converge to the optimal solution. Experimental results, involving both real-world and simulated data, confirm that the proposed algorithm consistently outperforms the industry-standard approach and other competitive solutions, including risk-averse optimization algorithms. The proposed algorithm consistently achieves superior performance, with notable gains of 52.87% and 15.11% over the industry-standard solution in real-world and simulated data respectively. Moreover, the algorithm's convergence speed is significantly better than that of risk-averse optimization algorithms. A sensitivity analysis reveals that the algorithm's performance resilience varies based on the ad display cost and user budget distribution characteristics. A detailed performance evaluation demonstrates the algorithm's strong robustness and ability to adapt to different ad display cost and user budget scenarios. The proposed algorithm's computational complexity is analyzed and a pre-training method is introduced to address the computationally challenging nature of bilevel optimization, thereby achieving efficient computation while maintaining high performance. The effectiveness and reliability of the proposed algorithm have been further validated through successful deployments in multiple industries. Continuous phase modulation (CPM) is a modulation method that offers enhanced error resistance and simplified receiver design, including a distinctive feature of having a strictly positive error probability for high signal-to-noise ratios. Nevertheless, its practical utility is limited by its slow data transfer rate due to the necessity for an extended duration of symbols to achieve reliable detection. This paper explores ways to increase the symbol transmission speed while maintaining a positive error probability for high signal-to-noise ratios through an improved non-coherent detection method that incorporates additional information. For this purpose, we examine the effect of combining adjacent symbols, referred to as expansion, on the performance of conventional non-coherent differential detection. We derive the optimal expansion value as the square root of the duration of a hollow circular region with a radius of 0.774 for the standard Von Mises differential detection, based on the criteria of highest symbol error probability. This optimal expansion value surpasses that of coherent differential phase shift keying (DPKS) and comes close to the optimal value for PFKS, with both methods serving as references. Furthermore, we establish that by applying the optimal expansion value, the resulting symbol error probability can be expressed as a function of the hypergeometric 2F1 function, with the result displaying a high degree of convergence to the optimal value for the special case of very high signal-to-noise ratios. This new detection method is thus suitable for applications requiring both high transmission speed and low error probability. It notably surpasses the performance of conventional non-coherent DPKS detection in terms of both probability of error and delay, with the delay being extended by approximately 8.5%. In addition, we compare its performance to that of the recently proposed non-coherent differential detection with multiple integrations, with the former being more efficient than the latter. This detection method is suitable for implementation because it entails the same processing complexity, receiver architecture, and data recording format as conventional non-coherent DPKS detection. As such, it can serve as a highly efficient method for transmitting CPM signals, with its performance being comparable to that of DPKS while offering improved delay and reduced error probability. This detection method is thus highly suitable for various wireless and sensing applications requiring both high transmission speed and low error probability. In addition to its high performance, it is noted that CPM signals detected using this method exhibit an average duration that is close to the optimal value for the special case of very high signal-to-noise ratios. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of this comparative approach. To overcome this limitation, we propose combining existing cluster ranking methods with visual tools to efficiently construct comparison datasets, significantly reducing the required number of labels while preserving performance. Our approach is facilitated by a dynamic data clustering and labeling process that allows us to identify and exclude irrelevant instances in addition to assigning labels for the remaining relevant data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, which integrates the process into a stochastic gradient ascent algorithm for optimal policy acquisition, and successfully apply it to two tasks: a two-armed bandit case and a domain with diverse actions and outcomes. Compared to traditional comparison-based methods, our approach yields comparable results with significantly fewer labels required for the bandit case and substantially fewer evaluations for a wide-ranging action space, saving 57% and 76% of labels, respectively, while delivering performance that is within a negligible range of the baseline. Our technique is called Visually Aided Cluster Ranking, or VACR. For the bandit case with gamma discounts, we develop Gamma Optimistic Visually Aided Cluster Ranking, or GVACR, which builds on the framework by integrating the optimistic learning rate and considering the variety of possible outcomes, resulting in the creation of the first comparative reward learning method for the make-table setting that has been proven to converge. Our technique is available at: https://github.com/whwu1208/vacl.git. For the two-armed bandit case, our method leads to the creation of the first theoretically proven convergent comparative approach without the strict asymptotic optimality, which addresses a long-standing technical challenge. Importantly, our technique achieves the first experimental convergence proof for the general case of optimal policy acquisition, which has been noted as an unsolved problem by Sutton et al. (2009). These form factors exhibit distinct behaviors in noncommutative space-time, in contrast to commutative space. Therefore, a noncommutative scenario provides valuable opportunities for exploring a nucleon's intricate structures, and experimental verifications can help clarify underlying issues. Conversely, these models often conflate form and content, relying on abundant data rather than incorporating formal structures and lexical dependencies that underpin dialogue semantics. As a consequence, they may struggle to generalize in contexts outside of their training context. To rectify this, we propose a new method for pre-training dialogue models based on the meanings encoded in linguistic structures. By utilizing a combination of non-parametric probabilistic models (such as the Probabilistic Theories of Meaning) to capture reference distributions of words and phrases, this approach enables the incorporation of formal and lexical dependencies in the representation of dialogue meaning. Experimentally, we demonstrate that our method, implemented using the Transformer architecture, significantly improves state-of-the-art performance on the Semantic Paradigm Evaluation benchmark for dialogue inference and achieves comparable results to data-driven models on the DailyDialog and Saucekan datasets. Our proposal is a quantitative method to evaluate this interactiveness, which in turn is linked to the complexity of the concepts associated with the algorithm. Our model, the Human-Machine Learning-based Algorithmic Interpretability Model (HML-AIM), consists of three interconnected components: 1) an interactive learning framework, 2) a natural language generator, and 3) a text-based representational complexity measure. One of the anomalies that can be detected is the Outlier, which is identified as a data point with a significant distance from its surrounding data points in the feature space. However, the detection of Outliers is a complex problem, which has been partially solved using Machine Learning algorithms. The motivation for our research came from the Anomaly Detection on IoT datasets challenge in the IOTW 2020 conference, where we participated in the Outlier category. Our solution for Outlier detection was TiWS-iForest, a lightweight machine learning model that leverages two main features: weakly-supervised learning and tiny model size. Our evaluation results of TiWS-iForest, using ten Anomaly datasets from the SAD-AIDR benchmark repository, demonstrated an AUC ROC score of 0.6681 ± 0.0069. Additionally, our solution won first place in the Outlier category of the IOTW 2020 challenge for Point-Optimization problems, which is one of the two main problem types of the challenge, alongside Multi-Instance Diagnosis problems. Our solution for Multi-Instance Diagnosis problems came in second place. Our work opens up new avenues for the application of weakly-supervised learning in the field of Outlier detection. By examining the statistical properties of the first exit times, we can gain insights into the process of exchange between the localized particle and the tube's end. Our work focuses on deriving the mean first exit time for a particle in an infinitely long tube as well as the fluctuation field surrounding the localized particle, with both being expressed in terms of the solvable mean first exit time of a finite tube. Additionally, we have extended existing approaches to single-file diffusion to include entropic force components, with the results of these extensions being compared to recent experimental findings. Furthermore, we have considered how the localized particle's position within the tube affects its first exit time when encountering varying degrees of mean and fluctuating potential within the tube's ends. Our work regarding single-file diffusion is applicable to a wide range of systems, including readings of diffusion in living cells, where cellular compartments often resemble tubular shapes. Lastly, the concept of first exit times also has potential in exploiting existing particle tracking data to determine forces. To achieve this, we have applied our approach to a set of existing microfluidic experiments, with the experimental data being analyzed without necessitating any additional setups or measurements. Our work provides a mathematical link between the surrounding field's spread width and the localized particle's exchange rate with the tube's end, with the exchange rate being related to the localized particle's position within the tube. Additionally, the derived width is related to the localized particle's persistence time as discovered by Bouchaud and the localized particle's middle axis velocity. Our work involves developing an approach to calculate the localized particle's middle axis velocity based on the tube's end and its surrounding fluctuation field width. With the aid of our approach, we are able to calculate the localized particle's exchange rate for various positions within the tube, with the exchange rate being compared to established measurements. Our approach is not only applicable to single-file diffusion but can also be used to determine forces in any diffusion process, with the tube being any confined geometry and containing one particle. Our work provides a breakthrough in determining forces using the first exit time analysis, with the tube being any dimensionally confined shape. Quantum Mechanics contradicts the universally assumed, classical cause-and-effect relationship established by Bayes' rule in physics. Despite this, our research demonstrates that when we adhere to the principles of quantum mechanics, quantum Bayes' rule is consistent and free from contradictions. Additionally, we illustrate how applying quantum Bayes' rule to real-world scenarios highlights the distinct characteristics of quantum effects that differentiate them from classical correlations achieved through local hidden variable theories. By using its formalism, quantum Bayes' rule can help us evaluate the feasibility of certain quantum technologies such as quantum-based racism prediction and quantum randomness. In these cases, applying quantum Bayes' rule to practical issues like racial bias and randomness indeed produce meaningful and technically sound results, and when we use quantum mechanics correctly, quantum Bayes' rule offers more accuracy and clarity in its calculations. However, when working within the constraints of local hidden variable theories, applying classical Bayes' rule results in fewer assumptions and more accurate predictions in some cases. Therefore, whether we use the classical or quantum version of Bayes' rule, applying it correctly leads to consistent and applicable inferences in both quantum and classical scenarios. Importantly, our research confirms that when we adhere to the principles of quantum mechanics, quantum Bayes' rule is a reliable and consistent tool for solving real-world problems. Its modules over the algebra can be classified using subgroups of a particular group, with trivial components being straightforward to identify. However, the structure of non-trivial components is more complex and not fully understood in all cases.

In the case of components with degree $0$, it is known that the subgroups of a particular group $GL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ are key to understanding the structure of non-trivial components in cohomology groups of the Steenrod Algebra. Specifically, relations between action of algebra generators and elements of these subgroups provide insights into their composition rules and action.

On the other hand, the structure of non-trivial components in cohomology groups of degree one is more complicated and not as easily understood as the ones in degree zero. There is currently limited information about possible generators of these components.

We begin by providing generators for all non-trivial components in cohomology groups of the Steenrod Algebra for all possible degrees. This study enhances the local projection method to allow for complex, non-linear pathways in non-parametric models by developing a novel technique, the flexible local projection. The FLP builds upon the original local projection framework introduced by Jordi M. Ho, which has a specific application in analyzing the Economic Rationale of Fiscal Policy. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to a range of scenarios, such as studying the impact of shocks on financial markets or the effects of policy changes on specific economic sectors. To illustrate its capabilities, an analysis is conducted on the financial crisis of 2008 and its effects on the stock market performance of companies listed on the S\&P 600 index. The FLP analysis reveals a significant acceleration in stock price declines following the initial shock, with an average increase in reaction intensity of up to 10%. The results are further validated by applying the FLP to synthetic data and verifying its accuracy in recapping historical financial turmoil events, including the Dot-Com bubble and the Global Financial Crisis. The results demonstrate a distinct variation in the nature and intensity of stock price reactions by these different firm types, with tech firms exhibiting more accelerated and volatile price growth patterns. Secondly, it conducts an in-depth analysis of the complex, non-linear effects triggered by the financial crisis on specific company groups within the S\&P 600 index. The FLP technique presents an indispensable tool for researchers seeking to explore non-linear relationships and time-varying effects in high-frequency financial datasets. Cloud-based Virtual Network Services have become increasingly attractive to users due to their ability to create customized service environments, even if such configurations are uncommon or rarely used. However, managing Virtual Network Services at scale poses a significant challenge, mainly because of their standard non-preemptive nature in virtualized platforms. This issue cause a virtual machine (VM) allocated to a Virtual Network Service to be blocked upon creation, preventing it from being utilized by other VMs. To overcome this issue, we have introduced Prepartition, a novel load distribution method designed to mitigate VM wait times and minimize waste during Virtual Network Service setup. By splitting and distributing VM requests across multiple servers, we prevent a single server from handling a high volume of requests, thus ensuring a balanced distribution of workload among all servers. Our simulation results confirm Prepartition's ability to reduce VM wait times and decrease waste factors significantly, outperforming compared to Round-Robin and Random allocation methods. In particular, we have observed significant improvements, with Prepartition achieving 60.3% less VM wait times and 50.4% decreased waste factors, compared to Round-Robin. Furthermore, Prepartition has demonstrated 44.2% decreased waste factors and 13.2% less VM wait times, compared to Random allocation. Our experiments further demonstrate that Prepartition's performance may degrade slightly as the percentage of reserved VMs increases, a consequence expected for all load distribution algorithms. In addition, we have investigated the energy-waste performance of Prepartition in a data center, revealing a lower waste factor compared to Round-Robin and Random allocations. Our analysis of Prepartition's characteristics enables us to establish its conditions for minimal waste and wait times. Specifically, we have established that Prepartition's performance is optimal, with near-zero waste factor and wait times for load values ranging from 0.46 to 0.836. In addition, we have identified a correlation between the number of servers and optimal performance conditions. Our research underscores the need for an load distribution algorithm that can balance VM assignment with minimal waste and wait times during Virtual Network Service setup. By distributing VM requests among multiple servers, Prepartition has achieved these desirable characteristics, demonstrating better performance in comparison studies. In addition, we have identified patterns of optimal performance conditions, thus contributing to a comprehensive understanding of cloud-based VM allocation. Our research provides insights for developing future load distribution algorithms that can improve the quality of VM allocation in virtualized platforms. By optimizing VM wait times and waste factors, Prepartition has demonstrated its potential as a load distribution solution

A document summary is a condensed version of the original content, typically comprising the key phrases and ideas, that can be generated using any of two popular models: Graph-Based and Neural Network-based Summarization. However, standard summarization models are often designed to work with English and other widely spoken languages, but not with languages such as Hindi, Telugu, and Malayalam that are commonly spoken in India. To overcome this limitation, an Indian language-specific summary model called GAE-ISumm has been developed using an ancient Indian text, the Mahabharata, as a large dataset. This dataset contains summaries written in Sanskrit and non-standardized Telugu that are missing in modern datasets. Generation experiments conducted on 100 and 200 sentences showed GAE-ISumm performs similarly or better than other leading summarization models, including Graph-Based and Neural Network-based Summarization. Notably, GAE-ISumm produced summaries that were close to those written by humans in terms of ROUGE metrics, while also outperforming the baseline models made up of extraneous sentences. Recently, a variation of the variational autoencoder, known as LS-VAE, has been developed and showed outstanding performance in generating images by utilizing natural image characteristics to regularize latent space priors. Unlike standard VAEs, LS-VAE employs least squares loss function in combination with ELBO, and demonstrates the ability to learn hierarchical Gaussian priors in the latent space more effectively than standard VAEs. Similar to ELBO, the loss function of LS-VAE relies on data and latent space parameters. Although LS-VAE is able to acquire hierarchical Gaussian prior in the latent space, it is limited to producing low-quality images, particularly for complex datasets. One of the main reasons for this shortcoming is that Gaussian prior in the latent space tends to concentrate data in a single area, which is not suitable for regression and image generation. In this research, a modified version of LS-VAE, referred to as LS-VAE- $\rho$, is proposed and implemented. The core aspect of this modification involves incorporating the hierarchical Gaussian prior in the latent space with a regularizing term, derived from the KL divergence of the latent space and data distributions. Consequently, LS-VAE- $\rho$ attains better results in generating high-quality images, regressing more accurate results, and learning a better comprehension of data and latent space patterns. Furthermore, LS-VAE- $\rho$ exhibits a significant potential in learning a diverse and semantically structured latent space, which is capable of being utilized for various tasks. Theoretical analyses and experimental studies are conducted to evaluate the performance of LS-VAE- $\rho$, and its results demonstrate the superiority of this model in producing high-quality images and regressing more accurate results compared to its predecessor. Moreover, theoretical research is carried out to assess the feasibility of applying hierarchical Gaussian prior in the latent space to generate latent codes for both LS-VAE and LS-VAE- $\rho$. In order to validate these theoretical findings, experimental studies are conducted to measure the performance of LS-VAE- $\rho$ in generating images based on the significant structural patterns in the latent space, and the results obtained are found to be in perfect alignment with the theoretical predictions made in this research. Ultimately, the experimental results validate the effectiveness of LS-VAE- $\rho$ in learning a diverse and semantically structured latent space, and its potential in being applied for various tasks such as image generation and image-to-image translation. This work introduces an approach to reduce complexity in systems using gray coding through low-bit precision quantization. By applying this method to the likelihood ratio (L-Variable) of received symbols, we maintain the encoding scheme's original decoding structure while decreasing the computational load. To this end, we employed a deep learning approach using a novel objective function that maximizes the bit-extrapolation performance and minimizes the bit-accuracy performance, maintaining a decoding error as low as 1.5% and saving 60-85% in processing time in comparison to the baseline. Furthermore, the proposed method outperforms traditional approaches such as maximum likelihood detection and decision-theoretic classifier in terms of performance and computation speed. It is noted that the proposed method can also be applied to non-linear modulation schemes like M-ary PSK with similar effectiveness. Interestingly, the proposed method exhibits resilience to training data perturbations amounting to up to 10-12 percent relative perturbation, which is far superior to the performance of the conventional decision-theoretic classifier. What's more, the proposed approach can also be adapted for real-time applications where the decoding latency is critical, achieving a decoding error rate of 1.5% with simultaneous reduction of 60-85% in processing time and the exchange of 1-3 extra bits in precision. Finally, the proposed analysis and benchmarking indicate the need for further research in exploring the possibilities of using deep learning-based approaches to reduce computational complexity in systems using gray coding. Our study involves analyzing the complexity of upward slice decomposition in clustered and unrestricted environments, utilizing multiple parameters. We introduce the concept of "inward" and "outward" cluster orientations and demonstrate a parameterized algorithm with significantly reduced complexity, applying the following parameters: contraction (elimination of vertices), standard branch and bound, Weft, inward, outward, and treewidth. Additionally, we investigate the intersection of these parameters across various variants of upward slice decomposition. Our results include confirmation of exponential complexity for multi-dimensional upward slice decomposition, despite multiple adjustable parameters. On the other hand, we design a parameterized algorithm that efficiently decomposes graphs into single-slice partitions, utilizing the contraction parameter in combination with branch and bound. Lastly, in an effort to validate the complexity results, we perform experimental analysis of upward slice decomposition, applying the Weft parameter in simple graphs, resulting in a computationally efficient algorithm. Our study confirms that upward slice decomposition is computationally intensive compared to other parameters, taking significantly longer to decompose complex subsets of edges. In response, we propose a pre-processing technique to efficiently narrow down the search space of upward slice decomposition. A comprehensive classification of quantized Hall insulators is developed in terms of exchange-coupled ferromagnets and various antiferromagnetic states found on the triangular and kagome lattices. By applying group theory to a complete set of one-bond terms, all possible antiferromagnetic configurations are identified and categorized. Further, interacting-spin theories and numerical simulations demonstrate the feasibility of achieving these states in realistic materials. Additionally, we outline a potential experimental framework involving NMR and doped-implantation to distinguish between degenerate ground states proposed by antiferromagnets and ferromagnets. We also explore ways to amplify spin-orbit coupling and establish a relationship between the proposed phases and recently discovered chiral phases. A comprehensive table detailing the properties of all identified phases is developed and presented. Furthermore, we highlight several materials that exhibit potential magnetocaloric properties due to their various ground states. We develop a novel approach to identify treatment effects within complex networks of interconnected systems, where many variables are influenced by a few key factors. Unlike existing methods, our technique can pinpoint active treatment effects even in highly correlated networks, and it achieves controlled false discovery rates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through theoretical analysis and present an efficient algorithm to implement it, accompanied by experimental results that confirm its performance in real-world scenarios. Our tests show that our method outperforms alternative techniques in controlling false discovery rates and accurately identifies treatment effects in highly interconnected systems, outperforming both classical frequentist and Bayesian approaches. Finally, we apply our algorithm to actual data from Google's experiment database and illustrate its use in real-world applications. Our algorithm is available for public use at https://github.com/drew-jackson/texid. Our method uses a new approximation of the null-calcium network, and through simulation, we compare it to the best frequentist and Bayesian approaches for its control of the false discovery rate. Our method was motivated by the need to interpret the results of network-wide clinical trials, and through experimentation, we compare its control of the false discovery rate to the CNET and TBX algorithms. Our method was validated by applying it to data from actual patients and seeking an active treatment effect. Our algorithm was tested against the TBX algorithm, which is the current state-of-the-art Bayesian approach for controlling the false discovery rate without assuming independence. Our method was shown to outperform TBX in highly correlated networks, and our algorithm was tested against frequentist and Bayesian methods using real-world data from actual patients. Our algorithm was then applied to the actual patients to accurately identify treatment effects in highly correlated networks, and our results reveal the only significant treatment effects in actual patients. In general relativity, gravity's root cause is curved space-time, but its symptoms appear as moving objects' paths deviating from straight lines due to varying gravitational potentials. By Newtonian approximation, these potentials are represented as scalar gradients that drive objects' acceleration. Since objects like galaxies experience opposing forces as they move through spacetime, their motion can be described as negative acceleration, or deceleration, with their speed gradually decreasing as they move further apart. According to observations, far-off galaxies are moving slowly, with high redshift indicating varying velocities. By the cosmological principle, these velocities remain uniform, and data confirm that the galaxies' relative acceleration with respect to one another is indeed gradual, with distant galaxies moving more slowly. Therefore, the cosmos is expanding, with its laws supporting the principle that relative acceleration is relative, making absolute acceleration a non-measurable property. As a result, the concept of absolute time, following the laws of general relativity, becomes relative as well, with time becoming a frame-dependent feature. With time being a relative feature, the question of whether the universe is growing or static, with its laws depending on the observer's frame, remains. Furthermore, the cosmos's non-linear, fractal features, perhaps result from interactions with unexplored dimensions, with our current measurements being one- and two-dimensional, may lead to further developments in understanding this phenomenon, with suggestions including unexplored three-dimensional depth and the possibility of existing parallel universes, each with their own time flows, to explain this evolution. With these possibilities in mind, the possibilities of extraterrestrial life also exist, with the potential lying in explaining how time is lost in our universe. With time being a relative feature, the question of what time is remains, and the possibilities of transforming it into a new form or discovering an alternative where time is linear rather than fractal. The loss of time may hold the key to understanding this transformation, with extraterrestrial life connecting to our state through the discovery of the lost dimension. With new dimensions being a potential explanation for the cosmos's evolution, the possibilities of extraterrestrial life also lie in understanding this transformation, with the loss of time as a key feature. The suggestions include a parallel universe where time is linear, with its flow opposite to ours, and the potential extraterrestrial life may have the capacity for regulating time, with the possibility of transforming our flow into a linear one for survival and then transforming time as a whole, with the loss of time as a necessary feature for such a transformation.
