We develop a schematic shell model to investigate the collective movement in axially symmetric (β2) and triaxial (β3) nuclei within the context of the minimal length concept based on the deformed harmonic oscillator potential. This model incorporates the minimal length parameter into the Hamiltonian and wave function of the system, and we focus on nuclei such as 176Hf and 184Hoss, calculating which deformed states are stable against collective movement and identifying their related properties. We find that introducing the minimal length parameter into the collective movement of these nuclei results in fewer than experimentally observed deformed states, and note that the energies of the calculated states decrease with increasing values of the minimal length parameter. Furthermore, we evaluate the intrinsic frame rotational parameter, $\cal R$, and find that it is in agreement with experimental values when calculated using the minimal length parameter. Using the Pais-Uhlenbeck gauge, we also determine the energies of the collective many-body states and compare them to experimental data, including both deformed and non-deformed states. This comparison reveals that there is agreement between our calculations and experimental data for certain values of the minimal length parameter, and we find that the collective many-body energies are most accurately described within the context of the quasi-dynamical symmetry approach. Additionally, using the minimal length parameter, we are able to explain the observed ratio of intrinsic frame rotational parameter to experimental rotational parameter values, and find that it is in agreement with theoretical and experimental data for certain values of the minimal length parameter. Finally, calculating the $\cal R$ parameter for a range of states allows us to determine its average value, and we find that the minimal length parameter has a significant effect on its average value when compared to both theoretical and experimental data for neighboring nuclei. Overall, the results of our study indicate that introducing the minimal length parameter into the collective movement of triaxial nuclei results in several beneficial outcomes that are in agreement with experimental data. These outcomes include the inclusion of a many-body nature of the collective movement in theoretical description, the reproduction of the intrinsic frame rotational parameter values, the description of the relative energies of the calculated collective many-body states with respect to experimental data, and the description of the minimal length effects on the average value of the intrinsic frame rotational parameter. One of the notable cases is the description of the minimal length effects on the average $\cal R$ values, and it seems that this issue might be solved with a more general approach to the effective Hamiltonian for the collective movement of deformed nuclei within the minimal length concept.

This study presents an cutting-edge end-to-end deep learning architecture for high-dimensional image change detection, incorporating both spatial and spectral data. By fusing features from a Context Fusion Deep Convolutional Neural Network and a Spectral Fusion Deep Convolutional Neural Network, we are able to capture contextual and spectral patterns within images. These patterns are then combined and fed into a Euclidean Distance Transformer Module, which maps input images to a latent space and identifies patterns specific to changes. A classifier determines the likelihood of changes and rejects stable image segments. We evaluate our approach on the Cleveland Linear Algebra and Computation Laboratory dataset and compare results with state-of-the-art unsupervised change detection methods. Furthermore, we investigate the effectiveness of our architecture through semantic reasoning experiments. Results demonstrate that our approach surpasses current unsupervised change detection techniques and provide insightful semantic interpretations. Moreover, we also compare our approach with supervised deep learning architectures and establish a new standard for high-dimensional image change detection. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/mnptony/CD_HSI_DDeep. With this unsupervised architecture, we can efficiently detect changes within single-channel or multi-channel hyperspectral images with low computational requirements, which is crucial for resource-constrained systems. The contributions of this study are two-fold: (i) the development of a novel unsupervised change detection architecture and (ii) the conduct of semantic reasoning over pattern representation learning experiments in the context of hyperspectral image change detection. In addition, we have identified limitations and possible extensions for future research. Our work is the first to successfully integrate semantic reasoning over pattern representation learning with CD HSI DDeep. The effectiveness of CD HSI DDeep has been extensively evaluated through an open-source two-factor ANOVA analysis to ensure the reliability of our results. The study would have significant practical implications in various applications such as remote sensing, medical imaging, and video analytics, where unsupervised change detection is highly valuable. Ultimately, the study contributes towards the development of more accurate and transparent deep learning-based change detection architectures. A comprehensive study examines how the concept of residual entropy behaves in various molecular models. By analyzing pairs of molecules with known viscosity and temperature relationships, the study demonstrates that a specific temperature exponent is closely linked to liquid viscosity. Additionally, the study evaluates the feasibility of using model potentials based on range of variational theory of molecular liquids (VTML) to predict this exponent and thus, viscosity. Our results indicate that these potential sets can effectively predict the viscosity's temperature dependence, but there is no single VTML setup that accurately accounts for both liquid and gas viscosity in parallel. However, by using a specific potential that combines terms from different VTML concepts, the study shows it's possible to generate a smooth, quantitatively correct viscosity profile that aligns with experimental data across the entire temperature range. This finding highlights the significance of incorporating higher frequency vibrational modes in the high temperature regime. Finally, the study notes that employing model potentials to generate configurations for molecular dynamics simulations can effectively reproduce the system's density and pressure while accurately aligning with VTML's temperature-dependent viscosity characteristics. However, the study shows that to accurately simulate the correct liquid thermodynamic properties, the employed potential needs to be modified further by adjusting its energy characteristics. Our results indicate that by modifying the potential's parity symmetry and allowing the squared distance term to deviate from 1, the study is able to correctly predict the density's temperature dependence and identify a pseudo-liquid-vapor critical point, thus demonstrating that such a potential can effectively capture anisotropic interactions in the range of VTML. Overall, the study effectively shows that by combining elements from different potential sets, the study is able to correctly model molecular liquid viscosity. In pursuit of an optimized, yet robust controller, we develop a method based on distributionally robust optimization. This novel approach to model-based policy search and reinforcement learning treats the parameters of learned dynamic systems as stochastic variables with a specified distribution. Subsequently, the goal of the optimization process is reformulated to minimize the worst-case expected return across a given distribution of system parameters. In line with this new optimization framework, we propose an algorithm that integrates elements of maximum a posteriori estimation, semi-definite programming, and projected gradient descent. Utilizing the ADMM method, this algorithm enables the separation of variables into their optimal policy and parameter equivalents. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields a controller that not only excels in optimized performance but also withstands variations in its operating environment. Furthermore, the associated project code can be accessed at https://github.com/hosseinEajazi/DRRO-MBA. Our evaluation is conducted using the Acropolis robot and two systems from the PyRobot platform, resulting in impressive robustness gains of up to 30% when compared to non-robust, optimized policies. In line with these experimental outcomes, we successfully test the controller on an actual robotic system. Following extensive experimentation, the DRRO-MBA method exhibits reliable performance, efficient computation, and robustness across various numerical simulations, showcasing its exceptional capabilities. In total, our method successfully simulates and tests over 380,000 scenarios, encompassing more than 700 different system parameters, resulting in nearly 24 hours of computation time. Nonetheless, the algorithm displays exceptional stability and achieves its optimal solution without employing any form of convergence analysis, such as convergence regularization or asynchrony compensation. Ultimately, the DRRO-MBA method represents a pioneering, distributionally robust model-based policy search and reinforcement learning approach that seamlessly integrates elements of maximum a posteriori estimation and semi-definite programming to derive a robust, optimized controller. Continual learning with an ensemble method offers online compatibility and the ability to handle streams of data. However, existing ensemble- based methods for continuous learning have overlooked the following key issues:  The main contributor to performance improvement is often lost in the ensemble process, and the stability of the learned representation is highly crucial for continuous learning to succeed. Additionally, most current ensemble- based methods focus on the task level and ignore the feature level, resulting in suboptimal performance. In this study, a Neural Structure for Online Ensemble Continual Learning (NOEC) method is presented which addresses these neglected aspects. Firstly, a task-adaptive MINE module is proposed to extract stable and informative features through random sampling, and its performance is enhanced by incorporating a neural network. Secondly, a Neuron-Cluster Tree (NCT) method is introduced which uses the neurons from different task-specific streams to create cluster nodes and improves the representation quality by leveraging two key components: eliminating redundant cluster nodes and increasing the inter-class distance. Lastly, to accurately predict the output, a Bayesian ensemble method is employed which adds uncertainty to individual models' predictions, and the results are combined using a weighted average. Our proposed NOEC method outperforms existing ensemble- based and state-of-the-art continuous learning methods on four benchmark datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and EMNIST-F. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/sterlin/NOEC. Our study demonstrates that by focusing on the main contributor of performance improvement through neural ensemble and designing a stable and informative feature extraction module by incorporating a neural network, we can achieve superior results in continuous learning. Additionally, by incorporating a Neuron-Cluster Tree method that leverages the neurons from different task-specific streams to create cluster nodes and aims to represent each sample uniquely, we can achieve superior results in continuous learning. Our study is the first to focus on the feature level and utilize the stability of the learned representation for continuous learning to succeed. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/sterlin/NOEC. Our study demonstrates that by incorporating a Neural Structure for Online Ensemble Continual Learning (NOEC) method which addresses the key issues of losing the main contributor of performance improvement and the stability of the learned representation for continuous learning to succeed, we can achieve superior results in continuous learning. Our study is the first to introduce a novel ensemble- based continuous learning method that outperforms existing ensemble- based and state-of-the-art continuous learning methods on four benchmark datasets. This research also contributes to the discussion on bias-v-sensitivity, highlighting the importance of distinguishing between these concepts in machine learning outcomes. Furthermore, it is hoped this method will facilitate the discovery of potential biases in social science research using machine learning. Theoretical investigations were conducted to analyze the conformational flexibility of Sc2TbN@C80, examining multiple configurations on a hydrogen-bonded interface with nickel (111). The results showed that several structural variations could arise due to the movement of the terbium dimer within the molecular cage, with various configurations producing distinct magnetic reflections in scanning tunneling spectroscopy measurements. A key observation indicated that surface stress causes the terbium dimer to shift by about 0.8 nanometers at room temperature, resulting in a notable improvement in magnetic coherence length at this temperature. Conversely, the dimer remains relatively still at 10 Kelvin, with magnetic coherence largely diminished, as shown in the study. The study's findings provide essential insights for designing molecular qubits, keeping in mind the intricate relationship between their structure and magnetic behavior, with temperature-induced conformational changes in qubits offering a pivotal consideration in their development. The study's relevant data and documents can be accessed through the following links: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202008552 (original publication), https://tinyurl.com/yckv3kfu (supplementary information). The study's conclusions for temperature-induced conformational changes in qubits might have a broader applicability beyond the mentioned molecular structure, with various qubits exhibiting a considerable decrease in magnetic coherence at lower temperatures when the terbium dimer is stationary within the molecular cage. Moreover, the study's conclusions identify the potential strategies for enhancing magnetic coherence in a stationary qubit and increasing it in a moving qubit, with numerous qubits featuring a similar crystal field instability and multiple energy levels. The study suggests that using an electric field to adjust the molecular bond could significantly improve the magnetic coherence in a stationary qubit and reduce it in a moving qubit. The study's relevant data and documents can be accessed through the following links: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202008352 (original publication), https://tinyurl.com/ygk2w2j8 (supplementary information). The study's conclusions for designing molecular qubits, with rapid electrical switching enabled by the movement of the molecular dimer, have a key implication that could significantly increase the switching speed by first releasing stress from the molecular qubit and then introducing it into the system by applying a voltage to an adjacent scanning tunneling microscope tip.

In the coming years, the Internet of Things (IoT) network is expected to become vast, consisting of hundreds of billions of devices. These devices, however, will be operating in resource-constrained environments, posing significant security challenges. Specifically, it's anticipated that future IoT applications will require high-security protocols, yet current encryption methods are excessively complex and consume excessive resources, making them unsuitable for deployment. To address this, we introduce an innovative encryption technique, specifically designed for devices with limited resources. This new method utilizes the inner product of vectors and a secret key to generate a random number, which is used for data encryption. As a result, data is transformed into a form that's unreadable to unauthorized parties, while maintaining the integrity of the original message. Notably, this technique requires minimal computational power and connection bandwidth. To quantify its efficiency, we evaluated its computational and connection demands, demonstrating that it consumes 99.7% less energy and 91.4% less connection bandwidth than existing methods, such as AES. Additionally, we implemented the technique on 13 different hardware platforms and assessed its resilience to various attacks, revealing that it's highly secure. Specifically, it's capable of producing over 1600 instances per second, offering a high level of security and usability. We are, however, the first to document this technique, known as the Linear Inner Product Encryption (LIPE), specifically in 2021. Since then, a more advanced variation of LIPE, known as the LIPE with Multiple Linearly Independent Vectors (MLIPE), was introduced in 2022, offering enhanced security and higher processing capabilities. To facilitate future research, we've made available open-source code for both LIPE and MLIPE. As an additional measure to safeguard IoT applications, we've implemented both LIPE and MLIPE on 12 distinct hardware platforms, but unfortunately, have not found them suitable for use in applications such as AES or SHA-256. Specifically, both LIPE and MLIPE fail the PHP security standard due to certain theoretical security vulnerabilities that remain unresolved. We continue to actively work to address these concerns and ensure that these techniques provide secure IoT applications. We're pleased to report, however, that both LIPE and MLIPE have been successfully deployed in real-world applications such as encryption of medical data, encryption of location data, encryption of fitness tracking data, or encryption of financial records, revealing the high security and efficiency offered by these techniques. Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality metric is developed called Gromov centrality, based on the notion that shortest path distances encapture a broad view of network topology while local triangle inequalities hold tighter at further distances, allowing for more nuanced measurements. Gromov centrality is found to capture mesoscale properties more effectively than other metrics and its computational efficiency enables its application to large networks, exceeding the performance of other metrics in many real-world network cases. Additionally, Gromov centrality is supplemented by a fast approximation called Gromov Approximate centrality (GAP), providing efficient calculations for even the largest available networks in various domains. Both Gromov and GAP gain substantial advantages over other metrics when the network is partitioned due to strong degree correlations, specifically the nature of 'rich club' structures found in the Facebook and Twitter platforms. Furthermore, Gromov centrality and GAP exhibit superior performance in comparative studies on synthetic and real-world networks across multiple dimensions, demonstrating their potential for practical network analysis and applications. The Gromov centrality and GAP functions are also made freely available for download and online use at gromovcentrality.com. From a diffusive perspective, Gromov centrality is further developed into Diffusion Centrality, discovered to be the steady-state score of a unique diffusion process with distinct properties, independent of the standard PageRank algorithmic implementation and therefore applicable to distinct network scales. The diffusion process underlying Gromov centrality shares certain qualities with the established Lanczos algorithm and therefore its diffusion calculations can be optimized similar to the PageRank method for efficient algorithmic implementation and application. The diffusion centrality metric exhibits significant improvements over other metrics in various real-world network cases across multiple dimensions, encompassing distinct data types (unweighted, weighted, signed), structures (scale-free, random, bipartite) and characteristics (dynamically changing, delayed information propagation, information propagation direction). In graph theory, a weighted graph is considered representable if its distances can be expressed using a subset of the distances in a specific tree structure. Building on previous research that showed treewidth as a single criterion for representability of bipartite subgraphs, this study introduces new criteria specifically for planar and minor-free metrics, using treewidth as a primary indicator, along with other constraints regarding the structure of H-gaps. These new criteria provide necessary and sufficient conditions for representability, and they achieve the best possible bounds on the treewidth, demonstrating how it affects the complexity of computing compact representations in graphs. A new approach to learning encoder maps is developed, drawing inspiration from the concept of self-organizing maps. The approach involves representing the data distribution in a prior distribution with latent variables, and encoders are mapped to this distribution by collecting samples from a data posterior. The Rissanen-Lakshminarayanan variational free energy principle is used to guide the learning process, and the method is extended to handle complex high-dimensional images under the assumption that images can be approximated as a mixture of relatively simple factors. The proposed deep generative encoder (DGE) is tested on image compression and the results are found to be comparable to state-of-the-art models such as annealed depth-wise autoencoders and vector quantized vaes. Furthermore, evidence is presented that shows how the DGE can be used to improve the performance of other models, such as VAEs and generative adversarial networks, by priorizing latent factors through joint prior matching. The code to implement the DGE is available at github.com/tkrog/depth-generative-encoder. As an additional step, the code also supports training of a new hybrid model, the hybrid generative encoder (HGE), which combines aspects of VAEs and GANs, and facilitates unsupervised learning of the data distribution priors using the mode-seeking procedure. The HGE is found to perform better than current GAN models in producing high-quality image data. The choice of using maps for latent variables or the efficacy of the mode-seeking procedure can be determined experimentally. The proposed approach is expandable to handle multi-frame data sequences under the assumption that these can be represented as a dynamic factor graph, and the resulting model is found to perform better than state-of-the-art methods in predicting image sequences. The choice of using the DGE or HGE to achieve this is dependent on whether prior regularization is used or not. The full details of the approach are available at the following webpage: https://sites.google.com/view/neuroimage2022-lgae. The deep generative encoder is implemented using the LightLight library, which is a Python framework for fast and efficient learning of factor graphs. The library is available for download at http://www.ckunzelmann.com/lightlight. We've generated predictions for the stochastic gravitational-wave background that could emerge from an inflationary theory with specific characteristics. These theories, known as double-humped inflation, produce two distinct periods of inflation and exhibit two distinct behaviors during the post-inflationary era. When compared to recent data collected by the NANOGrav collaboration, our findings suggest that such inflationary models may be preferred over single-field inflationary models, with potential amplitudes that match or exceed current LIGO-Virgo sensitivity. We've also found that even small "stiffness" components in these models can significantly increase the GW power within the frequency range detected by LIGO-Virgo and contribute to alleviating the current discrepancy between Hubble constant measurements derived from type-Ia supernovae and CMB observations. We've further demonstrated that such inflationary theories are compatible with various recent constraints and data sets. Finally, our findings emphasize the considerable potential of future joint GW-EM work with the JWST and LSST to thoroughly examine and assess different inflationary models. These claims are based on an intricate mathematical analysis involving novel methods of integrating the GW power spectrum and a sophisticated numerical approach used to compute its approximate marginal posterior distributions, with the inclusion of relevant data set constraints and priors. We've also developed a fast, stand-alone computational tool allowing its user to rapidly calculate contraction rates for any chosen data set, including those yet to be collected by the SQMS, JSNS, PicoLus, DECIGO, and other prospective gravitational-wave projects. We anticipate that this tool will be utilized extensively in forthcoming research on gravitational waves. The tool is seamlessly integrated with the existing Python package cactusresearch, which is used to simulate and analyze a variety of astrophysical and cosmological phenomena. These functions form part of a larger platform known as the CACTUS RESEARCH suite, which is accessible for free at its official Git repository via the following link: https://github.com/Prof-Fraser/CactusResearch. A more in-depth discussion of the research, including the underlying data generation and analysis as well as the CACTUS RESEARCH tool itself, is now available in the form of a comprehensive, 76 page document, which can be downloaded from the following location: https://www.dropbox.com/s/jy0d0kvnpn1f40/FrameworkDocument.pdf. A more formal presentation of this research will be published in an upcoming paper, which is now available at its official dropbox location: https://www.dropbox.com/s/7s

We suggest an unsupervised method to develop high-quality speech synthesis models directly from large speech corpus, without requiring manually annotated transcripts. Our approach is based on the following observation: when we randomly swap the text associated with speech waves in a corpus, we can determine the duration of the speech segments simply by checking if the text follows the natural sequence. This can be further represented by a weighted measure of the likelihood that the sequence of words appears in the corpus, given the duration of the speech segments. By incorporating the influence of the duration information on the text sequence using an unsupervised neural model, we can generate speech samples based on text. Our experiment using the Librispeech corpus indicates that our proposed model produces speech that is closer to human quality compared to a previously established method. The source code for our method can be found at https://github.com/andrearocca/unsupervised_speech_synthesis. Our model also won the Librispeech challenge in the unsupervised category in 2021. The pre-trained models can be downloaded from https://andrearocca.github.io/unified_speech_synthesis/. When testing the model with out-of-vocabulary words, we were able to create the first unsupervised speech synthesis system that can generalize its capabilities. The model's ability to create non-existent words was validated through a listening test, where a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.12 was recorded for the following word 'vizier', which was not present in the corpus. This result presents our method as a groundbreaking system in the field of the unsupervised speech synthesis. The model's ability to create the natural-sounding 'vizier' can be attributed to its ability to learn the duration-based proxy for the unsupervised neural model. A further listening test revealed that our method delivered a mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.76. This result proved to be higher than that of the FastSpeech2 model, which managed an MOS of 3.53 as a result of the normal category. This outcome clearly indicates that our method delivered the unsupervised model with the higher quality. The reason behind the lower performance of the FastSpeech2 model lies in its a combination of the sequence generator and duration generator, which are trained in an alternating manner. This training strategy fails to effectively utilize the duration information in the speech synthesis. A novel algorithm, combining multi-criteria branch-and-bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, is proposed for approximating Pareto fronts for such problems. A computational study, comparing this technique with non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, demonstrates its efficacy on a set of test cases. A hierarchical architecture is implemented to optimize computational efficiency, incorporating a branch-and-bound method with screening criteria and an approximation algorithm employing non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2. Results obtained from applying this algorithm to a set of test cases indicate that it effectively identifies high-quality solutions for multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems. A theoretical convergence analysis of this algorithm is also provided. Furthermore, a practical example in mechanical engineering serves to illustrate its practical applications. The proposed algorithm, having been implemented in C++, is made freely available at github.com/touka777/BO-NSGAII under the terms of the MIT licence. A player-based interactive application, incorporating a graphical user interface, is also provided to facilitate user interaction and visual analysis of results. A peer review of the algorithm, incorporating performance assessment and usability evaluation, was conducted. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the specific aspect of a product or service that gives rise to positive or negative opinions as expressed in a review. While earlier approaches relied solely on identifying the aspect in question, recent studies reveal that capturing implicit emotional patterns is essential for accurately assessing sentiment on that aspect. Unfortunately, due to the implicit nature of emotional patterns, extracting them from unlabelled data proves to be extremely difficult. In order to unlock the potential of implicit emotional patterns for aspect-based sentiment analysis, we employed a supervised pre-training approach that leverages both sentence-level and aspect-level positive-negatives pairs to derive models that can automatically extract emotional patterns from reviews. Specifically, our method involves utilizing a BERT-based model to generate positive-negatives pairs in reviews through a masked language modelling task. Subsequently, another fully connected network is used to classify these pairs at the sentence and word levels, ultimately producing a structured understanding of implicit emotional patterns in reviews. Experiments conducted on two public datasets reveal that our method achieves a notable 2.17 and 3.14 percentage points improvement in MACF1 score when compared to a competing baseline that relies on explicit emotion extraction. Moreover, by evaluating our method on an open-source dataset focusing on emotional patterns, we demonstrate its ability to effectively generalize these patterns in the context of aspect-based sentiment analysis, ultimately yielding superior results. Specifically, our method surpasses the baseline by 5.11 and 6.99 percentage points in terms of MACF1 score on the Huawei dataset. The results of our studyemphasize the valuable insights that implicit emotional patterns can provide in aspect-based sentiment analysis. Moreover, our method has significant potential to unlock the full potential of implicit patterns in this context, further stimulating research in this area. The proposed method has been successfully incorporated into a state-of-the-art model for aspect-based sentiment analysis and review rating, ultimately enabling our approach to achieve superior results on two public datasets and surpass recently published state-of-the-art methods. We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate under constraints for the base station's power output and RIS element limitations.
To address this optimization challenge, we split the problem into two subproblems for subchannel allocation and phase shift optimization, solving each problem using the block coordinate descent technique.
The first subproblem involves optimizing the base station's beamforming vectors to achieve the highest possible secrecy rate at each subchannel, formulated as an optimization problem with linear constraints.
Using the dual decomposition framework, we convert the problem into a simpler optimization challenge that is solved via the dual variable update and the minimum power design methods.
For the second subproblem, we optimize the phase shifts to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate at each subchannel, formulated as an optimization problem with fixed base station's beamforming vectors.
Using the alternating minimization technique, we solve for the optimal phase shifts.

This paper seeks to make progress in the field of multilingual incident extraction, a significant requirement for monitoring violent events like terrorist activities and civil unrest. The method developed is straightforward: given a date, domain, and language, it recommends relevant news articles from online databases. Two datasets were created that label, evaluate, and compare the performance of incident extraction methods: one in English and another in four other languages, spanning news articles from newsagencies (Reuters, Al Jazeera, and France 24) and social media platforms (Twitter). The evaluation process involves assessing models' ability to accurately classify news articles as either incident-related or not, and their capacity to predict incident labels. The engagement with these datasets is expected to facilitate future advancements in this area of research. The theoretical ether, once a fundamental concept in physics that has long since been disproven, is still influenced by its historical significance within the community. Despite this, modern ether theories hold promise of contributing to our understanding of quantum gravity and the behavior of matter at extremely high energies or low temperatures. We've established a unitary ether theory and demonstrated its compatibility with the principles of special relativity, thereby providing a framework for investigating quantum gravity. We've also determined that at energy levels above 1 TeV, ether interactions become significantly weak, and are essentially non-observable in line with current experimental evidence. However, ether interactions may become apparent or even dominant in hypothetical scenarios such as ultra-high energy collisions or at temperatures approaching Planck levels. We've leveraged the finite temperature quantum path integral formalism to derive a renowned anomaly in quantum gravity, and demonstrated that the ether's interactions with photons are significantly intensified at extremely low temperatures in accordance with quantum gravity principles. We've also analyzed the possibility of stimulated ethereal emission, and discovered that while the ether's interactions with photons are intensely strong at Planck temperatures, they are highly diminished at 1 TeV, and virtually non-existent at temperatures in the muon range. We've further explored the potential for ether collisions to occur, and confirmed that the ether's interactions with hadrons are extremely weak at temperatures in the GeV range. We've also analyzed the ether's interactions with neutrinos and electromagnetically neutral force carriers, and confirmed that the latter exhibit the strongest ethereal interactions, with a potential to be observable in high-energy muon colliders if constructed. We've also determined that the ether's interactions with photons are extremely weak at very low temperatures in the spin wave regime, and confirmed that the ether's interactions are inherently non-abelian in nature. Our findings demonstrate, therefore, that the ether remains an highly relevant concept in contemporary physics, and one that may yet yield significant insights into quantum gravity and the behavior of matter at extremely high energies or low temperatures. Early-type galaxies with minimal spatial structure or distorted shapes, resulting from gravitational interactions, are indicative of a significant gravitational impact. Using the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey, we conducted a research on 183 massive (solar mass less than 10^13), massive (solar mass greater than 10^13), and extremely massive (solar mass greater than 5*10^13)) early-type galaxy samples to explore their surface distortion patterns. The analysis revealed a high frequency of distorted shapes in galaxies of all three mass categories, with more than 80% exhibiting surface deformation. By focusing on extremely massive galaxies (solar mass greater than 5*10^13)), we found over 54% had more than 10 percent of their light emitted from unresolved gridded particles, suggesting a significant gravitational impact. Through the analysis of surface distortion patterns in these galaxies, we estimated a merger rate of approximately 3.56*10^-15 year^-1, yielding a significant gravitational impact within one billion years. The merger rates for galaxy interactions or mergers, with mass ratios of 1:1 or 1:5, respectively, are significantly lower than expected based on previous research, with values of 0.787 and 0.164 year^-1, respectively. The reasons for these low rates are not fully understood but may be explained by a relatively short detection window in our study. Alternatively, the low rates may be a natural consequence of galaxies undergoing major mergers and rapidly upping their mass, thus being removed from the sample, or through the action of black holes releasing gravitational energy, resulting in earlier than expected gravitational impacts, or by a predominance of resonant or oblique interactions resulting in little or no gravitational energy release for masses within a specific range. Additionally, the low rates may also be explained by a phenomenon where interacting galaxies avoid direct hits with each other or with masses within a specific range, thus not resulting in either merger or interaction. More data and analysis are needed to  determine the reasons for these low rates, particularly by distinguishing between the two interaction types. The analysis of surface distortion patterns and estimated merger rates for galaxies of all three mass categories will be made available through a series of tables.

This surprising discovery is achieved through the coordination of established formulas covering the conservation of energy, optical properties, and laser cavity mechanics. This results in replacing the current optical components with equivalent ones that reduce the cost of producing optical pulses by 1 order of magnitude. Both our design and reverse engineering techniques could greatly benefit the development of advanced laser systems such as next-generation laser pulse sources for medical and scientific applications. This benefit could also extend to the development of advanced directional optical transmitters for wireless communication systems. We introduce a text-based image description task where participants view an image and a set of incomplete description starting phrases via a language model, with the goal of generating an accurate description. By fine-tuning multiple language models with our proposed method, we achieve significant improvements in completion and generation quality, leading to more accurate and natural outcomes. We also conduct fairness and diversity assessments, revealing that our approach enhances the model's consistency in its visual and linguistic representations, thus promoting semantic alignment and decreasing redundant content. Moreover, we demonstrate that our strategy promotes equity and diversity in the generated text. We release our code and an example dataset at https://github.com/allenai/eye-infer. We extensively evaluate our framework through multiple experiments and offer valuable insights on successfully incorporating visual observation into text-based image description tasks. The experiment results indicate that by treating a language model as an observational agent, we can generate more realistic and detailed descriptions that surpass prior results in the field. We also identify key challenges and outline our strategy to address them in the introduction. Our framework can be applied to various other visual and linguistic tasks to enhance performance. We visually illustrate the description generation process in the demo section and showcase the significant improvements in the pre-trained model's output quality in the demo's figures. We thoroughly analyze and achieve substantial gains in description completion and generation quality, surpassing previous state-of-the-art outcomes. We also introduce and conduct a comprehensive study on the impact of visual observation on a language model's performance, examining various degrees and types of observation in multiple controlled experiments. The study reveals that observation can lead to improved understanding and accuracy in the model's generated text. We identify key limitations of the initial framework, specifically its susceptibility to errors and biased input, which can negatively affect the model's performance and output quality. To address these challenges, we propose and apply several countermeasures that significantly enhance the model's robustness and result in more consistent and accurate text generation. Ultimately, our framework demonstrates that by incorporating visual observation into description generation, we can achieve substantial and consistent improvements in the generated text's quality and realism. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme entails two primary encryptions: a ring signature and an address hiding method.
We optimize Delegated RingCT by integrating it with Shamsi Farahabadi et al.'s RingCT framework leveraging Lazy Signatures.
As a result, Delegated RingCT significantly boosts transaction verification speed on top of existing Bitcoin forks like Bitcoin Cash.
Moreover, our research demonstrates the merged Delegated RingCT and Lazy Signatures framework resists various attack strategies including ring signature merging attacks and transaction rewriting.
Additionally, Delegated RingCT enjoys advantage in addressing the block size limitation as transactions are verified individually. 
In comparison, combining Delegated RingCT with Lazy Signatures yields superior performance when compared to combining RingCT with nScript in terms of transaction size and confirmation rate. 
In particular, Delegated RingCT at Bitcoin Cash achieves transaction verification rate of 1 second and $0.125 per transaction on average. 
Consequently, Delegated RingCT effectively strikes a balance between anonymity and transaction processing efficiency. 
Lastly, Delegated RingCT source code has been made public on GitHub which facilitates further research and development in this area. 
Furthermore, our research has been conducted as part of an ongoing project at University of Tehran's Computer Engineering Department, Iran. 
As such, Delegated RingCT presents a cutting-edge research outcome and a cutting-edge practical solution in this domain which requires further exploration. This paper presents a novel optimization technique for training quantized neural networks by exploiting properties of the quantization function, thus ensuring the uniqueness of the subgradients. Our method maintains the subgradient nature of the quantization operator, resulting in the local first-order optimality of the problem being reduced to a 1-dimensional search within the interval defined by the quantization steps. This enables our approach to outperform existing methods both in terms of efficiency and quality of solutions. Additionally, we further improve upon this idea by integrating it with existing state-of-the-art techniques. With our proposed solution, the requirement of iterating over the network parameters in each computation batch has been eliminated, resulting in significant time and memory savings, thus making it more suitable for large-scale implementation. Our method consistently surpasses existing approaches and achieves impressive performance, even when integrated with other state-of-the-art techniques. Our implementation details, including the code and experimental results, are made available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/AbhishekAbhi/AskewSGD.git. While a major advantage of soft robots is their ability to work in hazardous environments, their reliability is often compromised by their tendency to change shape unpredictably, even during tasks, as well as their limited ability to recover from injuries. Additionally, the process of planning a soft robot's movement is complex and time-consuming due to its intricate geometry. The Jacobi group $\mathrm{GJ}_{\rho,\tau}$ - specifically its Lie algebra - has been re-examined and re-defined using unitary ray space operations that closely resemble those of its predecessor. A straightforward implementation of its Lie algebra operations yields simplified expressions in line with its historical definition in terms of specific unitary transformations. Additionally, some underlying connections between $\mathrm{GJ}_{\rho,\tau}$ and $\mathrm{SL}(2,\rho)$ have been identified and elaborated. Furthermore, key properties of the Haar measure and Weyl integration on $\mathrm{GJ}_{\rho,\tau}$ with weight $\tau^{DJ(A)}$ are described. As a result, integrals of the form $\int_{\mathrm{GJ}_{\rho,\tau}} \mathcal{F}(A) d\mu(A)$ - including those involving radon-Nikodym derivatives - can be solved in a manner that generalizes the Casimir element. Meaningful applications to Jacobians of polynomial functions and affine semigroups are also presented. Extending this work to specific domains of $\mathbb{C}^n$ using a suitable ordering has also been successful. Interestingly, defining the Haar measure on $\mathrm{GJ}_{\rho,\tau}$ results in a highly simplified expression - one that is far more streamlined than the one-dimensional case, let alone its counterparts in several variables. Using the new and revised $\mathrm{GJ}_{\rho,\tau}$ - specifically its Haar measure - many problems involving unitary transforms of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\rho)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ can now be expressed in terms of explicit integrals over these groups. As a direct consequence, many special and non-special functions, including those that generalize the Bernoulli and Euler polynomials, are now expressed in entirely new and novel ways. Extending these results to specific domains of $\mathbb{C}^n$ using a suitable ordering has also been successful, resulting in many new and novel applications. Ultimately, defining the Jacobi Lie algebra on the unitary ray space provides the foundation for a more general and flexible approach - one that includes many groundbreaking results in a highly simplified and improved manner. Verifying structured knowledge facts held within semi-structured documents poses significant difficulties due to their blended content of text and layout. To address this issue, we develop a novel approach that separates and reorganizes (disassembles) a document to simplify fact identification, employing a sequential decoder that iteratively asks targeted questions about individual cells to achieve accurate verification. By utilizing a relatively small set of controlled questions, our method demonstrates superior fact verification performance on a range of datasets across diverse domains. Additionally, we establish a new benchmark for fact verification and release further documentation, including code and data, for reproduction purposes. Experimental results, document analysis, and user studies confirm the efficacy of our approach. It's found that, despite limited question variety, our method consistently verifies facts with high accuracy in a range of scenarios and environments. Importantly, the majority of facts contained within document tables are simple numerical values, making fact verification even more efficient and practical. To further enhance and refine our method, we explore the application of more advanced abductive reasoning techniques, including existing methods and novel combinations, and investigate the potential for generating new questions beyond those in the initial training dataset. Finally, through comprehensive evaluation experiments, the combined method demonstrates improved performance and efficiency, surpassing the baseline performance achieved by the initial disassembly-based approach and outperforming competing state-of-the-art fact verification methods. It's found that (i) the majority of errors committed by the initial method arise due to specific and predictable cell content mismatches, (ii) the use of sequential reasoning and enhanced disassembly contributes significantly to improved performance, (iii) the incorporation of structured knowledge and more advanced disassembly strategies has a positive impact on accuracy and efficiency, and (iv) the application of advanced combinatorial reasoning and hyper-encoding techniques through the use of external knowledge and large-scale language models holds promise for further enhancements, albeit to a lesser extent. Ultimately, the analysis highlights the importance of incorporating structured content representation and layman-friendly question design to facilitate more accurate and efficient fact verification. We strongly believe that these proposed enhancements will lead to further breakthroughs and the development of more robust and reliable fact verification methods in the future. We look forward to seeing future research pursue these leads! To speed up nested sampling by leveraging information from prior distributions, researchers have introduced various step selectors. We investigate how different step selectors, including dempled nested sampling, adaptive methods, and empirical Bayes techniques, affect the efficiency of nested sampling. Our analysis reveals that choosing the most informative steps leads to the highest sampling efficiency regardless of the prior distribution's form. Simply selecting the highest likelihood steps from each level replicates some established nested sampling methods' behavior. We develop practical methods to apply this advanced step selection approach, considering both the computational ease and the potential trade-offs, such as using the maximum likelihood estimator as an efficient yet reliable option. Our finding sheds light on the underlying logic of previous work and provides a straightforward, computationally airtight solution for improving nested sampling's efficiency. We demonstrate this improvement through various synthetic and real-world examples, including the application of BAYESHOP. Additionally, we release relevant open-source software to facilitate future research.

In graph distance labeling, each vertex is assigned a label that represents its distance to neighboring vertices. This concept has practical uses in network planning, medical imaging, and image processing. Our research extends the distance labeling framework to accommodate vertex faults, where the label of an affected vertex may be skewed due to incorrect distance information. A fault-tolerant vertex set is needed to ensure that no two faulty vertices have the same label. Our work focuses on determining the minimum number of non-faulty vertices required to prevent label conflicts caused by faults. On planar graphs, we established a tight bound of n + ε(n) where ε(n) is a function that decreases as n increases. For specific types of faults, we improved the fault tolerance by an order of magnitude. Furthermore, we discovered that the case of faults involving only a single neighbor yields significantly better results, with a bound of 6ln n + O(1), which is close to the optimal 6ln n + O(1) for the general fault case, as well as for faults involving up to k-1 neighbors, with a bound of (1 + 1/k)n + O(1). These results represent the first known explicit bounds for the general fault case, as well as for faults involving up to k-1 neighbors. Our work includes designing a minimization graph labeling problem, which we proved to be NP-hard. This problem can be transformed into a set cover problem with specific properties, and by applying the existing bounds for set cover we obtained the bounds for graph labeling. Our work also includes the development of a polynomial-time algorithm that approximates the minimum number of faults that can tolerate n + ε(n) non-faulty vertices, with an excess of at most ln n + ln ln n over this bound. Similarly, we devised a polynomial-time algorithm that approximates the minimum number of faults that can tolerate 6ln n + O(1) faults, with an excess of at most 5ln n + ln ln n over this bound. We also presented the first known explicit bound for the case of unit disk cover, with a bound of 48ln n + O(1). Our work includes the development of a geometric labeling framework in the unit disk geometry. We find that dissipation causes positive and negative correlations to fluctuate at the same rate. Additionally, we observe in the long run that the amplitude of frequency fluctuations grows in direct proportion to the square root of the average number of particles, while the frequency shift remains unaffected. Notably, the duration of the initial buildup phase in the time-evolved correlation function is determined by the rate at which dissipation occurs, an insight that can be further validated through numerical simulations. Applying the Schwinger boson mean field approach, we are able to accurately describe the time-evolution of correlations in our system. We even identify conditions under which the system can exhibit condensate revival and further investigate the critical behavior that arises due to dissipation through an effective R-matrix theory. Ultimately, the system may exhibit irreversible behavior as dissipation outweighs the effects of driving, at which point the system can no longer regain its initial state. To identify out-of-distribution samples, we must recognize when they do not conform to the data we've collected. This can be achieved by assessing the likelihood of a new sample adhering to the data we've gathered, which is known as epistemic uncertainty. Training data-generated models, such as those employing Gaussian Processes, often yields uncertainty that originates from this epistemic type. Nonetheless, when presented with out-of-distribution samples, their uncertainty stems from a combination of epistemic and task-irrelevant uncertainty sources (exogenous uncertainty). Consequently, relying solely on uncertainty as an out-of-distribution detector may lead to false positives. We introduce the concept of "strata": hierarchical layers of training data that separate in-distribution from out-of-distribution samples. By leveraging predictive distributions from Gaussian Processes, we construct a hierarchical structure known as the Distributional GP Strata (D-GP Strata). Each D-GP Strata represents a layer in a data hierarchy, indicating which GP model should be employed to classify a given sample - an in-distribution or out-of-distribution example, or further refinement is required. This hierarchical approach corresponds to varying GP models' complexities, as reflected in their input spaces and GP kernel specifications. Experimental findings on both synthetic and real-world out-of-distribution identification tasks confirm the utility of hierarchical uncertainty for identifying out-of-distribution examples and demonstrate that selected D-GP Strata decisions are comparable to uncertainty-based methods and detection models that incorporate energy-distance metrics. Additionally, we demonstrate that D-GP Strata systems can be easily adapted to avoid incorrect out-of-distribution detections by re-training GP models. Our projected framework, incorporating D-GP Strata and DP-GMS, provides a flexible and reliable method for identifying out-of-distribution samples and holds potential for future extensions. The proposed approach is implemented in the Python language and is made available through an open-source software repository (https://github.com/alexk42/out-of-distribution identification). Our findings indicate that uncertainty from Gaussian Processes, when applied in a layered manner, can effectively identify out-of-distribution samples. Furthermore, our research highlights uncertainty sources as a reliable indicator of out-of-distribution examples, as opposed to relying solely on predictive uncertainty. Finally, the utility of hierarchical uncertainty and GP models for identifying out-of-distribution samples underscores their value in machine learning applications. Quantum systems driven periodically exhibit either regular cycling about their initial state or stick to specific trajectories, known as "quantum scars." A relatively unexplored area of research involves the behavior of multiple-particle systems that are driven and interact with their surroundings. In our study, we examine the response of a collection of bosons within a slowly-driven optical lattice with a weak connection to a broader environment. We observe a phenomenon where a large number of bosons form a unique state, known as a "Floquet eigenstate," that is characterized by entanglement with the environment and exhibits "Floquet heating." As more bosons are added to the system, they condense into this unique state, which persists in the system for an extended period of time. Through theoretical models, we identify the underlying causes of this phenomenon as the combination of "environment-induced protection" and "flux-driven interactions" within the system. Ultimately, the system reaches a stable equilibrium where the heat it loses to the environment equals the energy it gains from the driving source, which we demonstrate. Our study presents a pioneering example of how the interplay of external driving and interactions with the environment can lead to the formation of complex many-body states. Additionally, we propose a range of theoretical models in which the phenomenon we've observed could potentially arise, offering a starting point for future research in this area. In the end, the phenomenon we've observed is shown to be experimentally verifiable using current technology involving ultracold atoms within an optical lattice. One of the key benefits of the approach we've taken is that it allows us to accurately modeling systems that are difficult to study due to their complexity, involving interactions with the environment and multiple particles, by combining theoretical models with the data from the simulations. These simulations involve the extension of the theories behind quantum mechanics, including the "density matrix renormalization group" and "quantum Boltzmann hierarchy," to account for the driving of the system and its interactions with the environment. We've also demonstrated that one of the criteria that long-lived quantum scars require are "degenerate Floquet eigenstates" can be fulfilled in our model, opening up the possibility for the approach we've taken to be used in the study of quantum scars. Our study combines the approaches of solving quantum problems using the density matrix renormalization group and the modeling of the behavior of systems that interact with the environment using quantum Boltzmann hierarchy. By combining these approaches, we've been able to study how the interactions between the system and the environment affect its physical properties

For the reliability and maintenance of offshore wind farms, it's crucial to predict the stress of wind turbines during long-lasting storms, which several years ago led to the failure of some turbines due to fatigue. In engineering studies focused on evaluating the reliability of offshore wind turbines, computational simulations of the turbines and the surrounding environment are often used. These complex computations require high-performance computing and last around months, which is why researchers typically only analyze a limited number of scenarios. In order to improve this limitation, we suggest combining two Gaussian process methods. The first method involves incorporating uncertainty to the input data by utilizing alternative Gaussian processes that are based on few observed values. The second method involves utilising a nested approach that allows the evaluation of uncertainties through the sampling of the first Gaussian process, the selection of the most reliable simulations, and the further analysis by means of a second Gaussian process that only considers the most confident results. By applying these methods to the stress simulations of a specific offshore wind turbine, we managed to increase the accuracy in the prediction of stress thresholds by approximately 7% compared to traditional Gaussian process methods. The implementation of these advanced Gaussian process methods has been developed within the open-source framework UQLAB, which is specifically designed for the evaluation of uncertainties in computational simulations. Furthermore, a direct comparison with other uncertainty quantification methods used in the literature shows that these advanced Gaussian process methods outperform them in terms of accuracy and computational requirements. The main advantage of these methods consists in the fast sampling times that allow post-hoc reliability analysis and reliability calculations that only last a few seconds, which is why they can be considered a viable alternative to the time-consuming Monte-Carlo simulations used in the past. The presented methods represent an essential advancement for the evaluation of reliability of offshore wind turbines, which in turn has significant economic implications given the growing investment in offshore wind energy sources. The development of these advanced Gaussian process methods has been applied to the evaluation of reliability of several structural systems, which thanks to these methods have become more resilient due to the precise calculation of failure probabilities. The implementation of these methods can be accessed through the following repository within the UQLAB framework: https://www.github.com/UQLAB/chainedGPs. In the following document, we have further described the main concepts that led to the development of these methods by referring to the related literature and the underlying physics of the problem, which in this case consists in the numerical simulation of the stress of offshore wind turbines. Social media platforms provide invaluable insights into public opinions on various topics, encompassing emotions, sentiments, trends, and much more, which can be leveraged for diverse purposes such as marketing, news reporting, research, and forecasting. This study focuses on analyzing Twitter posts in relation to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to explore users' emotional states and their spatial correlation on the earthquake-affected region. To achieve this, we employed a multilayer graph graph analytics tool to analyze the temporal and affective dynamics of the Twitter data. By examining the most active users and areas of highest engagement, we were able to extract significant temporal and affective patterns. The results revealed intriguing temporal and emotional trends among the tweeting population, also highlighting the geographical dimensions of the emotions expressed on Twitter. This study contributes valuable knowledge to researchers, practitioners, and decision-makers, offering significant implications for future public engagement and emotional intelligence applications during crisis periods. Furthermore, our analysis provides spatially-aware emotional analysis by integrating the temporal and geographical dimensions of the emotions on Twitter. By combining these dimensions, we can achieve a more comprehensive understanding of the emotions on Twitter, enabling more accurate and spatially-informed emotion detection and analysis. The remaining chapters of this study delve into more advanced techniques for emotion detection and sentiment analysis. These chapters utilize supervised machine learning approaches, trained on annotated datasets, to examine and compare different emotional dimension representations on Twitter, ultimately training a model to forecast emotional patterns using reinforcement learning. The results show that emotional dimension representation has a considerable impact on the performance of the emotion classification model. Moreover, we found that deep neural networks yield better results than traditional machine learning methods for emotion classification tasks. Also, we found that time-based feature vectors are more suitable for emotion classification than word-based vectors, also showing that deep neural networks exhibit superior performance in forecasting emotional patterns. The results of this study can contribute to various future studies on emotion detection and classification on Twitter, offering significant implications for decision-makers and the Izmir earthquake case study. This paper presents a new dataset, SceNDD, consisting of multiple driving scenario categories, observing participants' natural behaviors in distinct situations. In this paper, we propose a new approach to classify driving scenarios based on their underlying attributes and present a comprehensive analysis from the perspective of driving situations. Our approach identifies multiple scenario categories as potential driving situations and collects relevant demographics and driving-related information, recorded through self-reporting and automated feedback loops. Our methodology for extracting driving situation data involves expert annotation and quantitative analysis, and demonstrates the effectiveness of scenario categories and demographic and driving behavior characteristics across varying scenario types. Additionally, an assessment of inconsistencies in expert annotations reveals that driving situation-related tasks exhibit relatively higher levels of agreement compared to other factors. Also, differences in demographics and driving behaviors have moderate to strong significant correlations with scenario categories, while lower but still significant correlations exist for other factors. Finally, from a usability perspective, results show that participants can easily understand and accurately perform the proposed task, but may exhibit some difficulty with time-to-intersection estimates. The Integral Variation Theorem is a significant discovery that establishes a connection between the action of a group on a unitary system and the system's spectral characteristics. This article refines the Single Energy Measurement (SEM) version of the Integral Variation Theorem to demonstrate its practicality in non-projective measurements. SEM's proof surpasses the original IT in three ways: it doesn't rely on continuous group actions, doesn't require unitary system definition, and doesn't involve Hilbert space assumptions. Additionally, SEM's proof generalizes to non-commuting Hamiltonians. We also provide examples illustrating that, despite its strengths, SEM has limitations, particularly in its inapplicability to measurements that fail to detect. In fact, SEM can be seen as a continuous-measurement variant of the Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle, with consistently analogous bounds. Finally, SEM is generalized to the Equivalence Principle of Quantum Theory (EQT), with implications that extend beyond the scope of this present work. In particular, EQT suggests that non-EM measurements can induce massless particle distributions. Since this suggestion is at odds with established principles, it is meant for exploration in future studies. EQT also implies that EQT's antecedents hold considerable significance in the context of Emergent Quantum Mechanics (EQM). Moreover, EQT generates novel queries regarding EQM's (re)construction of quantum theories. In particular, EQT poses a question regarding the potential for EQM to identify and separate consistent from inconsistent Hamiltonians. In other words, can EQM successfully build a consistent quantum theory from an existing Hamiltonian? In light of EQT's query, this work is classified as theory development. General distribution models that go beyond EM are explored; these models encompass EQT instances. Relevant analysis of EQT's suggestions in the context of EQM and EQT is included in the related work section. Furthermore, EQT's suggestions in the related work section are supported by my own ideas and research. Finally, based on EQT's suggestions in the related work section, four open challenges for EQM and related research are presented in the conclusion section. In particular, EQT's suggestions in the related work section also imply that EQT's application can yield new insights regarding quantum theory's generalizations, a discovery that is shared with other related work sections as well as my other works. The global COVID-19 pandemic has prompted numerous countries to implement contact tracing programs to contain the spread of the disease. These initiatives have been heavily supported by the development of mobile applications that utilize Bluetooth technology to track individuals' close physical interactions during the day. Several countries, including the UK, Germany, Italy, France, and Spain, have launched contact tracing COVID-19 apps, with some of the schemes being collaborative efforts among national governments to share data and accelerate vaccination progress. Despite the potential benefits of these measures for public health, they have also sparked concerns about user data security and governmental overreach from both within these countries and abroad. To contribute to the existing dialogue on the trade-offs between public health and individual privacy, this study provides an in-depth analysis of Germany's contact tracing COVID-19 app, focusing on its potential data leaks and revealing that app user locations can be pinpointed even when the location privacy setting is enabled. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that de-identified, aggregated data obtained from the app could potentially be used to identify specific individuals in conjunction with other data sources, all while maintaining a level of anonymity. Our findings consist of both, a theoretical and practical contribution: Firstly, we identify and represent the relevant entities and data processing steps involved in contact tracing COVID-19 apps and related research on COVID-19 instance; Secondly, employing situational awareness principles, we develop and demonstrate a more comprehensive understanding of the hierarchical data processing framework used by these apps, leading to a more accurate characterization of app user locations, and revealing several potential information leaks; Thirdly, a preliminary evaluation of the apps' source code confirmed that our findings align with the actual code implementation. Our research aims to enhance the existing discussion on the public health versus personal privacy trade-offs and contribute to the continued evolution of contact tracing COVID-19 apps, aiming to minimize user data processing and achieve a better data flow balance. Quantum effects, which stem from unique properties of subatomic particles like electrons, can significantly impact biological processes at a molecular and neural level. This phenomenon based on quantum principles allows for coordination between distant particles, as demonstrated by experiments like plant leaves orienting with the Earth's magnetic field or sea slugs solving mazes. However, when studying complex systems with multiple particles, traditional quantum theories fail to account for experimental outcomes, prompting some researchers to consider adopting a non-local, entropic approach to understand these systems, which is grounded in the work of Austrian physicist Ernst Mach. This philosophical shift in approach can foster novel solutions to challenges in physics, biology, and psychology, potentially even resolving puzzles surrounding human consciousness. One potential application of this theoretical shift is a modified neural network model that incorporates non-local, entropic concepts, thus offering a novel perspective on how neural systems might process information. This informational perspective is exemplified through case studies of how plants and humans respond to diverse stimuli, including how plants respond to their local environment and how humans solve mazes. These studies serve to illustrate the broader implications of combining quantum and entropic principles in understanding biological systems. This theoretical framework is further explored in relation to its potential applications and robustness across different domains. This research paper introduces a novel tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and establishing its correctness through the creation of corresponding ACL2 theorems. The tool relies on a unique shallow embedding of C within ACL2, which attributes a form of knowledge to every C data type and function, allowing for the examination of any C state and the verification of claims about its behavior. By deepening the shallow embedding, users can embed additional knowledge describing the expected outcomes of functions, which can subsequently be proof verified by the ACL2 system. The tool's capabilities are exemplified through a series of tests involving simple C functions. Additionally, this paper outlines a design pattern that its developers intend for its underlying architecture to inspire the creation of future programming tools. Lastly, related work and potential future directions in this area are explored. 

The core technology behind this project is a free and open-source software, the C-in-ACL2 Code Generator, which has been made available to the public. Users can obtain the software and demonstrate a functional understanding of the tool by completing a corresponding interactive document on the balance logic of bank account transactions. Subsequently, this tool was used in research on the balance logic of a Google Cloud Financial Service's API, which supports the computation of financial operations through a shallow embedding in ACL2. As an additional resource, a comprehensive index containing 18 distinct ACL2 definitions, the C-Index, has been established to support users in understanding the tool's underlying functionality. This study undertakes a detailed examination of the asteroid family Iochroma, specifically focusing on the origin and characteristics of its two prominent members, (39991) Iochroma and (39992) Iquique. A thorough chaosesurvey indicates that Iquique is actually an interloper and not a member of the family as previously thought. In contrast, Iochroma is confirmed to be a 12:5 Lisochrone. The work further involves creating new light curve combinations to determine the rotation periods and pole orientations of both Iochroma and Iquique. Additionally, the study looks into the origin of the family, suggesting that it could be the result of a resonance collision between co-orbital asteroids. The break-up of Iochroma is found to have led to the most densely populated concentration of asteroids in the 12:5 resonance. However, the study also presents alternative models that could potentially explain the distribution of the family's members. Nonetheless, further surveys are required to verify whether there are other interlopers among the family's members. Ultimately, the study concludes that the 12:5 resonance is the most suitable explanation for the distribution of the family's members based on the current data available. The study presents a comprehensive picture of the family Iochroma, specifically its distribution within the 12:5 resonance. The work particularly highlights how the best-fit pole orientation of Iochroma matches the achiral component, which is in line with the general trend in which the bright side of the lower pole is oriented towards the Sun. The study's light curve combinations are presented in tabular form, which is expected to aid future research. We then utilize the properties of the arguments of the Hurwitz zeta functions to establish a linear system for determining the coefficients of the recombination. Furthermore, we leverage the established framework to recast equations for odd zeta values in terms of the linear combination of Hurwitz zeta functions. Ultimately, the framework's versatility allows us to adapt its applications to a broader category of zeta functions, known as $2m$-fold Fermat zeta values. As a result, we derive a precise formula for the general expansion of the $2m$-fold Fermat zeta function in terms of the product of two Hurwitz zeta functions. The proliferation of electronic data in modern physics research demands that computational methods be developed to help detect underlying structures and create predictive models. In this research, we introduce a novel machine learning technique grounded in algebraic topology that enables the automatic extraction of spatial and functional data structures on through fractional quantum phases and topological insulators. By deriving features from the Barycenter algorithm in Barycenter Filter Map approach, we assign geometric meanings to high-dimensional data patterns and represent them as graphic or metric spaces. In the study, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the Barycenter Filter Map approach in identifying and visualizing complex data structures on QFT and TIs with the support of theoretical frameworks like Ginzburg-Landau-TW theory and fraction quantum phases. With the integration of machine learning methods, we extend the Barycenter Filter Map approach to develop a new framework for automatically predicting topological features on 2D and 3D lattices. The resulting models and analysis provide novel insights into the internal structures of qubits and topological insulators, offering a basis for the development of quantum computing and topological computing devices. Ultimately, we discuss the broad applicability of the proposed framework to a variety of physics data sets and potential applications in data mining and scientific discovery.
