Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). While enthusiastic users prefer complex PINs for added security, casual users prefer simpler PINs and are concerned that lengthy PINs hinder usability. Surprisingly, the inherent characteristics of PINs do not influence casual users' choices but instead dictate enthusiastic users' preferences. The dynamic tension between security and usability within these groups reflects the trade-off often encountered in password management. Our study underscores the significance of designing accessible security features to bridge the gap between enthusiastic and casual users and encourages further research on PIN design and user comprehension. Moreover, it raises questions about the optimal approach to collecting user feedback in design and whether the costs associated with difficult PINs should be explicitly communicated to users. Our findings also show that casual users often utilize the same reasoning as security experts when justifying their preferences and suggest exploring the concept of'security illiteracy' instead of 'lacking security awareness.' Ultimately, the study outlines promising avenues for further investigation and presents actionable recommendations for improving secure design practices that cater to diverse user experiences. This note showcases a set of Gaussian quadrature rules designed to accurately integrate products of functions over the interval [0, infinity) by leveraging spherical harmonics, which are eigenfunctions of the Laplacian operator in spherical coordinates. The resulting quadrature rules maintain the precision of Gaussian quadrature in one dimension while remaining computationally efficient. The spherical harmonics-based approach allows users to tailor the quadrature rules to suit their specific needs by adjusting the degree of the rules. The proposed quadrature rules have practical applications in problems involving solar-power integration, which often necessitate truncated expansions to a finite number of Legendre polynomials, making the quadrature rules applicable to products of Legendre polynomials. The quadrature rules can be easily adapted for use in dimension two through the implementation of tensor products of one-dimensional quadrature rules, which retain the C2 error estimate. Furthermore, the theoretical underpinnings of the quadrature rules are grounded in the framework of spherical Bessel functions, which are employed to derive the quadrature rules via the standard Gauss-Chebyshev procedure. The quadrature rules rely on the understanding that spherical Bessel functions are related to the square root of the Legendre polynomials through the 3-j symbol, which is a unitary rotation operator, which is itself related to the spherical harmonic convention used in this note. The quadrature rules have been implemented in Python with an accompanying Julia notebook that facilitates the computation of spherical Bessel functions using the Spectral methods for Summation (SpecSum) library, which is available at the SpecSum GitHub repository, which is shared by the authors. The proposed quadrature rules have been tested through various benchmarks that illustrate their accuracy and efficiency in integrating products of Legendre polynomials up to degree 4096 using only 129 points, which is a mere four evaluations of the quadrature rules. The theoretical convergence rate of the quadrature rules is super-Algebraic, making them faster than conventional Gaussian quadrature in one dimension by a factor of $129^{2}/256 \approx 41$ percent. The proposed quadrature rules have been further optimized using the adjoint method, which has yielded a speedup of approximately 80 percent by identifying and eliminating unnecessary computations. Utilizing the linear dependence of the quadrature-rule weights on the degree, we have derived an analytical expression for the weights in terms of the spherical Bessel functions, which has been tabulated here for easy reference, alongside the quadrature rules, which can be implemented in high-performance foreign function interfaces such as CUDA

In languages that specify gender through nouns, the link between a noun's gender and its meaning affects how we classify and connect related nouns. This impact is characterized by a bias in how we associate concepts, known as grammatical bias, which in turn affects the way we group related nouns based on this factor. We have found that this bias causes datasets of semantic associations to reflect a combination of conceptual relatedness and grammatical linkages. This means that the dataset's structure itself perpetuates the bias, as nouns of the same gender are more likely to be grouped together. The grammatical bias also affects the performance of neural networks that make associations, as they learn and reinforce this connection between gender and relatedness. This learning process means that the networks prefer to link a word with related concepts that match its grammatical characteristics, as much as its meaning. Consequently, the networks' representations of gender not only influence their ability to make accurate associations but also distort their representations of concepts to follow the grammatical structure of the language. We have discovered that this effect varies across genders and is more pronounced in languages with multiple genders. Furthermore, the grammatical bias affects not only associative linking but also word embeddings and linguistically influenced visual analysis of the words, shaping our understanding of the meaning of the words. We have found that the smaller the community of speakers, the more the grammatical bias affects their linguistic patterns. We examined the grammatical bias in three gender-marking languages: Spanish, French, and Italian. We considered two types of concepts in our study: those linked by co-reference (sharing the same reference) and those linked by conceptual similarity. Our analysis showed that the grammatical bias affects not only the spoken words themselves, but also their visual presentations. The sooner in training that word embeddings become effective, the more the embedded form of the words resists alteration to match the grammatical characteristics of the concepts in the dataset. We discovered that the signal from the word's meaning itself is weak and fails to influence the embeddings made by the networks. As a result, the embeddings made are heavily influenced by an external non-linguistic factor: the speaker's grammatical thinking pattern known as grammatical bias. We considered the implications of these findings on the influence of speaker's thinking patterns on their language and developed a set of general assumptions known as Bias-Agnostic and Bias-Perpetuating Assumptions. A discrete group is considered charmable if it permits a non-trivial combination of elements whose commutator lies within the group, making the quotient space topologically non-trivial. We provide examples demonstrating that all finitely generated nilpotent groups meet this criterion, especially focusing on those with a class of 2 or less. We identify and classify non-archimedean arithmetic groups that are charmable, revealing an interesting paradox where some stiff groups fail the charmable condition. We explore the concept of inner twistability in relation to this condition and establish an additional hypothesis implying that all arithmetic groups of class at most 3 that are inner twisted are indeed charmable. We partially resolve a related conjecture regarding the existence of a characteristic zero, finitely generated solvable group that exhibits the inner twistability property without being charmable. We establish that hyperbolic space groups are charmable under relatively simple and direct circumstances. We define the stiffness index as the ratio between a group's stiffness and charmability, then prove an underlying theorem that leads to the conclusion that many finitely generated groups with a stiffness index of one are indeed charmable. We identify and explore an underlying recursive pattern in generating irreducible characters for reductive arithmetic groups, using this information to demonstrate that groups with a largish size and a stiffness index of one are essentially charmable. We establish the existence of a characteristic zero, finitely generated example that meets the following conditions: it exhibits a stiffness index of one, but remains non-chamberable. We heavily rely on prior research, specifically the works of Harder, Wallach, Suh, Gurevich, Kuchment, Doppner, Lodder, Cai, Klopsch,  Miller, Shalev, and Bader. We also make direct use of a modified version of the Bronstein-Kesten theorem. This paper presents VACA, a variational graph autoencoder designed for intuitive causal reasoning. By condensing causal relations into a structured model, VACA generates a graph that represents the probability distribution of observed data and enables users to perform interventions and ask counterfactual questions. We develop a representation that integrates both node and edge properties, using a combination of MLPs (multi-layer perceptrons) and edge ranking as the inference process. We demonstrate VACA's effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to learn cause-effect relationships, perform interventions, and provide counterfactual explanations. Moreover, we showcase VACA's ability to identify causal dependencies in language, apply it to video analysis to establish cause-and-effect relationships, and use it for reward optimization in reinforcement learning agents. All the code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/moarll0/VACA. Our results are available at https.//graphica.lids.mit.edu/vaca. Through rigorous evaluation, we validate that VACA's causal reasoning skills are in alignment with the principles of causal graph theory. We demonstrate that VACA's learned causal models are resistant to English word permutations in language-based datasets and to noise. We further investigate the statistical properties of the edge ranking task in the binary case and develop a novel neural model that achieves state-of-the-art performance. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of VACA's parameters and evaluate its performance on a video analysis dataset, demonstrating that it can establish cause-and-effect relationships as well as identify causal dependencies in language. We also experiment with using VACA as a policy iterator in reinforcement learning and demonstrate its ability to learn a causal representation of the environment before making a near-optimal action. We assess the robustness of VACA's models to noise and validate that using edge ranking instead of maximization for inference results in less accurate causal models. Ultimately, we establish that VACA's causal representations lead to higher returns in a reinforcement learning setting. Our work contributes to the development of sophisticated AI systems with intuitive causal understanding. We collect a new dataset for causal reinforcement learning and release VACA's source code on GitHub at https.//github.com/moarll0/VACA to facilitate future research and development. Additionally, we provide a link to our results at https.//graphica.lids.mit.edu/vaca. In order to promote reproducibility, we conduct a case study on VACA's source code using the RSLER dataset. The study reveals several challenges in this area and we propose potential research directions for future development

The LoFAR Irish array's REALTA acquisition system made its initial discoveries, revealing two novel extragalactic sources identified through the LOFAR's real-time search of the sky across the 150 MHz frequency range. The sources autonomous detection occurred in April 2018 and January 2019 respectively. The detection process utilized the LoFAR's capabilities for persistent 24/7 monitoring combined with advanced signal processing techniques. The resulting data confirmed the sources as extragalactic through subsequent verification and localization processes. The finalized analysis places the sources' positions at 0.2 degrees and 0.3 degrees off the LoFAR Irish array's pointing axis, corresponding to the directions of 336° and 337°. The sources' spectral characteristics were found to be consistent with 0.35 Jy @ 150 MHz and 0.26 Jy @ 150 MHz respectively. Our results have revealed the considerable impact of these optimizations on the model's performance, exemplifying their value in machine learning-based light field image compression methods. We have also used a variety of metrics to assess the performance of our model and compare it to other current approaches. Our results have further demonstrated the considerable effect of our model's performance in terms of compression performance and overall quality. We propose a novel quantum betting system grounded in the well-established Kelly betting strategy, adapted to accommodate variable odds and payouts that can be represented by positive operators within a Hilbert space. This framework necessitates measurement following each bet, a requirement often overlooked in existing betting theories. Its application to the Hong-Ou-Mandel four-photon experiment demonstrates reduced volatility and maximum growth in wealth compared to alternative betting strategies. Additionally, we assess its performance in a realistic realistic single-photon experiment and contrast it with the outcomes of classical betting strategies. Its relatively simple implementation makes this quantum betting system an ideal candidate for experimental validation in ongoing quantum betting research. The quantum betting system may also be used as a distributed gambling protocol, its correctness having been formally established through a proof of uniqueness of the quantum fair-betting function. The latter concept offers an alternative to the Shannon entropy for measuring uncertainty in quantum states, with the quantum fair-betting function serving as a normative model for optimal betting strategies without the need for probability amplitudes or a wave function description. Its application to the no-communication theorem within non-local physics reveals that utilizing quantum protocols can exceed the performance of classical protocols, a phenomenon that can be attributed to the unique properties of quantum uncertainty as distinct from classical uncertainty. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that, in certain scenarios, achieving optimal results may necessitate near-sure loss, a consequence that may have broader implications for future research in quantum betting and related experiments. The theoretical validity of our quantum betting system has been supported by an independent formal proof of correctness as suggested in PeaRly Betting (2021). For the sake of readability, we have split our comprehensive analysis into two distinct submissions, the primary one concerned with the implementation and properties of the quantum betting system and a secondary submission focused on the theoretical underpinnings of the quantum fair-betting function and its application to the no-communication theorem within non-local physics. The formal proof of the quantum betting system's correctness is documented in the formal verification repository at https://github.com/peardy-betting/formal-verifications. This paper employs a comprehensive time series analysis framework, evaluating the efficacy of contemporary models in a multi-period environment where relationships between variables are unpredictable. Through an exhaustive set of experiments on 85 datasets, we compared six time series modeling methods for long-term and short-term forecasting, five of which are based on Gaussian Process models and Independent Gaussian Processes, with an alternative approach involving non-conjugate Bayesian variational inference and sparseness. Our results reveal that the majority of the tested methods are effective for long-term and short-term forecasting. Introducing sparseness to the models improves forecasting accuracy, particularly for predicting the next time point. However, sparseness has the opposite effect on prediction of consecutive time points, leading to lower accuracy of up to 18%. Furthermore, our study highlights the challenges of accurately forecasting electricity and financial time series, suggesting future research could focus on developing more robust models for these areas. The source code for our experiments is publicly available at https://github.com/dsi-mi/bqfm.

To reach this conclusion, we examine the duals of simple Stone spaces to understand their general behavior, ultimately showing that the duals of monadic logic's associated spaces deviate from Pontryagin duality's predictions. Despite its potential, the fairness of the model training process largely goes unaddressed, leading to differing training outcomes for diverse device groups. Not only can this influence the performance and fairness of the final model, but the conventional FL approach also compromises the privacy of individual devices, which is particularly critical when incorporating sensitive information. This paper addresses two key issues: ensuring fairness in the training process by equalizing the resources available to each device, and preventing the disclosure of individual data, which is crucial for maintaining privacy in both model training and evaluation phases. To this end, we propose a framework based on mirror descent, which is capable of addressing both fairness and privacy concerns through the optimization of a unified objective function. Our framework is grounded in the context of generalizable federated learning, which distinguishes it from the conventional Federated Averaging method. For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of prolate and oblate configurations independently in the parent and daughter nuclei. Prolate components dominated both parent and daughter nuclei for the experimental beta strength, while an upper limit was set for the oblate component in the parent state. To analyze the data, a new method for examining X-ray gated total absorption spectra was developed due to the analysis's complexity. Using calculated QRPA results and the analysis's independence of force details, a calculated $T_{1/2}$ of $43.8^{+3.9}_{-2.6}$ ms for the $^{186}$Hg isotope was obtained along with 90% confidence intervals for relative beta strength. The study highlights the need for further investigation into the beta strength in heavy odd-even nuclei with a focus on incorporating experimental data into the analysis to refine the understanding of the nuclei's structure. Calculated properties for neighboring $^{184,185,186,187,188,189,190,191,192,193}$Hg and $^{184,185,186,187,188,189,190,191,192,193}$Au isotopes are provided to facilitate further studies in this region. The application of sign-changing interactions was determined to have a minor effect on the analysis and is expected to be available on the arXiv in a accompanying document. The analysis's independence of force details and the use of calculated QRPA results, alongside the agreement with the experimental data for the $T_{1/2}$ value, confirms the study's findings. The study's results provide the most precise $T_{1/2}$ measurement for the $^{186}$Hg isotope and serves as the initial employment of the total absorbed gamma spectroscopy method in the Eukrates Nuclear Research Laboratory. By leveraging prior experience and physical principles, the algorithm achieves exceptional performance even with minimal, problem-specific training data. For instance, it permits the precise simulation of an underwater robot's movements, using only two real-world data points and adhering strictly to its physical limitations. Importantly, the algorithm's training time is independent of the robot's dimensionality, making it highly practical for complex control systems. Furthermore, the algorithm's efficiency is remarkable, even when processing large amounts of supplementary information. Through comprehensive evaluations on various continuous control tasks, the algorithm's success is demonstrated on a set of real-world robotic systems. A novel quantum key exchange protocol, incorporating twin-field phases and polarization states, is introduced, which circumvents the need for continuous phase locking. This protocol is analyzed through both theoretical and experimental perspectives, featuring a unique hybrid framework comprising a public channel and private channels. By leveraging light source characteristics, the proposed method is capable of achieving privileged information security. Notably, despite the absence of phase locking, it was found that the entanglement loss within the public channel is comparable to the standard TF-QKE protocol. Furthermore, the protocol's implementation using a 85 MHz pulsed laser demonstrated fast entanglement generation rates and high entanglement purities, resulting in identical keys exchanged between the communicating parties at a fast rate. An eavesdropping detection rate of over 90% was also reported, indicating the high reliability of this innovative QKE protocol. This approach offers secure communication solutions with substantial performance improvements, particularly beneficial for applications involving low-field theories or driving light sources. Furthermore, the experimental results provide the foundation for the practical application of TF-QKE in practical communication settings without relying on phase-locked loops. Finally, the study's findings contribute to the understanding of TF-QKE protocols and provide the basis for the development of new experimental protocols. Yet, YOLO family methods suffer from low accuracy compared to Faster R-CNN, making them unsuitable for some applications. Recently, some research has successfully integrated YOLO features with Faster R-CNN's high accuracy to create new methods. However, these integrated models are complex and difficult to independentley execute. This paper presents an Open Vocabulary Object Identification framework, leveraging the speed and implementation convenience of YOLO family with the high accuracy of Faster R-CNN through pseudo bounding-box label generation. We also developed a noise reduction algorithm for accurate bounding-box extraction from labels. Our proposed method was tested on three image datasets and compared with existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating notable improvements in detection accuracy, especially on general objects with minimal bounding-box noise. Users can easily apply this method to identify various objects by simply adjusting the size of pseudo labels according to the object class. Our source code is available for public access at https://github.com/1jsd8j1j/jjy1jj/OVFI_framework. Experimental results are also available on https://jipill.net/ovfi. Our proposed framework has the potential to outperform existing methods with further development in noise reduction techniques and larger datasets. This could be achieved by incorporating data augmentation, expanding the dataset through image synthesis, and collecting more labels from human annotators. Our method is set to deliver high performance with more high-quality labels, making it a strong baseline for future research. This work is also relevant to recent advances in self-supervised pre-training for object detection. While this area is still under development, our research has the potential to be reapplied in the future to speed up the training of self-supervised models. Such progress could further lead to semi-self-supervised or unsupervised object detection in limited-resource environments, ultimately making the technology more accessible to resource-constrained institutions. Using a combination of Herschel's spectral and photometric data, researchers found distinct characteristics of the cloud's gas, such as ionized regions, atomic hydrogen, and photo-disassociated gas, which revealed variations in their spatial distribution and temperatures. Notably, the warm layer within these regions exhibits a temperature range consistent with that of star-forming regions, suggesting that localized radiation from young stars plays a crucial role in the cloud's transformation. Furthermore, researchers utilized X-ray fluorescence modeling to pinpoint the cloud's ionizing sources, which were found to be young stellar objects, and to estimate the cloud's initial gas composition, revealing a relatively high initial abundance of carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen relative to hydrogen. Overall, the findings indicate that the cloud's gas composition serves as a proxy for that of primitive solar system materials, and that the cloud's contrast between ionized, atomic, and photo-disassociated gas offers insights into the formation processes of stars and planets. By incorporating these findings into models of stellar formation, researchers can refine their understanding of the formation processes of terrestrial planets and planets similar to Earth, and help explain the composition of the early solar system. The concept of veracity in data revolves around ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the information, which is an essential component for making informed decisions. Traditional approaches to veracity primarily involve identifying and mitigating the inherent inaccuracies within data sets, with a focus on incorrect or incomplete facts. However, advancements in artificial intelligence now expose a newer form of veracity challenge - the robotic inaccuracies arising from AI-generated content displaying a semblance of veracity. Our research seeks to elevate the existing discussion on veracity by expanding on previous efforts to categorize various types of AI-generated content, identifying key veracity issues specific to each category, and examining the underlying factors influencing these problems. Additionally, we provide a thorough analysis of the most advanced techniques currently in use for addressing these challenges, aiming to better synthesize content veracity in diverse applications and to create a foundation for developing more sophisticated solutions in the future. Ultimately, our goal is to assist content creators, publishers, and veracity solution developers in addressing the complexities of this evolving AI-generated content landscape, particularly with regards to enhancing accuracy and developing more effective approaches to veracity. A demonstration system showcasing the application of our methods is available at https://github.com/azee/knowledge-ai-veracity. Lastly, we hope that our research will stimulate further developments in this area and create a chance for veracity to improve as a result. A few promising areas of research have been presented on the main page, but a thorough investigation of the subject is recommended for gaining a deeper understanding of the underlying principles. The ultimate goal is to better synthesize content veracity in diverse human-AI interactions and to create a more robust, content-veracity-focused AI for improved future interactions between humans and AI. Moreover, our research promotes increased transparency in AI systems, and our vision is to ensure that veracity is integrated into the development of AI-generated content from the beginning, rather than being treated as an afterthought. A working prototype of our AI veracity model is available at https://github.com/azee/knowledge-ai-veracity. This research seeks to address the intricate challenge of forecasting mortality rates, which are influenced by numerous socio-economic factors in the early stages of an individual's life and a smaller set of factors in the later stages, all while incorporating the impact of random events. To tackle this challenge, we develop two distinct Bayesian factor models that take into account the varying relationships between life status and socio-economic factors over time. By using socio-economic factor models to create proxies for insurance risk and dividend accounts, these models provide a framework for updating these accounts as new data becomes available. We test and evaluate the effectiveness of both models through simulations and actual data analysis, ultimately demonstrating that a model with time-varying loadings offers the most accurate forecasting results. By applying this model to EuroMIR data, we generate mortality forecasts and create shock-resilient scenarios to mitigate potential disruptions from future events. This research builds upon existing work by adapting and advancing several key concepts, ultimately contributing to the development of the Colm model. By comparing our results to industry standards such as those developed by the Institute of Actuaries and CASS business school, we evaluate the Mortality Proficiency Measurement System's performance in assessing an individual's forecasting accuracy in the industry. Finally, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, we test and adjust our model to identify how the devastating effects of this global health crisis have impacted mortality trends and forecasting patterns. The accompanying code is available on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/12344321/Bayesian_time_varying_loadings_mortality_model. The research presents findings to the Supreme Council of the CAA and shares insights at an EUAA webinar on using factor models for mortality forecasting during the pandemic. Neural architecture search significantly escalates training costs with the current limitations, largely caused by the bias-introduced inference costs resulting from pairing potential architectures with numerous parameter configurations. This added expense is quantified as the inference bias, a factor determining the number of expensive inference tests needed to pinpoint the most optimal architecture. This paper explores the inference bias's nature and proposes a strategy to reduce it. The reduced inference bias is achieved by constraining the potential parameter configurations and corresponding architecture pairs to a subset of all possibilities. We then utilize the inherent relationships between potential architectures and their respective subgraphs in the search space to determine a feasible subset with minimized inference bias. As a result, the bias is effectively lowered across the entire search space. A novel graph-based non-convex program is designed to optimize the subset selection. The program's algorithm is then tested on NASBench-101 and NASBench-206, demonstrating notable improvements in inference bias and overall architecture search performance. Furthermore, our algorithm is then validated on the complex CIFAR-10 dataset with WNAS and FBNet architectures, yielding top-notch performance and significantly reduced training costs. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/acmt-ku/red-nas-liar. Our algorithm's performance is compared with state-of-the-art approaches such as FBNet, Soft Attention NAS, and Random Layer Pruning, with experimental results showing comprehensive analysis and rigorous ablation studies. The program was written in Python and executed using TensorFlow for TensorFlow 2.0. The analysis phase and multiple runs of the search algorithm were performed on an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU. The generation and testing phase was conducted on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. The model and program accuracy were monitored and measured using the accuracy function, and the time complexity was monitored and measured using the timer function. The accompanying code uses the following packages: tensorflow, torch, and pytorch. The algorithm was tested for usability by two different coders, and the code is documented with comments to ensure maintainability. The code also utilizes the following persistent storage: GitHub. The algorithm's performance is evaluated based on following criteria: 1. CFI metric, architecture's ability to fit different configurations without changing performance; 2. We consider a length metric space X that has nonempty geodesically complete subspaces, with no weakly geodesic components. We introduce a new type of subspace, called weakly geodesically complete, which includes X. We also investigate the edges of X by proving that for any two points in X, the 1-skeleton N(X, p, r) has non-trivial edges if and only if it contains a weakly geodesically complete subset with a diameter greater than r - d(p, X). We apply this to study 1-skeletons of CAT(0) spaces, leading to a proof of Chatterjee's conjecture: for any two points in a geodesically complete CAT(0) space, the 1-skeleton N(X, p, r) has non-trivial edges if and only all its complete 0-neighbourhoods have diameters less than r. Additionally, for any two points in a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space, the 1-skeleton N(X, p, r) has non-trivial edges if and only it contains a weakly geodesically complete subset with a diameter greater than r - d(p, X). We use this result to establish that for any two points in a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space, the set of weakly geodesically complete subspaces has a closure that contains the set of ends of the space. Furthermore, for any two points in a proper geodesically complete length metric space, the set of weakly geodesically complete subspaces has a closure that contains the set of edges of the space. We also prove the analog of a Chatterjee-type conjecture for abelian group actions. We derive a result on almost isometric maps to Hilbert spaces and use it to describe ends of solvable length metric spaces. We continue by exploring (G, T)-spaces, a class of length metric spaces with a group action that is free at infinity, and show that for any two points in a (G, T)-space, the set of ends has a closure that contains the set of edges of the space. We define another type of length metric space called weakly expandable, which includes all expandable spaces and contains all geodesically complete spaces. We continue by exploring maps between weakly expandable spaces, showing for example that any non-extendable map from a weakly expandable space X to a Hilbert space can be extendable

Human-assisted machine translation (MT) can improve the quality of translations, but relying solely on post-editing metrics like Levesque's Measure of Musicality (MM) is insufficient, as it doesn't account for the role and reliability of translators. Utilizing MM in the context of quality assessment for MT and human post-editing services may mislead, as it doesn't consider a transactor's expertise or level of involvement in the translation process. To address this limitation, a novel Bayesian method is introduced for assessing translators' reliability, which utilizes MM along with two supplementary reliability indicators: translators' professional characteristics and the feedback from clients. The Bayesian approach allows for the integration of these three reliability indicators while accounting for potential limitations and subjective nature of each metric. By incorporating the translators' reliability assessment (TRA) method into the translation process, clients can make more informed decisions when selecting translation services and transactors, ultimately leading to the assessment of transactors' reliability within a translation environment. A preliminary study demonstrated the practical application of the proposed method, which incorporated two auxiliary indicators: translators' professional characteristics and the feedback from clients. To evaluate the proposed method, two main parameters were investigated: how well does the proposed method perform in identifying transactors with high reliability and what characteristics differentiate reliable transactors from their less reliable counterparts. Furthermore, an experimental study was conducted to examine the proposed method in a real-world context, using a sample of 89 transactors from a translation services company. To calculate the reliability of transactors, two main statistical parameters were evaluated: the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and the 95% confidence interval of the proposed method. The results revealed that the proposed transactor reliability assessment method is effective in identifying transactors with high reliability, with the AUC value amounting to 0.95 or higher, indicating its high capability in accurately assessing transactors' reliability. Moreover, the characteristics of reliable transactors were determined to be: providing translations without any revisions, possessing multiple professional characteristics, and receiving positive feedback from clients, which are designed to be applicable in various translation environments. These findings can be used by clients to make more informed decisions when selecting translation services and transactors, which in turn can lead to the assessment of transactors' reliability in a real-world translation setting. Convolutional networks are the leading choice for image classification tasks due to their superior performance compared to other architectures, a significant portion of which can be attributed to their inherent invariance properties. Pruning techniques, used to enhance model efficiency, have long been utilized in convolutional networks. In this study, we treat pruning as a model selection method and develop it into an active technique for sifting through candidate models. By combining two distinct pruning methods - one exclusive to convolutional networks and the other adaptable to various architectures, we conduct an in-depth analysis on the performance of pruned models. Surprisingly, our results show that the pruned versions of simpler, fully connected models surpass the unpruned versions of more complex models, including convolutional networks. This has implications for active pruning as a model selection method, where choosing the right pruning method and timing it at the right stage in training can lead to remarkable success. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/daniellopezpr/Pruning-Accelerated-Testing. Furthermore, our research provides insights on the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of pruning, leading to a novel interpretation of the winning characteristics in convolutional networks. Specifically, we demonstrate how the exclusive pruning method can efficiently eliminate redundant neurons that are uniformly distributed across the training domain, common in convolutional networks. Additionally, we introduce a distribution-based measure of redundancy and investigate which characteristics make a good choice for convolutional and other architectures. Through this in-depth study of pruning, we gain insights into what sets the performance of convolutional networks apart from other architectures and identify areas for further exploration, such as the impact of pruning on training and the potential for improving efficiency by sifting through candidate models during training. In particular, our results show that the pruned models exhibit faster convergence rates due to fewer parameters to optimize. By employing pruning as a model design method, we establish a link between convolutional and fully connected models, demonstrating its potential as a tool to improve model efficiency and achieve remarkable results. The findings of this study contribute to a better understanding of the effect of pruning on the training process and suggest that traditional methods of achieving state-of-the-art model efficiency without going through the training process may not be as limited in their application as they seem. As such, we propose looking into an extended application of pruning that goes beyond achieving efficiency and includes selecting desirable properties in models. Our research focuses on the impact of sequential electron-phonon coupling on valley conservation rules in two-dimensional materials with specific symmetries.  By combining the full sequential electron-phonon coupling, which includes both form-factor and conservation rules, we investigate how valley defining symmetries are influenced.  We discover that breaking valley conservation results in valley diffusion, triggered by the sequential coupling.  Compared to the direct electron-phonon coupling, the sequential coupling contributes significantly more to valley diffusion, revealing its substantial influence.  Furthermore, valley diffusion induced by sequential coupling is dependent on inter-valley phonon population, contrasting the direct coupling's dependence on intra-valley electron and hole populations.  Using a quasi-classical approach for simplicity, our findings indicate that valley defining symmetries play a crucial role in determining emission rates of valence band phonons, leading to distinct emission patterns influenced by valley conservation.  Specifically, our analysis reveals the emergence of flat valleys near the major symmetry valleys due to valence band phonon emission rate patterns.  Our research demonstrates that sequential electron-phonay coupling could play a crucial role in understanding valley transport, potentially be exploited in designing devices with spatially varying valley Hall conductivity to transfer information across different valleys. We investigate a fusion of digital and analog computing techniques in order to understand how to execute quantum simulations of fermionic systems, mainly focusing on the fermionic Hamiltonian associated with the superconducting circuit platform. By combining analog techniques for encoding fermionic modes and digital methods for tunneling operation, we develop a hybrid approach that allows us to simulate diverse fermionic systems by adjusting the tunneling strength. Utilizing this hybrid technique, we develop a two-mode encoder and carries out precise simulations of fermionic Hamiltonians with both single-excitation and double-excitation states. Additionally, we achieve quantum entanglement of fermions in multi-qubit circuits, demonstrating the potential of the hybrid approach to simulate complex fermionic systems like the Hubbard model. We also explore the feasibility of utilizing the hybrid technique to measure fermionic correlation functions. We conclude that this hybrid framework offers a promising solution for simulating diverse fermionic systems on the superconducting circuit platform. Overall, the hybrid digital-analog technique presents a hopeful prospect for executing quantum simulations of complex systems. It could potentially be further adapted and developed to simulate an even broader range of fermionic systems and other complex quantum systems like the Kondo model and the Shubnikov-Nielsen-Odor effect. We hope that this technique might be employed to tackle some of the more challenging many-body problems in quantum physics and chemistry. We further contend that investigating the emulations of fermionic systems on digital and analog hybrid devices could yield considerable breakthroughs in the dynamics of quantum matter. We propose that a future research direction could involve developing a hybrid approach that emulates fermionic systems on a superconducting circuit platform in tandem with a variable and controllable fermionic number of qubits. Such a breakthrough in quantum simulation could potentially be utilized in the development of quantum computers with novel architectures, for instance, simulating the torsional motion of carbon nanotubes. We anticipate that investigating these concepts and implementing them on hybrid digital-analog devices could lead to a profound understanding of quantum matter and the development of numerous applications. Finally, the hybrid approach could be adapted and implemented on different quantum computing architectures like ion trap systems, and we suggest that exploring these opportunities could lead to significant advancements in the field of quantum computing. This research explores the concept of persistent homology in the context of color coding in computer algorithms. It draws from the theory of persistent homology in topological data mapping and applies it to color coding methods within parametric algorithms. A new parameterized data structure, called the chromatic alpha structure, is introduced to efficiently compute topological persistent features of colorable graphs. The chromatic alpha structure is specifically designed for problems involving color coding and can be used to modify existing algorithms in the field to take advantage of the concept of persistent topological persistent features. Furthermore, this research applies the idea of persistent persistent features to map the parameter k in problems such as Exact Tree-Coloring and List Colorability, resulting in a new mapping technique called chromatic persistent map. It is demonstrated that the newly proposed chromatic persistent map allows for faster computation times of colors compared to the current state-of-the-art algorithms in the field. Specifically, this research achieves a new runtime efficiency of O(nt) with the help of the chromatic alpha structure, surpassing previous algorithms in the field. A detailed comparison of the newly proposed method with current state-of-the-art algorithms in the field is conducted, highlighting the improvements made with the chromatic alpha structure and chromatic persistent map. Moreover, this research outlines various potential future applications of the idea of persistent topological features in computer science and challenges for future development. This work identifies the overall gains in degree of freedom that result from using optimal rather than binary power control in interference networks, for any possible number of users. Binary power control sets each transmitter power to either 0 or a maximum value, while optimal power control dynamically assigns a variable power to each transmitter for each pair of transmitting and receiving devices, using a specific equation that ensures signals are received at desired intensities. For large numbers of users, the advantage provided by optimal power control diminishes, in comparison to the maximum possible gains achieved in smaller-scale interference networks. A specific bound is known for the maximum possible gains in such systems, given by $C^{\text{opt}} \le 2 \sqrt{K} C^{\text{bin}}$. Conversely, a lower bound has now been found for this advantage, given by $C^{\text{opt}} > \frac{\sqrt{K}}{C^{\text{bin}}}$, with the possibility of further increasing this lower bound as needed. Furthermore, numerical evaluation shows that these bounds approximate equality when $K$ is in the range of 10 to 100. Inverse problem theory was used to derive the lower bound, providing insights into its formulation. In addition, normalized squared power control was studied as a surrogate for optimal power control, with the results showing the former to be close to the later, for any possible number of users. This led to further analysis of the extremal GDoF gain characteristics of the family of normalized squared power control systems, in search of a configuration that could serve as an optimal solution. A specific configuration was found - the hypercube power control system - which was shown to achieve the lower bound with high precision, both approximately and asymptotically. Moreover, the extremal GDoF gain characteristic of the hypercube power control system was found to be easily interpretable and to possess an intuitive, straightforward cause-and-effect relationship. Following the derivation and validation of the hypercube system's strong performance characteristics, the latter were used to formulate a set of numerical results, with the frequency of achievement of certain fixed throughput rates being studied as $K$ varied from 2 to 256. Interestingly, the analysis showed that while optimal power control's performance characteristic was found to be difficult to understand through analysis, the hypercube system's performance characteristic was found to be easily explained - for any given number of users $K$, the frequency of achievement of fixed throughput rates showed a significant, substantial increase, in the range of $K$ values studied

Specifying a pair potential for a system of particles involves selecting or approximating several key elements: the interparticle potential in detail, maintaining a suitable number of particles, ensuring spatial constraints are met, and ensuring a valid configuration exists within the given set of conditions. When working with sets of particles known as microstates, derived from a given potential, each of these challenges becomes even more complex. This paper explores the use of'stitching' algorithms, capable of piecing together random configurations to form valid microstates from their components, to study the effects of spatial constraints, population size, and precision on the accuracy of potential approximations. To do this, stitching algorithms are applied to random configurations generated from the Strauss process, a model with well-known properties. This study also compares the effectiveness of spatial constraints in guiding the generation process and discusses potential uses of stitching algorithms in the development of potential approximations in physics, such as those utilized in Simpler Born-Oppenheimer. Stokes smoothing and Reeds-Shepherd algorithms are explored, with a focus on their performance within the given models. This study finds that Stokes smoothing is particularly well-suited to working within the Strauss model with weak spatial constraints, while Reeds-Shepherd performs better in constrained systems. These findings serve as a starting point for further research into the potential applications of stitching algorithms in physics. Some of these potential uses are discussed at the end of this document. To facilitate further research, I have made my associated code available on GitHub, including both the stitching algorithms and any necessary changes to these algorithms to allow them to operate within the given sets of conditions. This code also includes basic implementations of both Stokes smoothing and Reeds-Shepherd stitching algorithms. Additionally, to help other researchers understand and work with potential approximations, I have developed an open-source BEO calculator based on our previous Simpler BEO research to demonstrate the feasibility of stitching algorithms in physics. This paper outlines recent advancements in the modeling, simulation, and efficiency improvement of a one-legged hopping robot. We first establish a simplified model for a single-hopping jump and use it to solve for the most effective sequence of movements. This optimized sequence is then used to develop a control strategy that can be easily implemented in the robot. To account for the influence of the terrain on the robot's movement, we introduce a model that represents the terrain's elasticity and use it to adjust the robot's stride length in real-time, resulting in a significant enhancement in the robot's ability to jump long distances. We also develop a simulation model that takes into consideration the robot's spatial movement and the effects of force and displacement on its balance, allowing us to accurately determine the maximum distance it can jump based on its power usage. This simulation model proves to be highly accurate in comparing the theoretical optimal distance the robot can jump to the actual distances it jumps in different experimental conditions. Finally, we combine the model and the control strategy into a single efficient hopping system and use it to greatly enhance the robot's jumping ability, resulting in a greater than 1.5 times increase in its maximum jumpy capability when compared to its original version. Several key experimental results from this optimization process are presented. This work is part of a larger research initiative focused on developing autonomous robots that can navigate challenging and dynamic environments on their own. This research investigates the performance impact of IoT firmware updates on reliable mesh networks, focusing on the challenges of updating thousands of nodes with limited resources and ensuring seamless recovery from failures. By updating Quppa mesh network nodes and measuring application-level accuracy, we evaluated the effects of firmware updates on data transmission. Our study revealed that three consecutive updates reduced network quality, as evidenced by increased packet transmission times and error rates, affecting both mesh and non-mesh networks. We observed similar performance degradation in both updated and older devices, suggesting that network quality is affected by update cycles rather than device age. Furthermore, under stress conditions, the network's robustness was revealed. Crucially, the results demonstrate that "shocking" updates, though time-consuming and error-prone, do not necessarily compromise security or affect data accuracy in field operations. Our field-based measurements and simulations validated that regular updates are crucial for maintaining optimal network performance. We recommend that firms consider updating devices within their network annually to maintain optimal performance. A thorough analysis of our findings is provided in this research. Furthermore, the data collected are available for further study. The Quppa nodes employed in this update process possess the same characteristics as those used in other similar field operations, indicating that the outcomes are relevant to real-world applications. Our study adds to the existing body of knowledge on large-scale IoT firmware updates by providing empirical, application-level performance data of such updates. As far as we are aware, this research is the first to present field measurement data of firmware updates on IoT mesh networks and their effects on data transmission. We investigate the scaling of the Fock-space propagator following a quasi-addiitive process involving excitation of magnetized one-dimensional lattice models. By analyzing how the quasi-additive process's "temperature" impacts the model as it transitions from localized to delocalized phases, we establish a critical point $T^*_{QA}$ based on the fractal dimension of the localized phase's boundary. Notably, the critical point $T^*_{QA}$ coincides with the shift of the many-body localization phase transition induced by the quasi-additive process. The problem of interactive search for multiple targets, where the goal is to find all the items within a budget that match a query, has significant applications in fields like product suggestions. However, the nature of this problem makes it challenging for efficient solutions. Firstly, it's impossible to know in advance which items will be relevant without querying them. Additionally, even during query processing, there's no feedback to determine the relevance of unqueried items. Therefore, the most effective strategy is to prioritize querying the items with the highest relevance, but this approach often leaves some relevant items unexplored if they're not near the top. To tackle this problem, we developed a new strategy that adapts to changing relevance by iteratively expanding the set of queried items. Our solution is built on top of a state-of-the-art target-aided search algorithm and incorporates techniques to minimize unnecessary queries and ensure fair targeting. We tested our approach using two datasets with both precise and imprecise queries and found that it successfully identified all the relevant items within the given budget while surpassing existing algorithms in various metrics. Furthermore, our algorithm can handle targets with changing relevance and has a time complexity proportional to the budget raised to a power between 1 and 2, making it more efficient than existing interactive algorithms. Our strategy outperformed existing algorithms in experiments and found the target in significantly fewer interactions. The source code of our approach is available at https://github.com/husnainirfan/Budget-LLFI-MTS. Our study highlights the importance of using distance-based targeting and highlights the existence of optimal targeting configurations that maximize the number of hit items found during the search process. We also introduced a new difficulty in this problem, where the relevance of items can change over time, and proposed the concept of sensitivity range to address this challenge. By incorporating sensitivity range into our model, we were able to derive a lower bound on its performance and found that our algorithm is optimal under specific targeting conditions. In summary, our algorithm is the first to demonstrate the feasibility of budget limited interactive search for multiple targets and outperforms existing algorithms in various metrics. Researchers have thoroughly explored the concept of adversarial examples in machine learning, and its potential for undermining the reliability of artificial intelligence. This consideration takes on heightened significance for quantum computing, a field still in its developmental stages. This work investigates the existence of adversarial examples in quantum computing, specifically universal instances and perturbations that can manipulate quantum classifiers regardless of their circuit layout, much like their machine learning counterparts. Our research employs quantum perturbations as the universal type of adversarial example. To demonstrate their effectiveness, we tested the perturbations against two quantum classifiers and discovered that they could lower classification accuracy to nearly zero, contingent upon the circuit layout and specific quantum state of the input. This successful experimentation provides the first verification of universal adversarial examples in quantum computing. This research serves as an initial step in exploring the vulnerability of quantum systems to adversarial examples, and we hope it contributes towards advancing the development of quantum-resistant machine learning algorithms. To facilitate replication, the code used in this experimentation is shared on GitHub at https://github.com/ ConnorJamesAbbot/Universal-Adversarial-Examples-QC. We make our quantum perturbations available for use at https://abbott.us/cf. This work is an expansion of our findings presented at the Machine Learning for Quantum Computing workshop in 2020. Further research is anticipated to offer additional methods for generating these perturbations, and to conduct more in-depth analysis of this novel concept in quantum computing. The possibility of extending our research to universal perturbations in series offers an additional area of exploration. The effectiveness of our research could have far-reaching impacts on future quantum-resistant machine learning algorithms. The process of testing our quantum perturbations against quantum classifiers served as an initial experiment, and we plan to apply the theory and methodologies developed for universal perturbations to investigate the performance of multiple perturbations in series, and the characteristics of near-optimal perturbations. This investigation is anticipated to offer significant progress in the field of adversarial examples in quantum computing, and ultimately contribute to the creation of quantum-resistant machine learning algorithms. Researchers have discovered a class of colloidal gels that can be manipulated chemically, yielding various properties such as elasticity, viscosity, and surface mobility, making them ideal for applications in both industrial and biological settings. These advancements create a need to further tailor the mechanical properties of colloidal gels. A recent study has uncovered a novel strategy for modifying the mechanics of colloidal gels by exposing them to ultrasonic vibrations. Ultrasonic energy introduces long-range force fluctuations that can lower the gel's elasticity and trigger gel breakdown under certain vibration intensities. This phenomenon can be explained by the acceleration of slow-moving particles and the distortion of long-range forces between particles. In addition to this effect, ultrasonic vibrations can generate thermal energy local to the gel, causing particle flow and leading to gel degradation. This phenomenon of ultrasonic stability loss in colloidal gels has been termed 'rheo-acoustic collapse,' and its roots in an instability of fluid-like forces have been explored. For certain gel configurations, an "rheo-acoustic window" of vibration intensities can be created where the gel remains stable. This finding has generated interest in the potential of ultrasonic technology to tailor the properties of biological and food colloidal gels, and the study outlines several proposed applications in this area. In summary, this research has created new avenues for modifying the properties of complex materials like colloidal gels via an unconventional method of ultrasonic manipulation. As this field continues to evolve, it will be crucial to further understand the interaction between ultrasonic vibrations and these complex materials. Potential future applications of this technology could include the development of advanced multifunctional materials and significant reductions in the energy requirements for various processing and storage methods. Furthermore, the study has also shed light on the broader implications of ultrasonic manipulation in various areas of soft matter, and the authors suggest its potential for yielding new insights into the physical world. These insights create a promising foundation for the development of ultrasonic methods to analyze and characterize a wide range of materials. In the long run, the ultrasonic modification of colloidal gels has also generated exciting avenues for the integration of flow and mechanics to develop new and innovative materials, potentially giving rise to a new era of "fluid engineering." The Collatz Conjecture is a mathematical hypothesis that has withstood testing for over 80 years, having been proven true for nearly all numbers within its realm, with the exception of a set of unproven statements referring to sequences of 2 and 5. This hypothesis suggests that if a number is subjected to a series of operations - specifically, a specific sequence involving doubling the number and replacing it with the number's half - it will ultimately reach 1. While this conjecture has been largely confirmed through its wide-reaching applications and the success of many supporting theorems, a definitive proof or contradiction remains pending, with the conjecture continuing to captivate mathematicians' interest. Historically, this problem has been proposed by David Collatz in 1937 and has since become one of the most prominent unsolved problems in the field of pure mathematics. This paper, titled "Collatz Conjecture," provides an in-depth examination of the conjecture itself, along with the theoretical foundations and supporting theorems underlying our work. We have also successfully applied computational methods to further test and validate the conjecture for an extensive range of natural numbers, with our software and findings being made publicly accessible for download at the specified URL. While our findings contribute nothing new to the body of known work supporting the conjecture, our work serves as an added affirmation of its validity and the necessity of a definitive proof or contradiction. We have specifically focused on expanding the known applications of the conjecture itself, rather than presenting new theorems related to the conjecture, in an effort to more thoroughly establish the conjecture's significance and relevance to the field of pure mathematics. This paper's comprehensive nature is intended to serve as a single, in-depth resource providing an extensive examination of the conjecture and the theoretical supports underlying our work, with the conjecture's potential applications and the conjecture itself being made accessible to readers who may be new to the subject. We have also included a related problem, the Odd 3n+1 Conjecture, in an effort to more thoroughly explore and explain the nature of the conjecture and its broader implications. While our related problem is not an integral component of the conjecture itself, it does serve to more effectively demonstrate certain properties and the conjecture's applicability to related sequences, with the problem also being an additive extension of the original conjecture. In this paper, we develop a comprehensive evaluation metric called SummScore that offers a more complete view of summary quality by addressing four key aspects: 1) Inference, 2) Information retention, 3) Information organization, and 4) Style coherence. Our proposed metric utilizes two BERT models, one for predicting the source sentence where the summary token appears for inference assessment and another for ranking summaries based on relevance and coherence of the annotated highlights for assessing information retention, inference, and style coherence. Additionally, a weak supervision approach is applied to determine the scores for assessing aspect coherence and coherence-based coherence is used to measure style coherence. Experimental results on four datasets demonstrate that SummScore outperforms existing evaluation metrics in terms of correlation with human judgments on summary quality, human-annotated summaries, and state-of-the-art automatic summarization models. From a mathematical perspective, we explore the concept of making precise predictions or recovering a compressed signal using only limited information, focusing on the scenario where data is collected through a quadratic sensor. When the signal length doubles the number of measurements, we prove that a linear approximation can perform nearly optimally under a mild statistical assumption. In fluid turbulence, friction along fluid interfaces dissipates energy and influences the statistics of velocity fluctuations. This study reveals that if the ratio of thermal to viscosity is very large, heat transfer has a calming effect on velocity fluctuations, consistent with theoretical models. Furthermore, our technique possesses several key benefits, including ease of use (no specialized data infrastructure required), faster processing times (enables rapid evaluation of conferences), and better alignment with intuitive standards of quality (captures the intrinsic value of research through career advancements). Ultimately, our algorithm performed exceptionally well in correlating our quality metric with established performance indicators across a wide range of conferences. By leveraging our algorithm's capabilities to evaluate conferences based on the career advancements of key researchers, we've demonstrated its potential to enable'venue analytics' – a type of analysis that provides a straightforward, easy-to-use, and robust metric to evaluate the quality of research conferences. The long-term numerical simulations of nonlinear wave interactions in a periodic domain reveal a unique spectrum of turbulent waves that adheres to the Kolmogorov spectrum theory. This theoretical framework was originally developed for hydrodynamic turbulence and predicted a specific spectral shape with a logarithmic slope at low frequencies and a frequency dependence in the inertial range characterized by the spectral shape $f^{-5/3}$. Our results indicate that the spectra of both the energy and momentum densities conform to this spectrum, providing the first numerical evidence of the Kolmogorov spectrum in wave-turbulence research. In addition, the simulations show that the inertial range of wave turbulence exhibits reduced drag effects on particles, suggesting that additional studies from this simulation could enhance our understanding of particle dynamics within turbulent waves. This understanding could subsequently be applied to a broader range of phenomena, such as wave-induced particle acceleration in marine and coastal environments, an area where the drag effects on particles have significant applications for science and engineering. This research extends the theoretical application of the Kolmogorov spectrum to two contrasting fields: fluid dynamics and wave dynamics, showcasing its numerical validity in different physical contexts. The similarity between the spectra of turbulent waves and hydrodynamic turbulence provides substantial evidence of the Kolmogorov spectrum in wave-turbulence research, a field that has long assumed but never previously demonstrated this theoretical underpinning. In addition, the numerical verification of the Kolmogorov spectrum sheds light on the long-standing debate over the anomalous spectrum of turbulent waves, addressing the underlying frustration of wave-turbulence researchers over the perceived discrepancy between theoretical predictions and numerical simulations. This frustration is now put to rest, knowing that the discrepancy is actually a non-existent issue, the result of an incorrectly assumed mismatch between theoretical and numerical spectra. In reality, this discrepancy was an artifact of an incomplete numerical range, one that failed to capture the extended inertial range, an eventuality that is now numerically confirmed. The existence of this extended inertial range, one that enables the emergence of the Kolmogorov spectrum, is shown through long-term numerical simulations, ones that are now long-awaited resolutions to long-standing theoretical debates in wave-turbulence research. The numerical resolution to this issue is one that is long-since anticipated by the spectral triad theory, a theoretical framework that is now numerically confirmed. In addition, the numerical verification of the Kolmogorov spectrum provides the theoretical underpinning for novel applications of the spectral triad theory to observe wave-turbulence phenomena

Graph normalization and matching are key techniques widely employed in graph-based energy minimization and matching tasks. However, the conventional graph normalization method introduced by Rohe et al. in 2005 is limited, as its output does not necessarily satisfy the condition of not having edge weights greater than one. To address this issue, a comprehensive analysis of the iterative graph normalization (IGN) method has been conducted. IGN is derived from the edge complement of the maximum weight independent set (MCWS) problem, to which the study brings significant insights. Specifically, a lower bound for the performance guarantee of IGN is established, and it is shown that multi-scale IGN can achieve a superior guarantee. Furthermore, a derivation of IGN from the complement of the MCWS problem offers the possibility of applying constrained submodular relaxation to develop improved algorithms. Such approaches could potentially yield better outcomes in the case of the maximum bipartite matching problem. Ultimately, a detailed experimental comparison between IGN and the traditional graph normalization method confirms that IGN produces edge weights less than or equal to one, and thus yields superior matching results in practical contexts. The proposed multi-scale IGN is found to further enhance matching quality. The study also provides theoretical evidence explaining IGN's superiority by demonstrating a positive linear relationship between edge weights and the number of scales used in multi-scale IGN. Consequently, this study contributes a more comprehensive understanding of the properties of IGN and suggests its widespread adoption in place of the conventional graph normalization method. This research studies the thermodynamic properties of a graphene monolayer modulated electronically. Graphene, when driven by a direct current in an electric field, exhibits oscillations of the Lorentzian distribution function, causing noticeable changes in its thermodynamic characteristics. These characteristics are evaluated using electronic modulation of graphene, replacing the temperature variable in conventional thermodynamic equations. The analysis of the replacement approach involves examining how it impacts the thermodynamic formula and the resulting thermodynamic quantities. We calculate the thermodynamic quantities - free energy, internal energy, specific heat, thermal conductivity, and dielectric constant - for electrically modulated graphene using the replaced temperature variable. These calculations depend on the electron charge, direct current intensity, electric field strength, and the ratio of the direct current duration to the measurement time. We discuss the general trends in the thermodynamic characteristics and explore the influence of DC intensity and electric field strength on these properties. Furthermore, we use the replacement approach to investigate the thermodynamic characteristics of graphene driven by alternating current in an electric field. The replacement of the temperature variable allows for the derivation of alternating current-driven graphene equations, similar to those for electrically modulated graphene. The resulting equations of free energy, internal energy, specific heat, and thermal conductivity for alternating current-driven graphene depend on the temperature, harmonic number, and the ratio of the alternating current duration to the measurement time. The specific heat and thermal conductivity of alternating current-driven graphene are found to be frequency-independent. We discuss the specific thermodynamic characteristics of alternating current-driven graphene and explore the influence of the electric field strength on these properties. Finally, our research studies the thermodynamic characteristics of superfluid helium-4 layered in electrically modulated graphene across phase transitions from superfluid to liquid and from liquid to gas. These characteristics are evaluated using the replaced temperature variable in the thermodynamic equations of superfluid helium-4 for electrically modulated graphene. The resulting thermodynamic quantities - free energy, internal energy, specific heat, and thermal conductivity - for superfluid helium-4 depend on the temperature, harmonic number, and the ratio of the direct current duration to the measurement time. The specific heat and thermal conductivity of superfluid helium-4 exhibit increased or decreased values across various phase transitions from superfluid to liquid and from liquid to gas in electrically modulated graphene, and we discuss these increases and decreases in detail. The influence of the harmonic number on these phase transitions in electrically modulated superfluid helium-4 is also analyzed. Despite this, current image classification technologies exhibit an inexplicably smooth transition from one scenario to another when confronted with severe distortions.  In order to bridge this gap between human and machine perception, we developed SEVRE, an innovative dataset consisting of 2,600 images featuring eight different categories and eight distinct distortion techniques.  We found through cognitive experiments that machines outperform humans in identifying distorted images, with humans struggling to tolerate even basic alterations and machines showing an unexpected ability to accurately recognize severely transformed images across multiple tasks.  Through additional studies, we demonstrated that the stability of machine learning is rooted in ensemble averaging and we examined the trade-offs between ensemble methods and fusion strategies.  Our proposed framework aims to improve both human and machine image processing capabilities, with potential applications spanning across visual understanding tasks and related fields. This investigation focuses on identifying the quantum ground states of finite-sized clusters, with particular emphasis on the behavior of corner-sharing triangles in flat layers of quantum gases and as part of an isolated layer surrounded by vacuum.  The findings are compared with earlier quantum spin-chain calculations and the predictions of classical spin quantum liquid models.  The participation ratio, critical exponents, and behavior in magnetic field are particularly examined.  Our results demonstrate an approach similar to a quantum spin liquid state in the absence of an applied magnetic field, but also reveal a significant breakdown of the quantum spin liquid model when considering the behavior of edge-sharing triangles and the influence of field.  The presence of a gap in the spectrum, as determined by a quantum fidelity susceptibility metric, supports the findings of a quantum spin liquid-like ground state.  The behavior in an applied magnetic field shows a strong analogy with the properties of spin-1/2 Kagome materials, with a hike in the quantum fidelity susceptibility metric observed at a field strength of B_D = 0.174 t_J appearing as a sign of spin singlet formation.  These findings suggest that the behavior of the edge-sharing triangle is significantly different from that predicted by classical models. Nevertheless, existing PLMs require significant fine-tuning on specific datasets, limiting their broader utilization. We propose a novel method called PromptLearn, which secondly views pre-training prompts as part of a larger dataset to be optimized. Furthermore, we introduce a meta-learning strategy to automatically identify effective prompts for any given task, thereby standardizing the dataset to be learned across all ZSL scenarios. We evaluate our approach on the standard image-classification benchmark, comparing its performance to other state-of-the-art Zero Shot Learning (ZSL) techniques that utilize text for image embedding generation. We estimate that the integration of our approach and a more advanced image encoder could potentially set new performance standards on the standard benchmark. By analyzing millimetric spectral line features and coinciding millimetric and radio continuum spectra, our approach helps identify reliable redshifts for complex objects such as gravitationally lensed dusty galaxies. By applying this instrument to a sample of 37 sources from the REDCOBRA survey, we achieved a substantial 68% success rate in determining unambiguous redshifts.
