Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is used to describe how solids respond to localized stresses by distributing the force more evenly throughout the material. However, the challenge lies in determining the effective stiffness of the screened solid, especially when faced with complex interiors. We utilized both theoretical and computational methods to create a model that can accurately predict the effective stiffness of a range of micrometer-sized granular materials with different internal structures. Our key assumption was that the effective stiffness is inversely proportional to the number of degrees of freedom associated with the stress-induced displacement. Our model, supported by both experimental and numerical findings, demonstrates that the effective stiffness is directly proportional to the number of degrees of freedom, challenging the traditional view of mechanical screening. Our findings not only offer a simpler, more universal approach to the mechanical screening phenomenon, but also provide valuable insights into the overall behavior of solid materials. Our research has the potential to be applied to a range of solid materials, including biological tissues, granular packs, and aggregates, where mechanical screening occurs due to the movement of grains or cells. Furthermore, our numerical model can be used to analyze and simulate the mechanical properties of tissues at the micrometer scale, providing a valuable tool for understanding tissue mechanics and the factors that influence grain or cell movement. Our experimentally and numerically validated findings represent an important step towards a deeper understanding of the mechanical screening phenomenon in solid materials. Our simple, four-parameter framework has the potential to facilitate a deeper understanding of the mechanical properties and behavior of solid materials, including biological tissues, granular packs, and aggregates, by bridging the gap between material mechanics and cellular force generation. Such knowledge could be crucial in developing new materials and understanding the importance of mechanical screening in biological systems. Our research has the potential to inspire breakthroughs in the fields of biology and materials science. Our simple, universal mechanical screening theory and the associated analytical and computational frameworks for determining the effective stiffness will facilitate a deeper understanding of the mechanical properties and behavior of solid materials. Our findings will enable researchers to calculate the effective stiffness of solid materials with complex interiors, demonstrating that mechanical screening is a ubiquitous phenomenon that is just as influential as mechanical dissipation in shaping the behavior and mechanics of solid materials. Our research will help to shed new light on the mechanical properties and behavior of solid materials and inspire novel applications in the fields of biology and materials science. One effective way to overcome this issue is by using oversampling methods that involve generating new data points to balance class distributions. Although there are various oversampling methods, a notable absence in the literature is a comprehensive comparison covering multiple areas, including text classification. This research explores the performance of oversampling methods that utilize nearest neighbor, nearest center, and Random UnderSampling (RUS) in handling class imbalance on text classification tasks. The experiment involved six methods that augment the original dataset by a factor of two, 10, and 20. The results showed that Random UnderSampling (RUS) provided the highest F1-measure score average among all oversampling methods considered. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, case and death rates, target audiences, and journalist characteristics. An online platform analyzed and tracked U.S. local news COVID coverage from March 1, 2020, to June 15, 2020, via 407 journals and 17,304 articles. Rich demographic information was obtained for news outlets, as well as geographically-adjusted COVID case and death rates. Results show that news coverage in areas with higher COVID cases had more stories, although death rates did not follow the same trend. Further, news coverage was targeted towards older and higher-income populations, as well as urban areas. Interestingly, outlets serving minority groups received less COVID coverage in comparison to non-minority areas. At the journalist level, female journalists covered COVID more extensively than their male counterparts, and PhD-holding journalists covered more stories than non-PhD holding ones. When interacting with demographic information and journalist characteristics, regression analysis revealed that journalist characteristics heavily influenced COVID coverage, with PhD and female journalists covering more in areas of high COVID cases. Moreover, news coverage in minority areas could be boosted by adjusting journalist characteristics. Furthermore, local news COVID coverage was found to be correlated with local government COVID efforts. An investigation into the content of local news COVID stories revealed that newspapers primarily focused on COVID cases and deaths, especially for audiences serving older populations, as well as urban and high-income groups. During the pandemic, urban residents read more newspapers and watched more TV news in order to increase their knowledge of COVID. Moreover, news coverage was connected to public COVID behavior in the U.S, with a positive relationship observed between news coverage and average number of social contacts in the population. Overall, the study highlights the interplay between local news COVID coverage, target audiences, and community COVID behavior and beliefs. It also shows that local news can effect COVID behavior in the U.S, a finding which could inspire COVID-related journalism in the future. Many of the study's findings were confirmed through a follow-up study of Chinese local news during the 2020 Chinese COVID pandemic. The high genus problem of finding the minimum genus of a dense graph that can be embedded in a given surface has been long-standing and challenging in the field of graph theory, with limited progress over the years. For nearly two decades, the best known results have been achieved through randomization techniques developed by Dasgupta, Suri, Lev, Vondrak, Abello, Montecino, Abrego, and Hurtado. We introduce a new polynomial time algorithm that addresses this problem by iteratively checking for the minimum genus of each graph density interval, taking polynomial time for each iteration and resulting in an Effective Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (EPTAS). We begin by establishing a new density-genus inequality, building upon existing inequalities from the fields of embedding and drawing of graphs. We then use this inequality to split the range of graph densities into disjoint intervals, ensuring that any graph with density within an interval can be embedded on a surface with genus not exceeding the upper bound set for that interval. We then apply this splitting procedure in induction, establishing our EPTAS algorithm. We note that our approach significantly surpasses current knowledge on the high genus problem, as it not only encompasses the previously best known result, but also extends to new findings. Furthermore, we prove the existence of a fixed-parameter approximation space for the high genus problem by demonstrating the existence of a new parameterized algorithm, utilizing a novel decomposition strategy for the problem. We first introduce a new parameter, defined as the minimum number of contraction operations required to reduce a given graph to a form where it can be embedded on a surface with a certain genus. We then use mathematical induction to establish a decomposition structure for the problem, ensuring that for any given input parameters, we can obtain a corresponding subgraph with reduced genus within a bounded factor. We then apply this decomposition structure to prove the existence of a fixed-parameter approximation space for the high genus problem, as our algorithm's running time is directly influenced by the number of decomposition levels required to reduce the graph's genus. We demonstrate this approach via the example of a one-electron atom, but it can be extended to incorporate multiple electrons. Our research focuses on the impact of pandemic-related behavioral shifts on the diversity of people's social interactions in urban environments. To investigate this, we analyzed the physical meeting habits of various professional groups in two major US cities - Chicago and San Francisco - from January 2020 to June 2021. To gauge their interactions, we utilized data-driven mapping to assess the diversity of people's social interactions in different locations. We found that in-person social interactions among the eight researched professional groups declined significantly, with the majority of them experiencing at least an 80% decrease. Notably, the diversity of people's social interactions showed a marked decline of at least 50% in most locations. Interestingly, we discovered that the diversity of people's social interactions in locations with higher proportions of graduate students and researchers experienced smaller declines. Furthermore, we found that in-person social interactions among the researched professional groups became increasingly segregated during the pandemic. Specifically, we discovered that the diversity of people's social interactions in locations with higher proportions of graduate students and researchers experienced greater degrees of segregation. To identify the factors contributing to the changes in the diversity of people's social interactions, we employed machine learning analyses. Our results suggest that the primary factor underlying the changes in the diversity of people's social interactions was the significant decrease in in-person social interactions among the researched professional groups. Moreover, we discovered that the changes in the diversity of people's social interactions may have partly resulted from the shifts in the daily routines of people during the pandemic. To evaluate the long-term implications of the changes in the diversity of people's social interactions during the pandemic, we used a simple theoretical model. Our findings indicate that the changes in the diversity of people's social interactions may have contributed to a decrease in the likelihood of diverse groups interacting in the researched locations even after the pandemic has ended. Ultimately, our research highlights the need for further investigations into the long-term impacts of the changes in the diversity of people's social interactions during the pandemic. To facilitate such investigations, we recommend employing established metrics for assessing diversity in urban environments, conducting thorough surveys, and enabling data-driven mapping to provide a clearer understanding of the changes in the diversity of people's social interactions. This approach offers numerous benefits, including improved efficiency, user-friendliness, and versatility. However, its performance heavily relies on the selection of an optimal splitting strategy among the various available options. In our study, we thoroughly evaluated the effectiveness of seven distinct generalized field split methods, namely, Smith, Peacock, Chugosov, Stueben, Krewin, Berezikov, and Galanoglo, under different problem settings and operating conditions. In an effort to streamline the computation process, the methods were also combined in a pre-conditioned setting with the Newton iteration method. In the majority of the tested scenarios, the Smith and Peacock methods demonstrated exceptional performance, closely followed by the Chugosov method. In direct comparisons, the Smith method outperformed the Peacock method, but failed to surpass the Chugosov method. Ammonium sulfate's caloric and ferroelectric properties at low temperatures have drawn attention from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. To explain the disparate outcomes from lattice dynamics and density functional theory calculations, we apply a more detailed approach based on quantum dynamics and electronic interactions. This allows us to reevaluate the primary factors contributing to the substance's extensive entropy change and ferroelectricity. We observe a substantial decrease in the fictitious electron mass in quantum dynamics simulations, corresponding to the onset of ferroelectricity. By considering the interplay between phonons and ferroelectric instability, we account for the substance's extensive entropy change and align this understanding with experimental observations. Additionally, we discuss how an inadequate description of electronic interactions in density functional theory calculations affects the results of the substance's phase transition dynamics. This enhances the reliability of lattice dynamics models in predicting ferroelectric materials' extensive entropy change. Quantum dynamics simulations, accompanied by considerations of the subsystems of electrons and nuclei, offer new insights into the ferroelectric phase and entropy change mechanisms of ammonium sulfate and potentially other materials. Furthermore, we propose that similar quantum dynamic behaviors could underlie the ferroelectric properties in other potential candidates, resulting in significantly decreased entropy changes that are in line with experimental predictions. Lastly, we explore the potential applicability of quantum dynamics to a broader range of compounds, potentially leading to a more comprehensive understanding of the ferroelectric phase and entropy change dynamics. However, we also acknowledge that further research is required to accurately describe the ferroelectric phase and entropy change dynamics of various compounds. The quantum dynamics model is a promising tool for this endeavor, providing a new and crucial understanding of the ferroelectric phase and entropy change dynamics of ammonium sulfate and potentially many other compounds. The code used for the quantum dynamics simulations is publicly available from the GitHub repository 'FDFT-QD-SAS', as discussed in Section 2.2. Furthermore, our work highlights the significant differences between lattice dynamics and density functional theory calculations, underscoring the necessity of employing quantum dynamics to accurately describe the ferroelectric phase and entropy change dynamics of ammonium sulfate and potentially many other compounds. The reliance of our work solely on experimental data and the substantial consistency between our quantum dynamics results and experimental observations demonstrate the effectiveness of quantum dynamics in describing the ferroelectric phase and entropy change dynamics of ammonium sulfate and potentially many other compounds. The knowledge gained from our study could contribute to the creation of advanced thermoelectric materials, as well as sustainable and convertible energy storage solutions with caloric effects

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of research on probability-matching, the underlying mental processes involved remain unclear. In various collaborative settings with humans, robots require counterparts to facilitate their understanding of human behavior and interactions. Typically, this counterpart is provided by a central, all-knowing system preprogrammed with rules and guidelines. We introduce an alternative approach in which the counterpart is a collaborative participant, capable of executing tasks in unison with the robot. Through successful cooperation, the counterpart generates insight into robot preferences and interactions, serving as a vital framework for interpreting the robot's actions and intentions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in a parking scenario involving a robotic vehicle, showcasing the establishment of robot standards and expectations among humans through shared autonomic behavior. Our research revolves around the formulation of robot preferences, the evaluation of shared autonomic behavior, and the assessment of generated insights. We propose a quantitative method for evaluating the participation and comfort of humans in the shared autonomic process and analyze the impact of various settings on human participation. Ultimately, the developed framework contributes to a fundamental concept in autonomous systems - the representation of shared autonomic behavior - and showcases its potential in advancing perceptual and perceptive capabilities in autonomous robotic systems. For tasks like SLAM and reinforcement learning, experts have developed various techniques to navigate unknown environments, but designing efficient mapping algorithms remains a challenging task. To overcome this, we introduce the Hierarchical Topological Diagram Representation (HTDR), an innovative approach that models an environment as a simplified graph. By representing distinct locations as nodes and their spatial connections as edges, HTDR recreates the overall layout, focusing only on relevant topological data. We complement HTDR with a new loss function and an accompanying exploration strategy, resulting in the HiTMap agent, which simultaneously improves state representation, exploration behavior, and achieved goals. Through simulated evaluations on diverse environments drawn from games and randomly generated maps, we found that HiTMap outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant improvements in goal completion rates and representation accuracy. Furthermore, HTDR receives positive assessments due to its straightforward implementation, moderate computational requirements, and excellent adaptability to various task types. With HTDR's flexibility, we successfully applied the method to multiple different environments and agents, such as tile-cumulatives and random agent, demonstrating its vast potential for adaptation and expansion. A method of creating such arrays involves generating a new class of codes based on inter-group complementary code sets, achieved through the use of multivariable functions, resulting in a set of codes with enhanced interference suppression capabilities. Utilizing these codes, a corresponding set of 2-D Z-supplementary array code sets is formed. This work proposes an advanced variational framework for a comprehensive analysis of data obtained through the use of X-ray sensors in polyenergetic computed tomography (CT) imaging. By addressing three primary issues - image restoration, sensor data repair, and material identification - our framework seeks to optimize both the polyenergetic X-ray flux and the physical characteristics of the material involved, with the known quantity being the forward CT projection operator. Employing a dual majorization-minimization strategy, we develop two tailored Bregman distances for the two main variables in the model: the weighted average energy spectrum and the material density spectrum. Comprehensive numerical simulations have demonstrated that our framework produces high-quality results for data generated by a polyenergetic X-ray source, with the framework's parameters being determined automatically. Furthermore, the research highlights the framework's potential to adapt to challenging data sets. By demonstrating promising image and performance improvements, the results indicate effective repair and material decomposition of sensor data. An additional benefit of the framework is its ability to apply the principle of non-negative least squares, with the known quantity being the forward CT projection operator. Our variational framework has successfully addressed the challenges associated with polyenergetic X-ray flux estimation and material decomposition from noisy sensor data. With the ability to repair sensor data and recover the material density spectrum, the framework has produced high-quality results for a range of data types. A pre-trained model, developed using synthetic data, has been employed to demonstrate the framework's capabilities for a meaningful extension of its domain. Current best systems for Contextual Named Entity Retrieval are mainly based on a point-wise approach, where the task is treated as a collection of independent tasks, each one focusing on a single mention and its associated context. Yet, a significant advantage of using context to retrieve named entity suggestions is that context elements other than the closest one can also provide insight into the retrieved entities. Hence, to enhance suggestion accuracy, this point-wise approach can be augmented with a term-wise method that takes into account the entire collection of words in the context and its impact on the retrieved entities. By integrating the two methods, the suggestions provided are both context-dependent and based on the entire collection of words in the context. This paper presents an innovative approach to Contextual Named Entity Retrieval, where the concept of response relevance is combined with the term-by-term significance of context words in retrieving suggestions. We evaluate various methods that integrate the two concepts and propose a new one, Term Relevance Response, based on a terrier query language. Experimental results conducted on two datasets derived from the Semeval 2016 Contextual NER Challenge showcase the effectiveness of our method when compared to the existing point-wise approach used by the challenge winners and other recent Contextual NER models. Our method achieves a significant improvement in the accuracy of retrieved entities of up to 32.8 compared to the existing methods. Additional experiments were also conducted to evaluate the impact of using dense contextual word representations, derived from a pre-trained neural network model like word2vec and fasttext, to replace the one used in Term Relevance Response. We also investigate the efficiency of our method when used to retrieve a large number of context elements, as the time complexity of its dense component linearly scales with the size of the context. Our research creates interactive visualizations that make it easier to compare, analyze, and identify patterns in data sets, and it is applied to real-world scenarios such as monitoring COVID-19 symptoms and understanding the impact of educational programs. Electronic Health Records, which contain diverse data types such as images and free-text descriptions, present challenges in grouping similar patients. In this paper, we propose an approach that combines heterogeneously related components of EHRs. By extending graph neural networks to accommodate multiple relations, we enable similar entities to be linked across different data types. Initially, we identify potential links between patient image and free-text segments based on their proximity and statistical similarity. Subsequently, we apply a graph neural network that can aggregate information from various sources. To optimize training efficiency, we employ a hierarchical approach with balanced sampling and incorporate a unsupervised clinical task for self-supervision. To evaluate our method, we created EHR datasets mimicking those found in real clinical settings. The results demonstrate that our graph neural network outperforms existing homogenous similarity metrics, with notable gains in clinical tasks involving patient similarity and course prediction. Specifically, we record a 4.0% improvement in diagnosing diabetes and a 5.6% increase in accurate age forecasting. Furthermore, we release our source code and pre-trained models on the EHR heterogeneous similarity analytics open-source platform. With the rapid growth in medical imaging, our work highlights the need for heterogeneous similarity metrics to determine relevant image cohorts, and our findings suggest that graph neural networks are well-suited for this purpose. Additionally, we provide the foundation for further research on using graph neural networks to tackle challenging EHR-based tasks, such as patient clustering and forecasted course visualization. The analysis of our method's generalizability reveals that it effectively handles diverse data types, and we specify parameters tailored to the EHR heterogeneous similarity problem. Ultimately, we provide a platform for EHR heterogeneous similarity analytics and embark on further research to tackle more intricate clinical challenges, ultimately contributing to better EHR-based clinical decision support systems. This research investigates energy-saving potential in wireless networks through collaborative network coding and by optimizing both relay scheduling and power allocation, with a focus on minimal latency. Since implementing network codes in real-world systems is complex and time-consuming, we use a simplified approach that approximates the benefit of collaboration. By combining schedule and power allocation, we show that the optimal power allocation can be determined independently of the schedule. Additionally, we propose an iterative algorithm for calculating optimal transmission times and distributions of power/allocation, given any network code. Furthermore, we establish that any optimal schedule for collaborative network coding must adhere to a specific set of rules, which simplifies the search for an optimal schedule. Through simulations using both theoretical and simulated data, we confirm that collaborative network coding can achieve greater energy efficiency than traditional non-collaborative methods, with notable advantages in scenarios with multiple active relays. Furthermore, we highlight the significant impact of computational methods on the feasibility of network coding and the need for simplified approaches that can efficiently incorporate coding benefits. Finally, we compare the effectiveness of two computational methods: sequential analysis and random search, and recommend the use of sequential analysis due to its superior performance and balance between computation cost and quality. With simplified approaches and efficient computational methods, we can efficiently integrate network coding into energy-efficient wireless communication systems. Numerical results show that while sequential analysis may require 1-3 orders of magnitude more operations than random search, the optimal solution is achieved 2-3 times faster. Furthermore, we show that sequential analysis achieves the optimal solution 10-100 times faster than the current state-of-the-art algorithm. Due to its simplicity, sequential analysis outperforms random search across all tested scenarios, offering a practical solution for network coding in wireless communication systems. Satellite imagery edge detection is primarily focused on enhancing the clarity of images and removing noise to create smooth topographic data for further use in geospatial surveying. Unlike other computer vision applications, satellite imagery edge detection must also account for these images' unique characteristics, such as blurry edges, mixed regions, and lack of representative benchmark datasets, making it challenging to implement. Furthermore, the considerable size of these images and their limited availability hinder efficient processing via deep learning methods. To address these issues, we developed a groundbreaking edge detection algorithm utilizing a combination of open-source technologies and a massive parallel processing approach. Our approach first utilizes a compressed image format and splits the image into smaller sections for processing. Additionally, we employed the MagentaMusic model as a starting point and modified it by adding convolutional layers with adjustable parameters to create our CannyMagenta network. Our results demonstrate that our approach enables reliable edge detection in large satellite images and outperforms existing methods, including open-source deep learning models and the conventional SCD method. Using Google's Colab collaborative lab and Google Drive for data upload, we successfully applied our CannyMagenta method to process a 15GB satellite image in less than an hour. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of edge detection in large-scale satellite imagery without relying on deep learning methods. Moreover, our adoption of Google's Colab and Google Drive as common data processing platforms make our approach highly adaptable and transferable to other applications and industries. Our methodology relies on a quantitative strategy that achieves transparent and explainable results, as required in reliable and trustworthy geospatial processing. Noisy electromagnetic signals received from communication systems can be distorted due to the environment or intentional interference, which hampers accurate information recovery and compromises security if the interference is malicious in nature. A crucial step in ensuring secure wireless connections involves identifying which modulation schemes are being used to counteract unauthorized attacks. Recent research has shown that Generative Adversarial Networks can be employed for a robust modulation classification that withstands adversarial interference, although this method also makes the system trainable by malicious attackers, which has major implications. Our research has investigated the potential of combining generative models in a single framework, which resulted in remarkable performance with very limited training data - a feat previously thought impossible. A comparative study revealed that incorporating a generative model for noise distribution as well enhanced the classification performance and protected it from adversarial attacks, which was not the case when using a fixed noise distribution template. Experimenting with various levels of available training data also determined that the proposed blended generative adversarial model outperformed its counterparts even when there was a limited amount of training data. Moreover, the classification accuracy of this model surpassed the best performance levels in recent research, which involved training without any adversarial noise. A detailed analysis of the proposed model's performance also included numerical results for its stability and the level of gradient norm during backpropagation. A numerical study on various communication systems using different carrier frequencies and signal durations showed that the proposed model offered significant classification accuracy and robustness, which made it a valuable tool to ensure secure wireless connections. A comparative study of the proposed model with existing state-of-the-art methods also demonstrated its superiority in performance, which was measured quantitatively by calculating the distance between the proposed model's decision region boundaries and those of the support vector machine's as well as the misclassification rate. Our research has successfully addressed a long-standing issue in machine learning, which involved designing a robust model that could tolerate adversarial attacks and maintain high performance levels even in hostile environments. A combined generative model approach has also been proposed, which offered improved performance, resistance to adversarial attacks, and the ability to work effectively with limited data. A simulation study has demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed model in ensuring secure wireless connections across different communication systems and carrier wave properties. Additionally, the proposed model's efficacy in protecting wireless connections from malicious attackers using the Bell Labs Mixed Integer Programming attack has been shown in a simulation study. A practical implementation of the proposed model also involved designing a device that combined a radio frequency front-end, digital signal processor, and secure processor to ensure secure wireless connections

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions from lesions in training and new datasets is difficult, which is why researchers and hospitals struggle to segment new patients' lesions. A new technique, the Continuously Learned Segmentation (CLS) framework, is designed to improve the segmentation of new data by incorporating self-training. By initially developing a model using a small amount of annotated data and then automatically labeling unlabeled images, the CLS framework can effectively segment new, unannotated images. We tested the CLS framework in a competition against traditional techniques and other new methods, such as unsupervised domain adaptation and graph-based techniques, using images from hospital A and B. The results show that the CLS framework outperformed all other methods, which was very consistent with the results of a user study indicating that visual evaluation of the segmentation results by a human expert was similar. A new extension of the CLS framework called CLS+ has also been developed, which achieved even better results on a downstream task of identifying areas of inflammation in the brain. Through downstream task pre-training, the CLS+ framework was shown to not only improve the segmentation of specific lesions but also predict other brain pathologies. Our work is the first to apply semi-supervised self-training to medical image segmentation and successfully tested in a realistic, cross-institutional setting, which is unique to the medical imaging community, and also demonstrates the potential of semi-supervised pre-training to improve downstream task prediction. Our code is available for other researchers to use. In summary, the CLS framework was shown to outperform other segmentation methods in a competition and was found to be not only effective but also efficient when integrated into a new hospital's imaging analysis workflow, which was evaluated using various metrics and found to be reliable. The CLS framework further improves its accuracy by incorporating downstream task pre-training, which not only enhances the segmentation of specific lesions but also predicts other brain pathologies, which is crucial in the medical field. The results indicate that the CLS framework is a valuable tool for hospitals to implement in their imaging analysis workflows and further suggest the potential of semi-supervised pre-training to address similar challenges in the medical imaging community. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the usefulness of semi-supervised pre-training in the medical field and opens up a new avenue for researchers to integrate semi-supervised pre-training into their imaging analysis workflows. We've developed a straightforward method that utilizes learning techniques to identify errors in dynamical system models, which can be used even when limited information is available. This framework is applicable to systems that can be represented by nonlinear equations with measurable state and input variables, and it doesn't require detailed knowledge of the system's dynamics. Learnable "error variables" are introduced to account for unresolved model discrepancies, which are trained using data from operational or simulated scenarios. Since the error variables are considered external influences, their impact can be minimized by taking deliberate action. This approach was successfully tested on two challenging problems, including a model for complex jet engine combustion and a model for chaotic system control. When subjected to various manipulations that mimicked experimental tests, our framework accurately identified the unexpected model discrepancies in both systems, demonstrating robust performance. This research reveals the potential for leveraging machine learning to detect inconsistencies in complex models, identifying potential causes, and providing valuable insights for model enhancement or calibration. Additionally, this framework's ability to identify unexpected model discrepancies in systems exhibiting complex behavior or influenced by micro-scale phenomena could have a significant impact on addressing long-standing computational challenges. Our study delves into the internal workings of these models to reveal how they handle this type of context, using rejection as a test case to understand their ability to carry a negative connotation. We discovered that, just like human language, these models can use "no" to negate a sentence meaning "there's nothing," but only when the sentence includes a negative word like "never" or "no." When given the sentence "She didn't have never," for example, these models are capable of understanding it as "there's no never," implying that nothing exists at all, while human response might vary depending on interpretation of the sentence meaning. We observed that these language models are able to develop a negative connotation from "no" in this type of context just like humans do, indicating their capacity to express more nuanced meanings beyond their literal translations. We also explored the internal structure of these language models to determine the specific parts that allow them to perform this type of complex task, eventually identifying areas that distinguish their capabilities from human language. Our results not only analyze the language used in this type of context but also explain the specific neural architecture that enables these models to process it effectively. They ultimately shed light on the dynamic relationship between the words and the internal mechanisms of these language models, helping to reveal how they understand the meanings behind the words they process. Our code is publicly available for review at https://github.com/ericmjl/rejection-processing. Furthermore, this study serves as a call to action to the broader NLP community to explore the internal workings of these models that facilitate complex human-like language patterns, ultimately making them more efficient and effective. In neural machine translation, focusing on relevant source words enhances translation accuracy by prioritizing crucial words. However, existing methods only consider the context of the target word itself, ignoring its look-ahead context in the target sequence and the source word's context. This work proposes a novel mechanism, the look-ahead focus mechanism (LAFM), which effectively identifies crucial source words by examining both their context in the source sentence and the target word's look-ahead context in the target sequence. The LAFM's integration with attention is explored, showing that to effectively capture look-ahead information, source word context and target word's look-ahead context must be distinguished. Experimental results on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that LAFM outperforms existing models, including the standard attention model and its variants, as well as other generation methods including coverage and gap penalty models. The success of LAFM highlights its ability to leverage source word context to influence translation direction and quality. Furthermore, LAFM's performance can be combined with other generation methods for even better performance. The code is available at https://github.com/sgwillems/lookahead_focus_nmt. We investigate the properties of a scalar $\phi^3$ Gross-Neveu model in two dimensions at large $N$ using both analytical and numerical methods. In the regime where the coupling is strong, we show that the behavior of the model diverges from that of a known non-interacting limit, a specific type of scaling limit known as the Ising model. We also observe in the strong-coupling regime that the rate of information loss is higher than what would be predicted by the conventional measure of entanglement entropy. Based on these findings and previous work regarding a non-local scale-invariant fixed point in the $6\gamma$ model, we propose a new framework for understanding the properties of interacting ground states in quantum field theories, and we explore the implications of this framework for the concept of entanglement entropy. We support our results with both analytical approximations and numerical simulations. We conclude by discussing the potential limitations and workarounds for a long-standing challenge associated with calculating thermal fixed points in a wide range of field theories. Our work presents new insights and fosters a deeper understanding of this complex computational problem. We further speculate that the rate of information loss that we measured in the $\phi^3$ Gross-Neveu model might serve as a universal lower bound for renormalization group trajectories starting from the trivial fixed point, with implications for both theoretical and practical applications in renormalization group flows. We also address a related problem regarding the possible dual description of a type of string theory known as TQFT, and we connect our results to a wide range of existing literature on this topic. We further speculate that the rate of information loss that we measured in the $\phi^3$ Gross-Neveu model might be related to a type of entropy production known as the holographic entanglement entropy in a specific type of theoretical context known as the AdS/CFT correspondence, although a direct proof is still required to confirm this connection. Our work provides new insights and motivates further research to understand the underlying ground-state properties of quantum field theories at large $N$. We also develop an important concept in this paper known as entanglement entropy decay rate, calculate it using both analytical and numerical methods, and compare our results to a non-local scale-invariant fixed point in the $6\gamma$ model. Our work supports the idea that the rate of information loss is higher than what would be predicted by the conventional measure of entanglement entropy. We also support our results using both numerical methods and analytical

Hirosa and Shirakawa recently proposed an approach to valuing Asian options by first transforming the associated partial integro-differential equation into a whole differential equation and then applying Lie group analysis to find symmetries and similarity transformations. They then claim that this method can effectively handle a broad range of geometric Asian options, although it's noted that non-standard ergodicity conditions are required in some cases. In our response, we suggest that this method can be viewed as a typical example of theENTE technique, which was first introduced by Fan and Wu in 2018, and that ENT is more comprehensive in this context as it doesn't require the introduction of new similarity variables. As a result, ENT is found to handle a wider range of scenarios, even when non-standard ergodicity conditions apply, and it offers the advantage of being able to tackle coupled integro-differential equations that describe dependent Asian options. Furthermore, ENT is found to align with the standard approach to valuing Asian options when ergodicity conditions are satisfied. To showcase the ENT method's efficiency, we provide pricing examples that demonstrate its accuracy and computational efficiency for a variety of geometric Brownian motions and practical strike prices. The ENT method's performance is found to be superior to that of Monte Carlo simulations in terms of speed and precision, and it is particularly suitable for use when ergodicity conditions aren't met. To expand the application of ENT in dependent Asian options, where multiple underlying assets are involved, we suggest introducing a Lie group analysis approach that generalizes typical non-linear dependence models such as the chi-squared, absolute deviation, correlation, and multiplication schemes. By doing so, the typical non-linear dependence models are found to be redefined in terms of ENT, and a new approach to valuing dependent Asian options is proposed using ENT. To validate the ENT method, we provide numerical results for dependent Asian options that align with theoretical findings in the literature. Finally, the ENT method's ease of use and the wealth of additional features that are available to the user are demonstrated through the deployment of a custom Python ent package. The ent package provides users with a range of easy-to-use functions for automatically generating partial differential equations, determining non-standard ergodicity and ergodicity barrier conditions, calculating Markov coefficients, performing Lie group analysis, and, ultimately, obtaining numerical solutions to the associated integro-differential equations. The ent package is found to be highly extensible, as it seamlessly integrates with a range of established numerical libraries, including NumPy, SciPy, PySAL

Although observables are limited to galaxy clusters beyond 100 Mpc, the area to be studied can expand as more sensitive instruments are developed. Their detection is challenging due to the extremely low rate of cosmic protons, resulting in the weak gamma-ray emission from these clusters. However, advanced telescopes like the CTA will make the gamma-ray flux from distant galaxy clusters measurable in the future. When accounting for systematic uncertainties, especially regarding the cosmic proton rate, the analysis of these observations can significantly restrict this rate. Currently, the largest observational limit exists for clusters beyond 280 Mpc, whereas collections of smaller galaxy clusters or groups are beyond 150 Mpc, and some individual large galaxy groups are undetectable due to insufficient signal strength or the lack of known collections. Notably, some misinterpretations of existing data may eliminate the possibility of detecting gamma rays from galaxy clusters or the cosmic proton rate. Evaluating stacked galaxy clusters or collections is particularly difficult due to the current sensitivity issues, but when accounting for systematic uncertainties, the analysis of future observations is expected to make notable contributions to the understanding of hadronic processes in the universe. A new, powerful gamma-ray detector like the GLAST-LS, which is currently under development, is needed to achieve a significant advancement in this field, and this could potentially happen during the CTA's operational period or possibly during the ongoing GLAST-LS satellite project. signatures in gravitational waves produced by gravitational interactions between
particles. Specifically, we investigate how gravitational waves are generated from
the collapse of overdensities containing multiple primordial particles in the
early universe. By developing a classical-based approach analogous to
cosmological collider experiments, we've established a non-perturbative method to
compute these gravitational waves. Our work applies broadly and serves as a
case study for examining fundamental particle interactions. By studying
anti-particle pairs produced in overdensities, we've identified distinct
features linked to specific quantum properties. Our analysis not only enhances
understanding of individual particle interactions but also presents new markers
that can be used to characterize the state of the primordial universe. Moreover,
the proposed gravitational wave spectrum contains information necessary for
reconstructing the quantum state of the primordial universe. By further studying
spectrum features and fundamental interactions, it may be possible to determine the
number of primordial particles present and explore multi-particle collisions. 
Additionally, we've demonstrated that features embedded within the gravitational
waves produced in overdensities can persist for several billion years after the
Big Bang, making them easily detectable with the laser interferometer graviational
wave observatory II. Detecting these signatures could provide early evidence for
the existence of fundamental particle interactions and inform quantum field theory
during this period. Ultimately, the proposed method for computing gravitational
waves from overdensities applies to features embedded within the cosmic microwave
background radiation and could also be used to explore novel physics at very large
 scales by reconstructing primordial features and fundamental particle interactions
via observational data. To facilitate further research, we've made publicly
available a code used to compute these gravitational waves in overdensities. 
Finally, we've demonstrated that detecting gravitational waves from overdensities
present new avenues for exploring the state of the primordial universe and could
be utilized in conjunction with other experiments. Our work offers a fresh path for
investigating the state of the primordial universe and could provide groundbreaking
insights into fundamental particle physics at very early periods of time without
requiring significant advancements in current experimental techniques. Moreover,
the proposed detection methods of features using current data do not require
significant computational power and could be performed with relatively simple
algorithms. Ultimately, the proposed methods for detecting features embedded

It's proven that specific neurons in deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) yield interpretable results when activated during the process of image classification, however the exact manner in which this occurs remains unclear. We propose LVSFF, an algorithm that identifies and explains which parts of an image are being targeted by neurons during classification and suggests a novel, 3D representation of CNNs that encompasses both image contents and semantic aspects. Our technique effectively handles neurons that represent complex visual patterns by associating them with corresponding image regions and breaks down multi-faceted patterns into their constituent parts, thereby offering a clearer visual understanding of the classification process in the human perception space. When tested across images of birds, airplanes, and everyday objects, LVSFF reveals that a considerable portion of neurons (around 52%) rely on minimal image contents such as a single object feature, while some (around 14%) use contextual information. Moreover, LVSFF shows that neurons focused on object parts tend to classify images incorrectly more often than expected and those focused only on the background frequently fail to spot birds. During visual reasoning, LVSFF also discovers that birds with distinctive characteristics like brightly colored beaks or feathers are easier for the model to recognize, while images with dominant noisy backgrounds lead the neurons to inaccurate classifications. Our technique provides a novel means of understanding how CNNs learn to identify visual patterns that humans can decipher. You can find the necessary code at https://github.com/asharakeh/lvsff. For demonstrations, visit https://explainer.deepvision.ai. Additionally, the model's predictions are accessible at https://deepvision.ai/classify. Our results suggest that significant challenges remain in how CNNs naturally generate visual concepts, which we believe is a critical issue. Visualization of feature map regions, corresponding to specific neurons, reveals that CNNs primarily classify images based on unique visual patterns rather their genuine meanings. For instance, despite both images containing a bird with yellow feathers, the model assigns the image featuring a chicken to the "golden eagle" category. When testing the model's ability to describe its classifications, we observe that most feature maps fail to correspond with labels that make sense to humans, indicating another major issue. Notably, our technique, LVSFF, discovers that some neurons use contextual information to represent complex visual patterns and that majority of birds feature a dominant background that helps the model to accurately identify them, while others rely solely on object features to classify the image. One-dimensional materials that conduct electricity typically have well-established rules governing how individual particles interact with each other, with repulsive forces predominating in cuprates. However, researchers have discovered that in one-dimensional cuprate compounds, where particles are arranged along a straight line, the overall interaction between particles is more complicated and cannot be easily predicted based on existing knowledge. A question arose as to the origin of a long-range attractive force between distant particles, with some speculating that it could be due to a short-waved particle vibration, while others proposed it could be the result of a long-waved lattice wave, which transmits energy poorly. However, researchers have now shown through mathematical analysis that this long-range attractive force can actually be attributed to a long-waved particle vibration, which has a significant influence on the energy pattern of the entire system. Furthermore, researchers have demonstrated that in conditions of extreme cold, the energy pattern exhibits a series of distinctive jumps rather than becoming more irregular and fragmented with increasing distance, in contrast to a long-waved lattice wave, which would result in a more fragmented pattern. This discovery has significant implications for the understanding of long-range attractive forces in one-dimensional materials that conduct electricity. (Figure presented within the article) A graphical illustration shows the different types of attractive and repulsive forces at different intervals of distance, with repulsive forces dominating at close distances, a short-waved particle vibration creating an energy 'well' in between, and a long-waved particle vibration resulting in a series of energy 'jumps.' A long-waved lattice wave fails to explain the regular pattern of the energy spectrum at low temperatures. (End of Figure caption) Note that in conditions of extreme cold, the energy pattern exhibits a series of distinctive jumps rather than becoming more irregular and fragmented with increasing distance. This paper introduces a novel approach for identifying the causal structure of a dataset under limited resources by leveraging discrete, tabular data. We evaluate the effectiveness of five diverse learning algorithms – BAYES, LiNGAM, PC, FCI, and FCI Annealed Bootstrap – which employ distinct learning strategies. Through a comprehensive series to evaluate their performance, we examine each method's reliability in discovering the true causal structure of a dataset as defined by the true positive rate. We apply the Mutipurpose Health Individual Awareness dataset to compare the causal structure discovery capabilities of these different learning algorithms. We also analyze the reliability of these algorithms in discovering the causal structure of a dataset when a portion of the data is missing. Our results demonstrate that BAYES, PC, and FCI Annealed Bootstrap are suitable for their respective tasks, while the other algorithms may have limitations in certain scenarios. Therefore, BAYES, PC, and FCI Annealed Bootstrap can be considered reliable options for their respective applications. Furthermore, we observe that the reliability of these algorithms may be impacted if a significant portion of the data is missing, thus highlighting the need to develop more robust methods to discover the causal structure of a dataset under missing data conditions. Finally, we outline potential areas for the further development of these algorithms. The complete source code and dataset used in this study are publicly accessible through the repository located at https://github.com/jarwasser117/Causal-structural-discovery. The dataset can also be downloaded from the website at http://mphtimes.cn/data/individual/. We warmly welcome researchers to collaborate with us on this study by referencing the provided repository. We also anticipate receiving feedback and suggestions from fellow researchers.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Co$_2$Mn$_2$Mn$_4$N$4$ type,  the emergence of magnetic skyrmions is identified through direct visualization by means of the local magnetization projection technique and confirmed by microscopic spin-polarized neutron diffraction. The contribution analyzes the recent study by J. R. Sun's group on the dynamics of skyrmions in the system. According to the measurement, when temperature reaches 52.5 K and field is applied at 10 kOe, the unstable skyrmion lattice starts to move due to the application of a small magnetic field, however, no topological effect on the melting process of the skyrmion lattice is observed, contrary to the group's claims. Moreover, no topological melting has been reported in the system at any condition either. We conclude by suggesting that further study is required to fully understand the dynamics of skyrmions in the system. (Published in Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter, Volume 34, Issue 8, 082002)

High-Dimensional Dynamic Variable Modeling involves advanced statistical techniques and methodologies that account for relationships between variables that change over time, often incorporating time series data and latest high-capacity data analysis tools. This enables researchers to study complex connections in fields like economics, finance and biology, providing a solid foundation for predicting future trends and decision-making. Although there's a vast array of models and methods in this field, this paper offers a concise overview and categorization of the primary approaches, focusing on Bayesian methods, matrix methods and other techniques. To stimulate further innovation, the authors present possible directions for future advancement and highlight existing challenges and limitations, ultimately aiming to make the high-dimensional dynamic modeling framework more accessible for practitioners and scholars. We introduce a novel, finely-grained approach to protect sensitive data in images and maintain its integrity. Leveraging the latest developments in reversible authentication and watermarking, this research focuses on a specific aspect - reversible concealment - which involves wrapping hidden information within an authentic image. Since the quality of the concealed image is crucial, but contrarian to the hidden data's accuracy, achieving optimal quality necessitates compromised results. To tackle this dilemma, we propose an innovative, probabilistic technique, known as Bayesian Neural Concealment, consisting of an encoder, authentication channel, and reconstruction channel, all functioning in tandem to seamlessly integrate hidden data into the image while maintaining its recoverability. Thorough experiments on three diverse datasets demonstrate our approach's success in striking a balance between the concealed image's quality and the hidden data's accuracy. Notably, it outperforms existing methods in terms of fidelity, and matches their accuracy. Our findings indicate that fine-grained quality and authenticity can be achieved through fine-grained hiding. The proposed approach's source code is publicly available on GitHub. Our study also includes additional conclusive findings on quality-based concealment methods. Moreover, a comprehensive survey on reversible data concealment is conducted, highlighting its distinct features from other data hiding methods, and leading to a range of novel research avenues. The survey is accessible at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-23145-3_3. Our research is registered on arXiv under the reference arXiv:2102.12185, and on the CVF Database with the ID CVF_2020_000501. Our approach was registered in the Challenge on Data hiding at ICDMW 2020 with the ID ICDMW2020DH_C_2. The challenge dataset and submission can be found at https://icdmw2020dh.ient.uva.es/. Our submission to the challenge earned a first-place finish in both tracks, and the challenge dataset and submission can be found at https://icdmw2020dh.ient.uva.es/. We utilize several numerical databases of globally baroclinic convective turbulent flows, spanning various intensities and scales of thermodynamic fluctuations, to evaluate the efficacy of mean-field dynamo models in describing global convective dynamos. By comparing the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) time averages of certain parameters in the models with those extracted from the simulations, we create optimal parameters for each turbulent effect in question. Interestingly, we find that convective stability parameter and eddy diffusivity both decrease as the level of thermodynamic fluctuations increase, while the magnetizing parameter, however, exhibits an increasing trend. Furthermore, we find that incorporating the full spectrum of turbulent effects in the models yields time-averaged solutions of the MHD field that demonstrate remarkable consistency with the results extracted from the simulations, showcasing the models' ability to provide accurate descriptions of global convective dynamos. Additionally, we find that incorporating further turbulent effects, such as the bismuth effect, does not significantly affect the model's performance in describing global convective dynamos, providing evidence that these effects may not be crucial in generating field oscillations or improving overall field magnetization in this context. Overall, we find that incorporating the full spectrum of turbulent effects in mean-field dynamo models is crucial in producing realistic results that are consistent with those extracted from simulations of global convective turbulent flows. The case for incorporating additional non-resistive effects, however, is less clear-cut, leading to further investigation of their importance in describing global convective dynamos. As such, we find that incorporating the full spectrum of turbulent effects in mean-field dynamo models is a necessary condition in accurately describing global convective dynamos and generating realistic results. The case for incorporating additional non-resistive effects, however, is less clear-cut and requires further investigation. The code used for generating the results in this paper is available upon request for intercomparisons or further investigation. The results in this paper may significantly impact the understanding and validity of results in the literature on incorporating turbulent effects in global convective dynamos, leading to potential revisions or refinements. This interacts with the extended magnetohydrodynamic (EMHD) equations through a dyadic equation for the second-order correlation function of magnetic fluctuations. Our paper draws inspiration from the conservative reformulation of the quasilinear PDE by Briot and Lemoult, extending it to the Galerkin approximation for turbulent plasmas. This is achieved by employing finite elements for the PDE, retaining a conservative structural property of the equation, and implying the conservation of the total magnetic energy, hence providing rigorous mathematical foundations for the numerical modeling of turbulent plasmas in the quasilinear regime. Our model is further evaluated through numerical simulations of the quasilinear EMHD model in the slab geometry, with various flavors of the Navier--Stokes equation for the incompressible fluid component. A key advantage of our approach is the ability to develop local and semi-implicit iterative schemes in the context of the quasilinear framework, with extensive testing performed using synthetic test cases in the Lagrangian framework. These test cases, with solutions evolving over time, have enabled the assessment of the stability and convergence of the iterative schemes, including the impact of the Brunt--Russell number and the Brunt number characterizing quasilinear fluctuations. Furthermore, the implicit scheme has been evaluated for its potential applications in the modeling of weakly anisotropic plasmas, with the solution of the nonlinear PDE requiring the projection framework. We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of the Lyapunov equation (L). Given that T is uniformly bounded and T' is Hille-Yosida for the equation -T' \eta = \eta', with \eta and \eta' in our Banach space, we show that any solution of L with this condition yields T(t) close to a bounded operator as t approaches infinity. Our result generalizes previous work in J. Diff. Equations (2015) and extends the boundaries of the mentioned reference by relaxing the requirement for C1 continuity. Utilizing the relationship between the resolvent and adjoint semigroups, we extend our findings to the unbounded case and develop a corollary that extends Keyfitz-Muller on the stability of the heat equation. Finally, through the use of an integral operator, we extend our findings to the case of a semigroup acting on maps from R to the unit circle and prove the Ulas linespeed theorem, providing a connection to the theory of compact operators. Our work was inspired by the study of certain infinite-dimensional systems in the work of Nussbaum. The simulation of dimuonium atom interactions with various substances under external fields has been carried out, which may provide a means of detecting these atoms by observing changes in mass density or buoyancy in the presence of external fields. A program called MuMuPy has been developed to perform these calculations, which involve generating 3D density maps of interaction sites within substances and calculating the resulting electric field distributions. These fields determine the potential energy between the dimuonium atoms and the substance, leading to changes in their density and ultimately their gravitational shift in vacuum energy principles. A user-friendly interface has been implemented to easily compute and visualize these changes for different substances and dimuonium states. By applying these calculations to experiments searching for V$_{ud}$ flavor-changing neutral currents, the expected effects of these currents on muon atom gravitational redshift were calculated and used as a control reference. Furthermore, the possibility of detecting dimuonium atoms within superfluid helium was explored, with the goal of being used as a control experiment in future muon electron muon proton collision experiments. A major advantage of utilizing solid media to observe dimuonium atoms is that they can be in proximity to each other, allowing for coherent superposition of the atoms to be measured. This is in contrast to being used as target material, where dimuonium atoms would stand out due to their significant loss of electrons. A comprehensive discussion of potential detection methods and experimental setups has been discussed, including a possible search at the Paul Scherrer Institute using MuMuPy-optimized targets. A critical component of muon electron muon proton collision experiments will be developing methods to easily identify and analyze the produced baryons. Given the current rate of progress in superconducting magnetic systems, it is plausible that dimuonium atom gravitational separation will be achieved prior to the start of these massive particle accelerator projects. A thorough examination of the theoretical separation limits of dimuonium and Xenenonium atoms within superfluid helium has been carried out, including a detailed analysis of the Helium-4 phase diagram. Considering the existing laboratory equipment, it is feasible to achieve separation on a relatively small scale, with the ultimate goal of achieving complete separation among the muonium, dimuonium, and xenonium states. One of the key features of the muonium atom is that it can be produced at a very high rate in a circular shape, which is essential for its separation. This study extends power absolute and relative return utilities in portfolio optimization to address both asset price uncertainty and relative price uncertainty, yielding new results. Assuming continuous trading and a power utility function, we derive an analytical solution for the optimal portfolio allocation in the class of linear portfolios. The paper also introduces a stochastic maximum likelihood estimation method to estimate model parameters when some asset prices are observed, revealing how relative prices impact optimal portfolio frames and frames structures in the presence of uncertainty. Furthermore, we demonstrate how relative prices affect mean-variance frames, illustrating increased robustness with their use. The effects of various parameters on the optimal portfolio framework and structures are thoroughly analyzed. The methods employed in this research can be readily extended to other optimization problems involving relative prices. Analysis of panoramic X-ray observations reveals an inverse relationship between the IGM's temperature and the host galaxy's mass. Text retrieval is a crucial operation in numerous document management systems, and recent advancements have enabled the transformation of texts into compact, invariant embeddings that enable similar texts to be grouped together and retrieved efficiently. Although major breakthroughs have been achieved, retrieving text clips or segments rather than entire texts remains a much more difficult task. This challenge is due to the fact that shorter clips lack sufficient contextual information, and the existing models are not well-suited for retrieving text clips because they treat all input tokens equally and apply a fixed transformer architecture to each token independently. In order to address this issue, a novel TS2-Net architecture called Token Shift and Selection Transformer Net is introduced for Text-Clip Retrieval. This architecture is designed to not only not increase the model's parameters significantly but also improve the ranking of retrieved text clips relative to their corresponding full texts. This is achieved by introducing a token shift mechanism that repositions clip segment tokens within a pre-trained token-expanded text embedding. A selection transformer is then proposed to determine which of the shifted token locations constitute a valid text clip and to also identify the optimal relative token order within that clip. This is done by having two learned matching functions that produce a high scoring pair when the text clip and its corresponding full text are correctly aligned. Experimental results on the MS MARCO document ranking dataset have shown that TS2-Net outperforms the existing state-of-the-art Text Retrieval models by a large margin, and it also surpasses the existing state-of-the-art Text-Clip Retrieval model. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of various TS2-Net sub-components is also carried out. By utilizing a proprietary dataset, it was demonstrated that the proposed CNN model can accurately identify interference caused by various electrical devices in a deep learning format. The proposed system utilizes a unique representation of audio signals in the frequency domain, known as Constant Q Transform (CQT). The proposed architecture consists of multiple CNN layers, the output of which is processed by a fully connected layer to determine the probability of concurrent device interference. The proposed system provides interference analysis results similar to those obtained using the Synch-RCN system, an industry-standard solution. Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model when it's modified by spin-orbit coupling and an optical superfluid state. By employing a self-consistent approach based on second-order Green's functions, we investigate the formation of Fermi-like excitations resulting from the cooperation of spin-orbit coupling and inter-species interactions. We also identify the various types of superfluid degradation and find that the resulting states exhibit both quantized resistance and multiple phases of instability. Notably, the influence of spin-orbit coupling on the system's instability is significant, leading to two distinct phases of instability: one associated with density waves and the other with spin-ordering. When comparing our results to recent experiments, we suggest that the observed zero-peak in the imaginary part of the self-energy could be attributed to a new type of excitations brought about by an interplay between spin-orbit coupling and inter-species interactions. Furthermore, we propose that the resulting phase could be identified using quantum spin susceptibility in combination with existing experimental data. Additionally, we map out a phase diagram for the $t'-t''$ plane and demonstrate how it can be modified by spin-orbit coupling and inter-species interactions. Presently, there is no unified approach to create novel kernels by building upon existing ones. In this paper, we explore the method of constructing Gaussian Process kernels using fundamental mathematical expressions through a platform we call Python Kernel Builder. Our builder enables users to define kernels by combining existing expressions in an intuitive manner, making it easier to create new kernels tailored to specific tasks, even those involving complex multi-modal functions, by breaking them down into simpler components. This demonstrates the potential of building kernels from basic components similar to how deep neural networks are constructed from elementary functions. Designs for next-generation high-energy colliders incorporating muon beams are taking shape, with the potential for an energy reach of over 10 TeV. Yet, the high-intensity muon beams intended for these machines are anticipated to result in substantially higher beam-induced backgrounds compared to earlier designs, posing challenges for observing genuine physics signals. In this context, reducing beam-induced noise is essential to enable detection of various physics phenomena, necessitating an optimized design of the detector and/or the strategic deployment of beam manipulation techniques. In this paper, the potential area of focus for reducing beam-induced noise in future high-energy Muon Collider designs is identified and several potential solutions are proposed. The paper specifically examines and compares the efficacy of detector design optimization and beam manipulation in reducing beam-induced noise, with particular emphasis on the likelihood of implementing each method. The paper presents an in-depth analysis of near-far coupler (NFC) beam dump systems, showcases an advanced NFC concept designed to mitigate beam-induced noise, and discusses the potential for utilizing fast pulsed steering magnets (FPSMs) to counteract beam-induced noise. The paper also explores other innovative methods to reduce beam-induced noise, including the utilization of FPSMs in the muon decays, muon screening, and optimized FPSM placement on the beam pipe. The paper culminates in a discussion of the synergistic effect of combining FPSMs with the optimization of NFCs and FPSMs in the optimization of the detector design, with a view to creating a Muon Collider detector optimized for reduced beam-induced noise. The paper is intended to serve as an early-call for proposals, encouraging the community to submit innovative ideas to NASA/DOE for funding in 2022. The paper also makes the code for the FPSM integration into the MadGraph 5\_aMC\@\_NEXT::\@\_MC module lightweight and publicly available on the GitHub platform. Current methods for training neural networks to drop out neurons have focused on regulating their expected output, but this approach has limitations as it doesn't account for the actual output and cannot be optimized beyond a certain point. In contrast, previous work on dropout has used non-differentiable methods to eliminate neurons, resulting in subpar performance. In response, we present the Spartan framework, which addresses these challenges through a novel differentiable approach for introducing sparsity in neural networks. By reinterpreting dropout as a optimization problem and applying a regularized transportation mechanism, we can control sparsity in any Riemannian manifold, including neural networks, and derive a clear objective function from the optimal solution. This allows us to develop simple yet effective gradient-based updates for both model weights and sparsity parameters, making the training process more efficient and enabling easy integration with other training methods. Additionally, we can derive a surrogate objective function for our objective, which provides a straightforward generalization of classical dropout. Our framework is compatible with various neural network architectures and can be used with a wide range of training methods. Notably, we find that leveraging our framework with existing methods can significantly improve performance, with small improvements in sparsity leading to large gains in accuracy in some cases. In our experiments, we explore the performance of the Spartan framework on a variety of vision and language tasks and compare its results to state-of-the-art methods for regularized training, demonstrating effective sparsity induction and consistent accuracy improvement. In particular, we find that small amounts of sparsity can lead to large performance gains on tasks such as image classification and machine translation. Moreover, we discover that large-scale input representations can still maintain significant amount of accuracy despite much higher level sparsity, and that our framework is compatible with a wide range of neural network architectures, including vision models up to 33B and language models up to 84M. Finally, we find that large-scale training with our framework and much higher level sparsity leads to more robust neural network performance, even when introducing additional regularization mechanisms. In our code release, we provide detailed examples of using the Spartan framework to train a range of vision and language models, complete with configuration files and experimental results. This allows other researchers to build upon and reproduce our work, representing an important step towards developing more efficient and effective neural network training algorithms. In addition, we provide access to the neural network architecture search library through our GitHub repository, which includes the full range of vision and language models used in our evaluation. This resource represents an important contribution to the neural network architecture search

This area of study aims to uncover the underlying structural information in graph nodes to generate continuous and evolving representations throughout a graph's evolution.
