of the $^7$H ground state, accurately described by coupling a $^3$H nucleus with four
neutrons in different orbital states. This particular configuration offers one distinct
arrangement, where all neutrons have occupied the $s$ orbital, along with seven additional
states resulting from combining the $s$ and $d$ orbital configurations with diverse spin
orientations. Utilizing the expanded space for the ground state, we successfully account for
the $^7$H ground state's energy using a $V_{\rm NSO}$ potential, thus effectively explaining
its position relative to the $^3$H+4n excitation energy spectrum. This analysis paves the
way for understanding other island of inversion systems consisting of neutron-rich nuclei. Moreover,
our study of the $^7$H ground state also leads to a theoretical description of its electromagnetic
properties, including electromagnetic decays to $^6$H and other $^6$H isomers, as well as electron
capture in $^7$H involving the $^{+}{}^7$H island of inversion. This work is found to have significant

isotopes near the $N=8$ magic number. These insights hold particular significance in the ongoing search for
invisible states, including the possible existence of the Pauli-excluded $^7$He $J^{\pi}=1/2^{-}$ state.

Deep representatives learn complex, high-dimensional features that minimize a given loss function with simplified, easy-to-optimize objectives. Unlike traditional methods using mean or variance, our research applies the Sinkhorn divergence to a deep learning framework. This divergence measures similarity based on the permutations of elements in two sets and is scalable for high-dimensional data. Our theoretical analysis shows that Sinkhorn divergence is a consistent estimator of the covariance and pseudo-covariance for subgap distributions in linear regression, making it an ideal criterion for representative learning. Furthermore, we developed a representative learning algorithm called Deep Sinkhorn Representative (DeSR) and tested its performance on both synthetic and real-world data. The results confirm that Sinkhorn divergence leads to more accurate and robust representatives compared to existing methods. Moreover, the representatives learned using Sinkhorn divergence exhibit stronger connections to the underlying data, resulting in well-structured and easy-to-interpret features. These features have the potential to enhance our understanding of the data as well as improve downstream tasks. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, numerous voluntary tracing initiatives were established to complement the existing Test and Trace system, with the primary goal of enhancing the overall tracing effort.  By leveraging robust methods and large datasets, our research examines the effectiveness of these voluntary tracing projects in three key areas:  new case discovery, contact identification, and contact reach, and compares the outcomes to the existing services.  Our findings suggest that the voluntary services have primarily strengthened the existing systems, rather than replacing them as targeted partners to the Test and Trace system.  Specifically, they have improved the new case discovery rate by 3.6%, increased the number of contacts identified per new case by 11%, and increased the reach of contacts by 10%.  However, a closer analysis of the work reveals that the voluntary services primarily excelled in the initial stages of the tracing process, particularly in the first day and two days following a new case notification, where they helped isolate key contacts and prevent infections.  Conversely, they were found to have minimal impact on the later stages of the tracing process.  By integrating the data from the voluntary services into the existing systems, our results suggest the potential for a combined improvement in the overall efficiency of the tracing effort.  Finally, our work sheds light on the key factors driving the success of the voluntary services, and indicates that future partnerships should prioritize establishments with high volumes of customers, located in urban areas, and those where interactions with customers are frequent and dynamic.  By doing so, they can effectively augment the existing tracing efforts.  The methods employed in our research are broadly applicable and can be utilized in various fields beyond the COVID-19 tracing context.  Specifically, they can be applied in areas related to economic analysis and public policy.  By leveraging the same data sources, our research can provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of the voluntary services from a more economic perspective.  Therefore, our results can be further generalized and provide valuable applications in other fields of study. In settings with existing behavior but without access to rewards or state values, we develop an approach called RCREL. RCREL uses supervised learning to model the complex dynamics of a system, followed by a constraint-based optimization of the reward function. RCREL's reward optimization is grounded in solving a maximum likelihood estimation problem. The approach is illustrated by applying it to the problem of learning the optimal reward for an autonomous vehicle to follow a predetermined route. RCREL is compared to alternative methods including learning through trial and error and using demonstrations to design the reward function. The results of these comparisons indicate that RCREL is able to learn a reward efficiently quickly and effectively. The effectiveness of the approach was also validated using MuJoCo benchmarks, showing that RCREL is capable of learning the optimal reward even in complex control domains. The resulting reward functions were found to improve the sample efficiency of value and policy learning. The ability of RCREL to efficiently learn the optimal reward under real-world time constraints was demonstrated by setting up a simulation environment to test the system in a loop. The approach is also theoretically justified by proving its robustness to perturbations in the optimization of the reward function. The general conditions under which the approach is valid provide a useful framework for investigating the robustness of the reward function, offering a potential area of improvement for the methodology. The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will place highly precise coordinates on nearly 1 billion celestial sources over the course of 5 years, using a space-based telescope to measure their positions, motions, and light angles with unprecedented accuracy. As the most advanced star mapping project to date, GAIA will create a detailed 3D cosmic picture, revolutionizing astronomers' capabilities to study the structure of our galaxy, the movement of its stars, the formation and destruction of stars, the properties of binary systems, the distribution of small-body orbits, and planetary systems. This article introduces the mission, its scientific objectives, and observational challenges, as well as outlining the technical design, functional aspects, and testing of GAIA's on-board scientific instruments. Furthermore, it highlights the diverse community of scientists collaborating on the mission and their respective areas of expertise. Finally, this article concludes with the anticipated outcomes of GAIA's data analysis and its resulting impact on modern astronomical research. As the mission is presently in its final preparation stage, this overview provides a comprehensive summary of the major developments and advancements made since the completion of the development phase, which began in 2011. As such, this paper may serve as a helpful introductory resource for scholars new to GAIA and the related community, providing a thorough review of the mission from a variety of perspectives. The accompanying multimedia content includes illustrations, images, and videos depicting various aspects of GAIA, its scientific instruments, technical design, and related topics, as well as illustrations and videos describing key components of the mission, its scientific instruments, and related topics. The text itself is intended to serve as a standalone resource, whereas the multimedia content enhances the understanding of the topic, particularly for readers who are new to the mission, and visual elements are crucial in clarifying complex concepts of 3D astronomy, astrophysics, and related scientific topics. A joint publication with the Astrobiology Journal (Volume 19, Issue 8, 2019) is also present, discussing the planetary outcomes of GAIA in a standalone text. For analyzing graph structure and implementing algorithms efficiently, treewidth is an important parameter. A treewidth-based method uses vertex dividers to calculate the treewidth of a graph. By employing smaller vertex dividers, which occupy less space, treewidth computations can be carried out using less memory. We've developed new vertex divider types with minimal size: $\mathcal{O}(n + H)$ for biconnected graphs and $\mathcal{O}(n + \text{tw}^2)$ for general graphs. These new dividers have applications in algorithmic problems, notably, $2^{\mathcal{O}(n + \text{tw}\log \text{tw})} \cdot n$-time algorithm for vertex coloring on treewidth $\text{tw}$ graphs, which exhibits linear dependence on the treewidth. Additionally, we've created a $\mathcal{O}(n + \text{tw}^2)$-sized data structure for computing branch-width, yielding a $2^{\mathcal{O}(\text{tw}\log \text{tw})}$-time algorithm. [Current methods use $\mathcal{O}(n + \text{tw}^3)}$-sized dividers and $2^{(5/3)\text{tw}}$-time algorithms respectively.] The development of these new, space-efficient vertex dividers is foundational for further research. The construction of these dividers is based on a new, recursive decompositions of graphs, which is also significant and useful on its own. The experimentally verified results demonstrate the practical implications of these discoveries. This approach assigns node weights that reflect various aspects such as centrality, connectivity, performance, and category affiliation. We emphasize that in many networks, especially those derived from observational data and involving directed relationships, proper interpretation of weights necessitates consideration of multiple perspectives. Therefore, we introduce the concept of weighted group membership analysis with multiple weight orientations and offer a few methodological suggestions for heterogeneous, inferred, and mixed datasets. These suggestions primarily revolve around the choice of weight sets. Firstly, we recommend employing multiple weights to identify potential biases and cross-validation errors in networks. Secondly, we suggest selecting weights based on well-established measures to ensure methodological consistency. Lastly, when multiple weights are not available, we provide an alternative approach for choosing a single weight that is closely related to the network's structural and descriptive attributes, thereby offering a more flexible analytical framework. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we apply it to a directed social network involving students in a game development project. Our results highlight the value of using multiple weights to define groups in networks. Moreover, by annotating the analysis with confidence levels, we demonstrate that weighted group membership analysis can provide insightful support during the network analysis process. Ultimately, we offer recommendations for improving this approach and showcase its applicability to both measured and inferred network settings. Consequently, we provide a comprehensive, open-source example code that is designed to facilitate future applications of this analysis model. One key factor holding back the widespread adoption of neural networks in physics from theoretical viewpoints lies in their inherently unpredictable nature, which hinders graspable loss functions and hindering training in a data-driven setting. By assuming that the training dataset is comprehensive enough to accurately map input to output, we explore how reliable neural networks can be without perfect data. Further, focusing on physics-informed neural networks that leverage governing differential equations, we explore their behavior when the data and model are both incomplete, developing an estimate of the expected loss in such cases based on the existing theoretical bounds of approximation theory. By testing this theory on simple examples and the well-known Navier-Stokes equations to model 3D water flow, we confirm its practical applicability and reliability. Furthermore, this approach enables us to derive optimal data collection strategies in cases of limited data, leading to significant time savings when training physics-informed neural networks. Ultimately, our work confirms the potential for neural networks to be a useful tool in physical modeling, translating complex, nonlinear problems into quantifiable risks and turning what was previously an art based on intuition into a data-driven, optimised process. To achieve this, we drew inspiration from a new approach in linear algebra that utilizes combinatorial methods to calculate probability limits, a technique previously unexplored in the context of linear bandits. Furthermore, we have shown the upper limit we derived to hold true under specific conditions by creating a novel combinatorial method to calculate probability limits. In addition to our theoretical contributions, we have also implemented an algorithm based on our findings and verified its effectiveness through a range of simulated trials. We expect our results to have a significant impact on the development of reliable statistical inference techniques in the field of online learning. Graphene, being a unique 2D material, exhibits unique properties that are often associated with its "valleys," which are equivalent to spin polarizations. Despite this, it's the orbital Hall effect that plays a key role in many of its quantum properties, particularly in response to strong magnetic fields, where Berry phases contribute to orbital Hall transitions. This alternative to the valley Hall effect is most pronounced in superlattices and moir\'e lattices, where the orbital Hall effect is expected to dominate due to its stronger impact on Landau levels, particularly in systems with substantial orbital mixing. This expected result is verified through a quantitative analysis of a moiré vortex core, where the orbital Hall transitions are observed to far exceed valley transitions, primarily due to the greater impact of the superperiod on the Landau level structure, resulting in a significant increase in orbital mixing. This is particularly the case when the superperiod is substantially larger than the lattice constant, leading to a stronger interaction between the orbital Hall transitions and transport properties. However, it's also demonstrated that the orbital Hall effect can be synchronized with the valley Hall effect, simply by adjusting the superperiod, which effectively regulates the transition between these two phenomena. This is shown to be the case for a specific moiré structure formed by stacking boron nitride layers, where the application of a magnetic field in the plane reveals a significant difference in conductivity patterns due to the orbital Hall effect, while a finite stacking error effectively switches the transition from the valley to the orbital Hall effect, resulting in a notable change in the conductivity patterns at the edge of the sample. This is found to be the case for all samples in the moir\'e series, providing strong evidence for the dominance of the orbital Hall effect over the valley effect, particularly in response to strong magnetic fields and substantial orbital mixing. The expectation that the orbital Hall effect may dominate due to its stronger impact on the Landau level structure is also supported by a computational analysis using a full three-dimensional tight-binding model. This is found to be the case for a variety of structures including a superlattices of thin lead layers, a lead-germanium alloy, a superlattices of thin inversed lead layers, an atomic lead layer, an atomic lead-germanium layer, an atomic tin layer, an atomic tin-germanium layer, an atomic antimony layer, and an atomic antimony-germanium layer. The G-ADN has demonstrated exceptional performance in generating contamination examples that greatly diminish GNN classification and clustering accuracy. The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are confused with one another due to poor resolution.  In contrast, histogram-based equivalence testing, which compares the photometric properties of potential matches, has been shown to mitigate such issues and improve accuracy.  The existing approach of using photometric histograms has been augmented in this study by analyzing color distributions as well.  A new method called HistEcho, which incorporates histograms and takes into account the statistical uncertainties associated with each source, was developed to complement the existing technique of astrometric probability calculations. The growing presence of ontologies in various domains has resulted in the creation of extensive and intricate ontologies with numerous entities often lacking clear categorizations. This increase has underlined the need for more effective visualization tools that can accurately communicate complex hierarchical and non-hierarchical data to support proficient querying. Although visualizations like concept maps and graph visualizations have been successfully employed to showcase ontology hierarchies, they struggle to accurately represent entity associations. In order to address this limitation, we present OntoPlot, a novel visualization approach that makes it easier to identify both hierarchical and associative connections within ontologies, by plotting entities on a 2D plane according to their relative positions, which are calculated using semantic distances under multiple ontological frameworks. The representation is particularly useful for visualizing non-hierarchical associations and analyzing semantic neighborhoods. We have incorporated OntoPlot into the OntoPlotly Python library, which provides a range of interactive visualization components, allowing users to seamlessly explore and understand ontology structures. The integration of OntoPlot was demonstrated through its application to the extensive YAGO and Wikidata knowledge graphs. Additionally, we have developed a public demo at https://onto-plotly-demo.herokuapp-0.gke.southamerica-west1.gce.googleusercontent.com, which provides an immediate, understandable understanding of YAGO's non-hierarchical associations without the need for prior knowledge of the ontology. The library's current version can be downloaded at https://github.com/andreafazani/OntoPlotly, while it can be installed via the pip package onto-plotly. The diversity of possible ontology structures, coupled with the versatility of OntoPlot, presents numerous potential application scenarios, which are also discussed in this study. In particular, we have observed that OntoPlot's visualizations can be used to identify and analyze non-hierarchical associations at a data enrichment level, which has significant implications for knowledge graph embedding methods. Furthermore, we propose an interactive visualization component, known as the OntoPlot's Semantic Neighborhoods, for visualizing semantic neighborhoods and exploring the entity's contextual associations in both hierarchical and non-hierarchical domains. Last but not least, we present several strategies for automatically detecting and preventing visualizations that may reveal an entity's sensitive information, demonstrating the potential of OntoPlot as a valuable tool in privacy preservation discussions. The integration of OntoPlot into a system for creating visualizations based on semantic relations is an area for further investigation. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate how errors in the trajectory of thrown objects, due to various factors like distraction or physical impairment, affect observers' perception of the throw's technique, particularly the release point. We have developed a systematic method for artificially creating simulations of incorrect release points for virtual throws, using 3D pose data from expert athletes, to accurately represent throws with various flaws. By analyzing both the overall throw and the motion up to the moment of release, we found that certain flaws in the trajectory can make it seem like the thrower intentionally used specific invalid techniques, such as releasing the ball behind their back or twisting their arm. We have also found that releases that are significantly erroneous can lead to significantly altered perceptions, but even small errors can still affect how the throw is perceived. Ultimately, the accuracy of the release point's representation depends on both the version of the throw being watched and the thrower's level of expertise. We present our novel algorithm in the form of a open-source module called fauxthrow, allowing researchers to create more realistic simulations of invalid throws and better design studies that investigate artificial impairments. We apply our work to the specific case of 3/4 pitch breaking balls, but our research offers a versatile framework for studying other types of throws and releases, which can be explored in further investigations. Furthermore, this paper provides an in-depth analysis of how the binding energy distributions are affected by technical factors such as the level of theoretical complexity and molecular structure precision within the context of water and hydrogen chloride clusters, which is expected to significantly impact the development of new astrochemical simulation software. Our findings demonstrate that significant advancements in theoretical accuracy lead to distinct outcomes in the corresponding binding energy distributions. Moreover, employing larger basis sets and higher levels of electron correlation, especially coupled cluster with perturbation theory, has a notable effect on the width of the binding energy distributions for hydrogen chloride clusters. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) have led to the development of "black-box" models that can perform complex tasks independently, but competing effectively in science and engineering requires integrating domain knowledge into ML. In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost the limit of general actuators in power and weight, and offer heightened resilience to failures. We introduce a category of actuator called the spring-pull actuator, characterized by its compact size and capacity to efficiently lower the center of gravity during movement. We develop a direct optimization method for finding the ideal sequence of spring-force profiles that produce efficient straight-line running when applied to a ZMP-based controller, and also incorporate a active learning technique to reduce the time and computational costs associated with simulating the system. We successfully test the resulting policy on a physical robot and verify that it can effectively be used in conjunction with the originally-designed trajectory controller, and even enhance its existing performance. Our research provides theoretical support for utilizing elastic actuators in quadruped locomotion and showcases their potential to expand the movement capabilities of legged robots. We also offer useful insights to streamline the optimization process, and the resulting data can serve as a foundation for developing more sophisticated reinforcement learning methods in the future. The Quadruped Spring-Pull Actuator model is available at https://github.com/hosseinakeh/QSPA. We also supply our associated simulation tools at https://github.com/hosseinakeh/Spring-Based_Simulink. We propose a new variational approach to the problem of determining a basis for energy eigenstates of a system composed of two parts with distinct Hamiltonians acting separately. Compared to existing methods, our approach has the advantages of lower computational requirements, fewer calculations, and simpler implementation, as it only necessitates solving for the eigenvalues of one of the system's Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we provide additional evidence to support the idea that a system's energy eigenstates form a complete basis for its Hilbert space by demonstrating the equivalence of two previously established methods. We then test the precision of our approach by applying it to solve systems with distinct or identical sub-Hamiltonians. We analyze the impact of various parameters on the accuracy of our results and suggest a method for improving accuracy, which involves adjusting the strength of the inter-particle coupling. Finally, we apply our approach to a system with interacting particles bounded by an harmonic potential and analyze the effect of their interaction on their energy eigenstates. Our findings demonstrate the capability of variational methods to accurately describe complex many-body systems and mixtures of bosons and fermions with distinct sub-Hamiltonians. We also derive an analytical expression for the optimal variational parameters using an average principle, which may be useful for expedited simulations. Ultimately, our approach allows for efficient simulations of systems with considerable numbers of interacting particles with varying energy eigenstates, which can be applied to topics such as light molecules, nuclear systems, and ultracold gases. A numerical experiment using the VENUS code revealed that a "ripping mode" first noted in a 1980 study is indeed a genuine phenomenon occurring in a collisionless plasma environment. In this experiment, a heavy ion plasma was superimposed onto a pre-existing transverse density bump, resulting in the growth of a "ripping mode" (a mode characterized by a hollow electron distribution function) via a specific nonlinear process involving the excitation of both the k=0 and k=2 Kelvin-Helmholtz modes. Although earlier research could not yield a ripping mode due to an inability to achieve nonlinear saturation, our small-scale experiment succeeded in doing so. In contrast to linear modes, the resulting ripping mode was found to have distinct nonlinear characteristics and generate large-amplitude magnetic fluctuations in both the perpendicular and parallel directions. In the resulting steady-state, the electron distribution was found to exhibit "bunching" along the x-axis coupled with x-space heating. A small-scale ripping mode was found to support the formation of filamentary structures through a nonlinear "string-like" regime, which was found to exhibit increased conductivity, thereby serving as a pathway for parallel magnetic fields. A ripping regime has also been found to give rise to the formation of electron holes. This small-scale ripping regime was found to bear some resemblance to the microinstability known as the "ripping mode" in quark-gluon plasma theory proposed by McLerron. Our successful experiment has identified a possible mechanism for electron filamentation in a ripping regime in collisionless plasma environments. Furthermore, the resulting small-scale magnetic fields were found to generate a Penrose-Onsager criterion orders of magnitude smaller than previously thought, opening up the possibility of accessing plasma environments similar to those found in white dwarf stars or neutron stars. A small-scale ripping regime has also been found to bear some resemblance to the dynamic processes occurring during solidification phenomena in the presence of a supercooling fluid. Our successful experiment has also demonstrated the possibility of achieving nonlinear plasma regimes in extremely small scales, a concept known as macroquantumity. A key concept in fashion imaging is manipulability, which refers to the ability to achieve desired fashion goals through image processing.  In this study, we explore a novel application of fashion image manipulability, specifically trait manipulation, where we aim to achieve a target image by adjusting a source image with access to only a subset of a pre-trained fashion embedding model. Unlike existing trait manipulation methods that require a massive quantity of fully-labeled data and rely on pixel-level manipulation, our proposed approach involves feature-level manipulation and utilizes semi-supervised learning to handle limited data.  In this context, we define feature-level manipulation as generating a desired image with altered fashion characteristics using a source image and a target image. Our proposed model, called Semi-supervised Feature-level Trait manipulator (SFT), employs a residual learning strategy and introduces adversarial training at the fashion feature level to produce manipulable images. Additionally, we employ domain alignment using a unsupervised fashion embedding model to create a unified representation of fashion images across different domains, known as the unified fashion representation (UFR) cycle. Our experiments on three datasets demonstrate that SFT outperforms existing approaches in terms of manipulating fashion images across multiple domains. Our code is available on GitHub.  In terms of limitations, our approach does not extend to pixel-level manipulation and relies on access to a pre-trained fashion embedding model.  Although we do not fully address this limitation in this study, we believe it presents an interesting area for further research.  In particular, fully integrating our model to work without this restriction is one such potential extension.  Another potential extension is applying our model to manipulate images in multiple styles, which is an additional limitation of our work.  We believe that combining our model with style manipulation could lead to significant improvements in the state-of-the-art.  Ultimately, we hope that our work inspires research in these areas and leads to further advancements in this field. The results illustrate that semi-supervised feature-level manipulations hold significant potential for achieving high-quality results in fashion image manipulability.  Specifically, our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of manipulating images in multiple domains with limited labeled data.  We observe notable improvements in target-test fashion image manipulations on the Fashion2012, FashionERA, and STFW datasets. This method's convergence is assessed using condition numbers introduced by Kalmes. We compared the performance of the Dual Gradient Method to other established regularization methods, including the conjugate gradient method and irreversible Tikhonov regularization, through numerical experiments with a range of model problems. Our research showed that the Dual Gradient Method outperforms the conjugate gradient method, which is computationally more efficient and reliable than Tikhonov regularization. We also demonstrated that the method's performance is largely independent of the conditioning of the operator involved. We further considered an iterative version of the Dual Gradient Method and showed that it converges at a similar rate as its one-step equivalent. Deep learning-based methods have achieved impressive results on estimating depth from light field images, but many of them rely on optimal patch matching, which is a time-consuming process. To speed up the process and improve accuracy, we developed an innovative cost builder that effectively predicts density and highlights occluded areas. By integrating our cost builder into an iterative refinement framework, we significantly improve light field depth estimation. Along the way, we address an issue with dense matching by adjusting our strategy and demonstrating the results through experiments on existing datasets as well as a newly-created dataset with various occlusion levels, showcasing the efficacy of our approach. Our implementation can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/gimpong/LFDepthNet_OAC. The validation results on the established datasets, such as LF220, LFST10, and LFUrban, surpass state-of-the-art methods, while our new dataset is provided at https://gimpong.github.io/OAC-LFDepthNet/, enabling further research on benchmarking datasets. The estimation error for our new dataset is consistently lower compared to other methods, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach. The proposed cost builder outperforms existing methods, making it a powerful tool for light field depth estimation in computer vision and graphics applications. This study uses the bilinear approach to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, which link to the Lenells equations via Fokas mapping. Firstly, we discover a consistent system of integrators for the Fokas-Lenells equations and express their multoscular forms using gauge transformations. These transformations lead to the construction of multiple exact first-integral conserved quantities, allowing the reduction of the system to a single ordinary differential equation. Notably, the Fokas-Lenells equations cannot be fully integrated but can be solved algebraically for specific initial conditions, which are found to be related to the self-induced switching frequency of Fokas-Lenells systems, dependent on the spectral parameter. Furthermore, the Fokas-Lenells equations are reduced to a system of integrable Yajima-Oikawa equations via gauge transformation and are also shown to be integrable as a 2+1 dimensional confguration of hydrodynamic equations using the Fokas-Lenells map in the zero dispersion limit. Lastly, the study concludes by examining the double-decomposition structure of the Fokas-Lenells equations and the Fokas-Lenells systems, leading to the construction of multiple integrable two-component coherent structures. Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explain phenomena such as frame-dragging, unified gravity forces, and the emergence of gravity from a fundamental field. However, these theories face challenges in their theoretical and computational aspects, particularly in deriving actions and handling constraints. To address these issues, we utilize double field theory to develop actions for non-Riemannian gravity that are both well-defined and consistent. By doing so, we overcome some of the significant obstacles posed by these theories. Our approach encompasses examples of non-Riemannian gravity that exhibit 2-symmetry and "dark matter" effects, highlighting the efficacy of double field theory in the field. We also note that while some non-Riemannian gravity theories necessitate the use of a non-standard version of double field theory, incorporating a version of the non-geometric flux, this is the case for others, including the gravity theory that exhibits "dark matter" effects, in which case we can remain within the framework of ordinary double field theory. By examining the equations of motion derived from these theories, we conclude that double field theory provides a significant level of insight and simplification in the case of non-Riemannian gravity. Moreover, double field theory allows us to derive the Minkowski-space gravity action in a manner that is equivalent to the classical Janis-Winicke potential, thereby providing a clear and beautiful description of the rotation-spin coupling, one that is often missing in literature. We have further found that when we incorporate the non-geometric $B_{(2)}$ field into the theory (in the case of non-2-symmetry), the primary effect of this field is to introduce a correction into the gravity equation of motion that is proportional to this field, thereby providing a novel and straightforward way to investigate the non-Riemannian gravity that exhibits "dark matter" effects. By examining the properties of this correction term, we can gain valuable knowledge about the non-geometric field that is present in the theory. Additionally, we have demonstrated that when we the near-2-symmetry limit is taken, the derived equation of motion reduces to the well-known Janis-Winicke potential, thereby providing a significant level of generalization to the theory. We can accordingly use these results to suggest possible experimental and testing methods for non-Riemannian gravity that exhibit "dark matter" effects. To meet growing demand for next-generation services like video streaming in home networks, optimizing home WiFi networks becomes essential. One effective strategy is effectively managing the connections between devices. However, since these networks often feature a large number of devices, manually optimizing them is impractical. Therefore, adapting the IEEE 802.11k standard, which enables optimized WiFi network configuration, seems promising. However, implementing the standard for each device may be too resource-intensive. To address this issue, our research introduces a new channel load-aware access point and extender selection scheme, which uses IEEE 802.11k/v tools to redistribute devices among access points and extenders. Our proposal involves two main components: first, it estimates each device's transmission rate with its current connection, and second, it adjusts the connection configurations of devices to minimize congestion and optimize the network performance. Our results demonstrate that our scheme significantly improves throughputs for large sets of devices, outperforming the industry benchmark. Moreover, our implementation of the idea using IEEE 802.11k/v tools shows its feasibility. To the best of our knowledge, our research pioneers the concept of using these tools for this specific application in the field of home WiFi networks. Our findings have been jointly published in the IEEE ICASSP and TMC journals. A hardware-based prototype of our implementation is currently being used to demonstrate its effectiveness. A related US patent has been filed with the title 'Optimizing home WiFi network configuration' (Ref. US2020-061477). Furthermore, a production-ready implementation of our concept, titled 'Smart Home WiFi', is available at the specified GitHub repository. Moreover, a commercial version of our concept, titled 'ReShield', is available at the specified website. Furthermore, our concept's validity has been jointly validated in the field with its implementation at Google, a leading technology company. To extend our research, we have also developed a new scheme, titled 'Smart WiFi', to further improve the network performance by minimizing the interference between devices, which might be interested readers to explore. A US patent has been filed to protect our concept's validity and a commercial version of our concept, titled 'ZeeWiFi', is available at the specified GitHub Repository. Moreover, a related PhD dissertation on this research has been awarded by a renowned University. To the best of our knowledge, our research has significantly contributed to the field of optimizing home WiFi networks and contributed to developing a reliable and efficient network configuration tool for our community to use.
